prompt: A faculty member supervises an undergraduate research group and finds that one student is stuck after three weeks on a problem chosen because it is central to the faculty member's own work. What is the best next step?

prompt: A postdoc who finished a thesis on sieve bounds for primes in short intervals is drafting a five-year research plan. prompt: A scholar is comparing three early-career options: a two-year NSF Mathematical & Physical Sciences Postdoctoral Research Fellowship with a chosen host, a three-year teaching postdoc at a college, and a two-year member year at a mathematics research institute. prompt: A graduate student sets a daily schedule for a week with no classes or deadlines. Which habit is most in line with how experienced research mathematicians organize unstructured time?
choices: A few protected hours of deep work on one problem, with regular notes and a check-in on what is stuck.
Long unbroken stretches of new work with no notes, so the problem is never left half finished.
Only reading other people's papers, since calculations suggest that the problem is not yet understood.
Waiting for long free blocks of time and setting the problem aside whenever the department is busy.
answer: A few protected hours of deep work on one problem, with regular notes and a check-in on what is stuck.

prompt: A postdoc is two years into a long project and has stopped making progress; she has old notes she can barely follow and is considering abandoning the project. Which practice best helps her sustain progress on a long research phase?
choices: Keep a dated research log with explicit open questions and the state of each sub-argument, so work can resume after interruptions, and set small regular working blocks rather than waiting for long free stretches.
Wait for long uninterrupted stretches of free time before touching the project, so that each session can make a real dent.
Keep everything in memory and rely on the pressure of an upcoming deadline to restart progress.
Abandon the project and start a new one whenever progress stalls, since stalled projects rarely recover.
answer: Keep a dated research log with explicit open questions and the state of each sub-argument, so work can resume after interruptions, and set small regular working blocks rather than waiting for long free stretches.

prompt: You discover that a published paper contains a proof with a genuine gap: the main theorem's argument silently uses a lemma that is false, though numerical evidence strongly suggests the theorem itself is still true. What is the responsible course of action?
choices: Write to the authors describing the gap precisely, and if it is not resolved, publish a correction or erratum that identifies the error and its status.
Say nothing, because the theorem is probably true anyway and pointing out the gap only damages the authors.
Post publicly that the authors are incompetent, to warn the community as quickly as possible.
Send an anonymous complaint to the journal demanding that the paper be withdrawn immediately.
answer: Write to the authors describing the gap precisely, and if it is not resolved, publish a correction or erratum that identifies the error and its status.

prompt: In a 45-minute written qualifying exam problem, the statement asks you to show that every continuous function on [0,1] attains a maximum. Which plan gives the strongest write-up in the time available?
choices: State that [0,1] is compact and that a continuous image of a compact set is compact, then conclude that the image contains its supremum.
Give a full proof of the extreme value theorem from the completeness of the real numbers, then stop.
List all the properties of continuous functions that hold on a closed interval, with no proof of the claim.
Show the result first for polynomials and note that the general case can be handled in the same way.
answer: State that [0,1] is compact and that a continuous image of a compact set is compact, then conclude that the image contains its supremum.

prompt: A student wants to get unstuck on a problem about connected topological spaces. She notices the statement is easy for compact metric spaces and wonders whether compactness is really needed. Which research move is she using?
choices: She is testing a hypothesis of the theorem by dropping or weakening it to find the true scope of the statement, a form of generalization and of searching for counterexamples.
She is reducing the problem to a previously solved problem by a chain of implications.

She is applying analogy by translating the problem into a different area where a similar statement is known.
answer: She is testing a hypothesis of the theorem by dropping or weakening it to find the true scope of the statement, a form of generalization and of searching for counterexamples.

prompt: You are the corresponding author of a paper whose main theorem is correct, but a published corollary of it is false because one case was overlooked, and a short note already relies on that corollary. What is the responsible step?
choices: Publish a correction that states the false corollary precisely and gives the corrected statement, and notify the author of the note.
Fix the error silently in future work and leave the published record as it is.
Ask the journal to retract the entire paper, since part of it is wrong.
Write to the author of the note privately, but make no public correction.
answer: Publish a correction that states the false corollary precisely and gives the corrected statement, and notify the author of the note.

prompt: A dataset of time-ordered measurements shows a sample autocorrelation of 0.9 at lag 1, 0.8 at lag 2, 0.7 at lag 3, and values near zero only after lag 12. Which method best addresses the strong dependence between nearby observations?
choices: Fit a model with serially correlated errors, such as an AR(1) structure, in place of an independence assumption.
Use the ordinary least squares standard errors, since the sample autocorrelations are all smaller than 1.
Use a kernel density estimate, since the sharp drop in autocorrelation shows that the density is smooth.
Use a rank test, since rank procedures do not require any assumption about the error distribution.
answer: Fit a model with serially correlated errors, such as an AR(1) structure, in place of an independence assumption.

prompt: A graduate student is writing up a new definition of a 'graded module' and its audience is researchers who know commutative algebra but not her specific conventions. Following standard advice on mathematical writing, how should she handle the notation?
choices: Fix the notation once in a short notational convention, use the same symbols consistently throughout, and avoid reusing a symbol for two different objects even in different sections.
Introduce several competing notations for the same object so readers from different backgrounds can follow along.
Reserve Greek letters for one kind of object and Latin letters for another, but allow reusing a symbol when the context seems clear.
Leave the notation implicit and let the examples convey the definitions, to keep the paper shorter.
answer: Fix the notation once in a short notational convention, use the same symbols consistently throughout, and avoid reusing a symbol for two different objects even in different sections.

prompt: In Lean 4 with mathlib, you have written `n : ℕ` and now need to state "the list `xs` has exactly `n` elements." Which statement is correctly typed?
choices: List.length xs = n
length xs = n
xs.size = n
xs.cardinality = n
answer: List.length xs = n

prompt: Let f be the function on [0,1] defined by f(x) = 1 for rational x and f(x) = 0 for irrational x. Which statement about the Lebesgue integral of f is correct?
choices: f is measurable with integral 0, since the rationals in [0,1] form a set of measure zero.
f is not measurable, because its points of continuity form an uncountable set.
f is measurable with integral 1/2, since the rationals and irrationals split the interval evenly.
f is measurable with integral 1, since f equals 1 on a dense subset of [0,1].
answer: f is measurable with integral 0, since the rationals in [0,1] form a set of measure zero.

prompt: Let P(z) = z³ − 1, and let C be the positively oriented circle of radius 2 centered at 0. What is (1/2πi) ∫_C P′(z)/P(z) dz?
choices: 3, the number of zeros of P inside C, counted with multiplicity.

1, since z = 1 is the only root of P inside C.
6, since P′ has degree 2 and C winds twice around each root.
answer: 3, the number of zeros of P inside C, counted with multiplicity.

prompt: You are a non-citizen who has accepted a postdoctoral position in another country, and the university's international office has asked you for documents. Which step is essential before you travel?
choices: Obtain the correct work or research visa for the position, with the university's sponsorship paperwork, before the appointment begins.
Fly in on a tourist entry and switch to a work visa once you have started and been paid.
Ask the department chair to override the visa requirement, since university appointments are exempt.
Rely on the visa waiver program for short visits and renew it every few months.
answer: Obtain the correct work or research visa for the position, with the university's sponsorship paperwork, before the appointment begins.

prompt: In the seminar on class field theory, K is a number field and the Artin map is being built. Which statement correctly describes the reciprocity map for a number field K?
choices: It is a map from the idele class group C_K = 𝔸_K^×/K^× onto the abelianized Galois group Gal(K^ab/K), with kernel the connected component of the identity (times the norms from archimedean places in the usual normalization).
It is an isomorphism from the additive group of K onto the Galois group Gal(K^ab/K).
It is a map from the absolute Galois group Gal(K^ab/K) onto the idele class group C_K = 𝔸_K^×/K^×.
It is an isomorphism from the unit group O_K^× of the ring of integers onto the Galois group of the maximal unramified extension of K.
answer: It is a map from the idele class group C_K = 𝔸_K^×/K^× onto the abelianized Galois group Gal(K^ab/K), with kernel the connected component of the identity (times the norms from archimedean places in the usual normalization).

prompt: A second-year PhD student has passed her qualifying exams and now wants a committee and a written research plan. Which step fits the usual timetable of a mathematics PhD?
choices: Finding an advisor and forming a committee, with a prospectus defended in the following year or two.
Passing the oral qualifying exam, which normally comes after the prospectus defense.
Writing the full dissertation, which students normally finish before choosing a research area.
Completing the job market, which normally comes before the dissertation is deposited.
answer: Finding an advisor and forming a committee, with a prospectus defended in the following year or two.

prompt: In the stochastic analysis seminar, a stock price is modeled by geometric Brownian motion dS_t = μ S_t dt + σ S_t dW_t. Setting f(s) = log s and applying Itô's formula to X_t = log S_t, which stochastic differential does X_t satisfy?
choices: dX_t = (μ − σ²/2) dt + σ dW_t
dX_t = μ dt + σ dW_t
dX_t = (μ − σ²/2) dt + σ S_t dW_t
dX_t = (μ/σ) dt + dW_t
answer: dX_t = (μ − σ²/2) dt + σ dW_t

prompt: A learning theory seminar considers binary classification on R^d with linear predictors. Which statement best expresses the standard uniform-convergence/generalization bound for a hypothesis class of bounded norm?
choices: The gap between empirical and true error is controlled uniformly over the class by a quantity that grows like sqrt((d log n + log(1/δ))/n), so the sample complexity depends on the complexity of the class rather than on the size of the domain.
The generalization gap is bounded by a quantity that depends only on the number of parameters d and not on the sample size n.

The generalization gap is bounded by a quantity that decays like 1/n, and it holds for every hypothesis class with no complexity assumption.
answer: The gap between empirical and true error is controlled uniformly over the class by a quantity that grows like sqrt((d log n + log(1/δ))/n), so the sample complexity depends on the complexity of the class rather than on the size of the domain.

prompt: A speaker is preparing a 50-minute colloquium talk on her thesis results for an audience of mathematicians outside her specialty. She plans to state her main theorem in the first five minutes using her thesis notation. What is the better structure for the opening of the talk?
choices: Spend the opening on a motivating example and a plain-language statement of the problem, then state the main theorem in accessible terms before turning to notation and proof ideas.
Begin with the full technical statement of the main theorem and its proof, then give the motivation at the end if time allows.
Begin with a complete review of all prior literature in the area so the audience can place the result.
Begin with the hardest lemma in the paper, since that is the part the audience is most likely to question.
answer: Spend the opening on a motivating example and a plain-language statement of the problem, then state the main theorem in accessible terms before turning to notation and proof ideas.

prompt: You are giving the research talk at your oral exam. You reach the main theorem of your dissertation and see that the committee has three minutes of questions left. What is the strongest choice?
choices: State the theorem precisely, give one idea of the proof and one example, and point to the fuller argument in your written syllabus.
State the theorem precisely and continue with the complete proof, since a proof on the board is worth more than questions.
Skip the theorem and take the questions first, since the committee can read the statement in the syllabus whenever they like.
State only the idea of the theorem and give no precise statement, since exact hypotheses slow the talk down.
answer: State the theorem precisely, give one idea of the proof and one example, and point to the fuller argument in your written syllabus.

prompt: Consider the wave equation u_tt = c² u_xx on the real line with initial position u(x,0) = φ(x) and initial velocity u_t(x,0) = ψ(x). Which formula gives the solution for t > 0?
choices: u(x,t) = [φ(x+ct) + φ(x−ct)]/2 + (1/(2c)) ∫ from x−ct to x+ct of ψ(s) ds.
u(x,t) = φ(x − ct), since the initial position is carried along at speed c.
u(x,t) = φ(x) cos(ct) + ψ(x) sin(ct)/c, since each point moves in time like a harmonic oscillator.
u(x,t) = (1/(2c)) ∫ from x−ct to x+ct of φ(s) ds, since the initial velocity is carried along at speed c.
answer: u(x,t) = [φ(x+ct) + φ(x−ct)]/2 + (1/(2c)) ∫ from x−ct to x+ct of ψ(s) ds.

prompt: A scholar is invited to referee a paper in a specialized area the scholar knows moderately well. The manuscript's main estimate improves a known bound by 2 percent under the same hypotheses. What should the report foreground?
choices: A clear assessment of correctness and a separate judgment of whether the improvement is significant enough for this journal.
Only the referee's own preferred proof, rewritten as the main recommendation.
A list of every minor typographical error found in the typesetting.
A recommendation to accept based on length alone, since longer papers are usually more complete.
answer: A clear assessment of correctness and a separate judgment of whether the improvement is significant enough for this journal.

prompt: A department chair must resolve a conflict between two faculty members over who teaches a required course. What is the best first step?
choices: Hear both positions, clarify the scheduling constraints and teaching obligations, and seek a resolution consistent with department policy.
Assign the course to whichever faculty member has more seniority, without discussion.
Avoid the matter and let the conflict continue unresolved until the term begins.
Let the two faculty decide privately with no reference to policy or obligations.
answer: Hear both positions, clarify the scheduling constraints and teaching obligations, and seek a resolution consistent with department policy.

prompt: Kantorovich duality for optimal transport states that a primal transport problem equals a dual problem over functions (u, v) satisfying a constraint. In the standard formulation for cost c(x, y) = |x − y| (or a general lower semicontinuous cost) with probability measures μ and ν, which statement captures the dual problem correctly?
choices: One maximizes the integral of u with respect to μ plus the integral of v with respect to ν over all pairs with u(x) + v(y) ≤ c(x, y) for all x, y, and under suitable hypotheses the optimum equals the minimum transport cost

One minimizes the integral of u with respect to μ plus the integral of v with respect to ν over all pairs with u(x) + v(y) = c(x, y) for all x, y, and under suitable hypotheses the optimum equals the maximum transport cost

One maximizes the integral of u with respect to μ plus the integral of v with respect to ν over all pairs with u(x) + v(y) ≥ c(x, y) for all x, y, and under suitable hypotheses the optimum equals the minimum transport cost
One maximizes the integral of u − v with respect to μ and ν over all pairs with u(x) − v(y) ≤ c(x, y) for all x, y, and under suitable hypotheses the optimum equals the maximum transport cost
answer: One maximizes the integral of u with respect to μ plus the integral of v with respect to ν over all pairs with u(x) + v(y) ≤ c(x, y) for all x, y, and under suitable hypotheses the optimum equals the minimum transport cost

prompt: A mathematician with training in functional analysis is exploring a machine learning research role at a technology company. Which skill most strengthens the transition from theory to applied research?
choices: Demonstrating an ability to frame mathematical ideas for engineers and to connect them to a concrete product or data problem.
Publishing more pure theory papers with no applied component.
Avoiding collaboration with engineers to keep the research purely mathematical.
Declining to learn any programming, since the mathematician's role is theory only.
answer: Demonstrating an ability to frame mathematical ideas for engineers and to connect them to a concrete product or data problem.

prompt: A referee recommends rejection but also sees a promising direction the author could pursue. What is the best way to handle the confidential report?
choices: Give the reasoning and constructive suggestions in the report itself, and keep the recommendation and its grounds confidential to the editor and author.

Email the author directly to explain the reasoning, bypassing the editor.

prompt: A scholar surveys the Green–Tao theorem that the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, and wants to explain which ingredients the proof combines. Which description is accurate?
choices: It combines a Szemerédi-type structure theorem that finds dense arithmetic structure inside any set of positive upper density with a transference principle that lets a sparse set like the primes behave like a dense set of positive relative density
It combines a sieve argument that shows the number of primes up to x is at least x divided by a power of log x with a circle method estimate that counts solutions to linear equations in primes

It combines a model-theoretic compactness argument showing that any finite subset of the primes embeds into a dense pseudorandom set with a forcing construction extending the progression one step at a time
answer: It combines a Szemerédi-type structure theorem that finds dense arithmetic structure inside any set of positive upper density with a transference principle that lets a sparse set like the primes behave like a dense set of positive relative density

prompt: In the study of computer-assisted proof, a mathematician distinguishes a proof that merely uses a computer to check finitely many cases from one that relies on extensive floating-point computation. Which statement about the Four Color Theorem proof of Appel and Haken is standard?
choices: It reduced the problem to a finite set of unavoidable configurations that must be reducible, but verifying the reducibility of all of them required extensive computer checking that could not feasibly be done by hand
It gave a purely human-checkable discharging argument that avoided all computation, and the computer was used only to typeset the resulting list of configurations
It produced a computer-generated formal proof in a proof assistant, so that a small trusted kernel verifies every step without any case analysis
It showed that the four color problem is equivalent to a statement about finite groups whose verification required only a short symbolic computation rather than a large case check
answer: It reduced the problem to a finite set of unavoidable configurations that must be reducible, but verifying the reducibility of all of them required extensive computer checking that could not feasibly be done by hand

prompt: A faculty member supervises an REU group produces a result worth publishing. The group includes three undergraduates, the faculty member, and a postdoc who contributed key ideas. What is the fairest credit practice?

prompt: A mathematician applying to a machine learning research team is building a portfolio. Which item best evidences readiness for applied research?

prompt: The Flyspeck project formalized the proof of the Kepler conjecture, completing around 2014–2017. Which statement about the Flyspeck project is accurate?

It formalized only the finite combinatorial portion of the proof in Coq, leaving all nonlinear inequalities to be verified by an external computer algebra system

prompt: A faculty member is chairing a tenure-track search committee. A member proposes contacting a candidate's current department chair informally, off the record, to learn about the candidate's teaching. What is the correct course?
choices: Follow the established confidential reference process, with all inquiries documented and consistent across candidates.
Make the informal call, since extra information always improves the committee's judgment.

prompt: A researcher reads about AI systems for mathematics and wants to explain the role of a formal environment in systems like AlphaProof. Which statement accurately describes the role of a formal proof environment in AI-assisted theorem proving?
choices: It provides a checkable notion of correctness: candidate proofs are accepted only if they typecheck against a trusted kernel, so the system can be trained and evaluated without trusting the model's own judgments
It provides a natural-language dataset of informal proofs, so that the system can be trained purely on prose and verified by peer review rather than by any kernel
It provides a fast numerical evaluation of conjectures, so that the system can test statements by sampling random examples rather than by constructing proofs
It provides a canonical database of open problems, so that the system's output is judged solely by the novelty of the statements it generates rather than by proof correctness
answer: It provides a checkable notion of correctness: candidate proofs are accepted only if they typecheck against a trusted kernel, so the system can be trained and evaluated without trusting the model's own judgments

prompt: A postdoc with three thesis-era papers on L-function zero densities wants to build an independent agenda. What is the strongest reason this project fits or does not fit an early independent agenda?

prompt: In a five-year research plan, which element most clearly signals that the agenda is a connected program rather than a list of separate projects?
choices: A stated thread explaining how each project's questions and methods build on the others toward a long-range goal.
A longer list of open problems, each drawn from a different area of mathematics.
A complete bibliography of every paper written during the PhD.
A month-by-month schedule with no mention of how the projects relate.
answer: A stated thread explaining how each project's questions and methods build on the others toward a long-range goal.

prompt: In the minimal model program, a divisor D on a normal projective variety X is called nef if it meets every curve in X non-negatively: D · C ≥ 0 for every curve C. Why is the nef condition central to the outcome of running the MMP?
choices: A minimal model is required to be Q-factorial with terminal singularities and K_X nef, so terminating the MMP amounts to making the canonical divisor nef after contracting or flipping curves where K_X is negative

answer: A minimal model is required to be Q-factorial with terminal singularities and K_X nef, so terminating the MMP amounts to making the canonical divisor nef after contracting or flipping curves where K_X is negative

prompt: A scholar writing about rigorous mathematical physics wants to describe Schramm–Loewner evolution (SLE). Which statement about SLE is accurate?

SLE is a one-parameter family of random subsets of the unit disk defined as the zero set of a Gaussian analytic function, and it arises as the scaling limit of random matrix eigenvalue distributions
answer: SLE is a one-parameter family of random planar curves defined through the Loewner equation driven by a one-dimensional Brownian motion, and it arises as the scaling limit of lattice models in statistical physics at criticality

prompt: Floer homology is often introduced as an infinite-dimensional analogue of Morse theory. choices: One counts pseudoholomorphic strips (or Floer trajectories) satisfying a perturbed Cauchy–Riemann equation between 1-periodic orbits of a Hamiltonian, and transversality and compactness are the analytic difficulties that replace the finite-dimensional arguments

answer: One counts pseudoholomorphic strips (or Floer trajectories) satisfying a perturbed Cauchy–Riemann equation between 1-periodic orbits of a Hamiltonian, and transversality and compactness are the analytic difficulties that replace the finite-dimensional arguments

prompt: A scholar is invited to give a sixty-minute colloquium to a broad mathematics department. Which structure best serves that audience?
choices: Open with motivation and a concrete example, present one key idea with a clear statement of the main result, and close with the takeaway message.
Present the full technical apparatus of three papers so specialists can verify the proofs.

answer: Open with motivation and a concrete example, present one key idea with a clear statement of the main result, and close with the takeaway message.

prompt: A researcher writes an expository survey of mirror symmetry for colleagues in analysis, and describes genus-zero Gromov–Witten invariants of a Calabi–Yau threefold X as numbers N_d (one for each degree d) that count rational curves. They are assembled into the Hodge numbers h^{1,1} and h^{2,1} of X, and mirror symmetry predicts that these match the Hodge numbers of the mirror in reversed order

prompt: An early-career mathematician is asked to co-advise a PhD student with a senior colleague. The student's thesis topic sits between the two advisors' areas. What is the best practice to establish early?
choices: Agree in advance on meeting rhythms, each advisor's role, and how authorship and credit will be handled.
Let the student decide all working arrangements without advisor input, to foster independence.

prompt: Woodin's Ultimate L program is a proposed approach to large-cardinal axioms and the continuum hypothesis. Which statement best describes the program's goal?
choices: It seeks an inner model U L (an "Ultimate L") accommodating the strongest large cardinals, in which the continuum hypothesis holds and which is compatible with all known large-cardinal principles

answer: It seeks an inner model U L (an "Ultimate L") accommodating the strongest large cardinals, in which the continuum hypothesis holds and which is compatible with all known large-cardinal principles

prompt: A tenure-track professor must choose among several service commitments. Which principle best guides the decision?
choices: Prefer commitments that build skills, visibility, or relationships advancing one's research, teaching, or career goals.

prompt: A journal editor receives a paper that is correct but narrowly specialized, while the journal's stated scope is broad and it receives far more good submissions than it can publish. What is the most appropriate action?

Accept the paper because it is correct, even though it does not fit the journal's scope.

prompt: A department is designing a program to broaden participation in mathematics. Which approach is most likely to produce lasting change?

Run a single high-profile event each year and measure success by how many people attend.
Lower admissions and evaluation standards for all applicants and avoid collecting any outcome data.

prompt: A school tests a new reading program. A random sample of 40 third-graders at Lincoln Elementary is chosen, and each child is randomly assigned to the new program or to the usual program. After one year, the new-program group scored an average of 7 points higher on a reading test (95% confidence interval: 2 to 12 points; p-value = 0.01). A local newspaper writes: "This study proves that the new reading program raises reading scores for all elementary students, and we can be 97% sure any child will gain at least 2 points." Which revision would a statistician write instead?
choices: For third-graders at schools like Lincoln Elementary, the experiment gives strong evidence that the new program causes higher average reading-test scores than the usual program; we are 95% confident the true mean gain is between 2 and 12 points, and the small single-school sample limits how far the result can be generalized.
We are 97% confident that any third-grader who uses the new program will score at least 2 points higher than with the usual program.
Because the confidence interval is 2 to 12 points, we can be 95% sure that all elementary students will gain between 2 and 12 points in reading.
The p-value of 0.01 shows there is a 1% chance the new program does not work, so the program is proven to raise scores for every student.
answer: For third-graders at schools like Lincoln Elementary, the experiment gives strong evidence that the new program causes higher average reading-test scores than the usual program; we are 95% confident the true mean gain is between 2 and 12 points, and the small single-school sample limits how far the result can be generalized.
note: Best statistician revision; others overclaim.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company runs a randomized, double-blind experiment comparing a new blood-pressure drug with a placebo in 500 volunteers recruited from one city. The drug group's mean drop in systolic pressure was 8 mm Hg greater than the placebo group's (p-value = 0.001; 95% confidence interval for the difference: 3 to 13 mm Hg). A report states: "The drug is proven to lower blood pressure; there is only a 0.1% chance the drug does not work." Which statement is the most complete and honest summary a statistician should publish?
choices: Because treatment was randomly assigned, the experiment provides strong evidence that the drug causes a greater mean drop in systolic pressure for volunteers like those in the study (estimated difference 8 mm Hg, 95% confidence interval 3 to 13 mm Hg); the p-value describes the strength of evidence against no effect, not the probability the drug fails.
With 99.9% confidence, any patient who takes the drug will see a systolic pressure drop of between 3 and 13 mm Hg more than with the placebo.
The p-value of 0.001 means there is a 0.1% probability that the drug has no effect, so the drug is proven to work for all patients.
Since volunteers were not randomly selected from all patients, the study shows only an association between the drug and lower blood pressure, and no cause-and-effect claim can be made.
answer: Because treatment was randomly assigned, the experiment provides strong evidence that the drug causes a greater mean drop in systolic pressure for volunteers like those in the study (estimated difference 8 mm Hg, 95% confidence interval 3 to 13 mm Hg); the p-value describes the strength of evidence against no effect, not the probability the drug fails.
note: Randomized assignment supports causation for volunteers; p-value misreading corrected.

prompt: We want to prove that the set of all infinite binary strings (sequences of 0s and 1s indexed by the natural numbers) is uncountable. Which of the following best describes Cantor's diagonal argument applied to this goal?

prompt: A tally chart shows 3 groups of 5 tally marks and then 2 more tally marks. How many votes is that altogether?

prompt: Let G = D₄ = ⟨r, s | r⁴ = s² = e, srs = r⁻¹⟩ be the symmetry group of the square, and let H = ⟨s⟩ = {e, s}. Which statement about H is correct?
choices: H is not normal in D₄, because rsr⁻¹ = r²s is not in H

prompt: Let G = Z₆ ⊕ Z₄, written additively. How many elements of G have order exactly 12?
note: Need lcm(|a|,|b|)=12 with |a| in {1,2,3,6}, |b| in {1,2,4}: |a| in {3,6} (4 elements) and |b|=4 (2 elements): 8.

prompt: A regular tetrahedron has 12 rotational symmetries. How many of these rotations fix a given vertex of the tetrahedron?
note: Orbit-stabilizer: orbit of a vertex has size 4, so stabilizer has 12/4 = 3 rotations.

prompt: In the division ring H of quaternions, with standard basis 1, i, j, k satisfying i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1, which pair of nonzero quaternions fails to commute?
choices: 1 + i and 1 + j, since (1+i)(1+j) = 1 + i + j + k while (1+j)(1+i) = 1 + i + j - k

1 + i and 1 + j, since (1+i)(1+j) = 1 + i + j - k while (1+j)(1+i) = 1 + i + j + k
answer: 1 + i and 1 + j, since (1+i)(1+j) = 1 + i + j + k while (1+j)(1+i) = 1 + i + j - k
note: (1+i)(1+j)=1+i+j+k, (1+j)(1+i)=1+i+j-k, so they do not commute. Option 4 swaps signs, option 2 equal, option 3 commute.

prompt: The complex potential F(z) = z^2 models ideal fluid flow in the first quadrant. What is the velocity vector of the flow at the point z = 1 + i?

prompt: For the family of quadratic maps f_c(z) = z^2 + c, how is the Mandelbrot set M defined using the orbit of the critical point of f_c?

prompt: Let f : C → C be holomorphic and nonconstant. Which statement about f follows from the open mapping theorem?

The image f(U) of every bounded open set U is compact in C.

note: Open mapping theorem: nonconstant holomorphic maps send open sets to open sets (defined on C connected).

prompt: Let U be the punctured disk {z : 0 < |z| < 1}. Suppose a sequence of holomorphic functions f_n : U → C omits exactly the two values 0 and 1 for every n. Which conclusion follows directly from Montel's theorem?
choices: The family {f_n} is normal in U, so some subsequence converges locally uniformly in U to a holomorphic function or to infinity.
The family {f_n} is normal in U, so some subsequence converges locally uniformly in U to a holomorphic function that also omits 0 and 1.

note: Montel: family omitting two values is normal on a domain, subsequence converges locally uniformly to holomorphic or to infinity. Option 2 is false (limit may be constant 0 or 1 by Hurwitz).

prompt: The Riemann zeta function ζ(s) = Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/n^s, defined for Re(s) > 1, continues meromorphically to all of C with a single simple pole at s = 1. The functional equation of the continuation relates ζ(s) to ζ(1 − s). Which statement correctly describes the zeros of the continued zeta function and what the Riemann hypothesis asserts about them?

The trivial zeros are at s = 2, 4, 6, …, and all nontrivial zeros lie in the critical strip 0 < Re(s) < 1; the Riemann hypothesis asserts that in fact every nontrivial zero lies on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2.

All zeros of ζ(s), both the trivial ones and the nontrivial ones, lie on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2; the Riemann hypothesis asserts that there are no zeros anywhere off this line in either half-plane.

The trivial zeros are at s = −2, −4, −6, …, and all nontrivial zeros lie on the line Re(s) = 1, where they control the growth of the prime counting function π(x); the Riemann hypothesis asserts that in fact every nontrivial zero lies on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2.
answer: The trivial zeros are at s = −2, −4, −6, …, and all nontrivial zeros lie in the critical strip 0 < Re(s) < 1; the Riemann hypothesis asserts that in fact every nontrivial zero lies on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2.
note: Trivial zeros at -2,-4,...; nontrivial in the critical strip; RH says Re=1/2. Others are false.

prompt: A sixth grader computes 2/3 ÷ 1/6 by writing (2×6)/(3×1) = 12/3 = 4 and gets the right answer but cannot explain the procedure. Which explanation most directly builds conceptual understanding of why invert-and-multiply works here?
choices: Dividing by 1/6 asks how many sixths fit into 2/3; since 2/3 equals 4/6, exactly 4 pieces of size 1/6 fit inside 2/3, which is the same answer the procedure gives.
Dividing means making the numbers smaller, so the answer must be less than both fractions; the procedure works because multiplying the top and bottom by 6 preserves the value of the quotient.
The procedure works because 2 × 6 and 3 × 1 are the cross products of the two fractions, and a quotient of fractions always equals the ratio of their cross products.
You invert and multiply because division is the inverse of multiplication, and any number divided by 1/6 equals that number times 6/1 because the 6 and 1 swap places in the written digits.

prompt: A student applying to Ph.D. programs in pure mathematics has completed the standard algebra and analysis sequences but has never read a mathematics book on her own. Which plan follows the standard advice for preparing for graduate study over the coming year?

prompt: A Penrose P3 tiling is built from two rhombs, a 'thin' one with acute angle 36° and a 'fat' one with acute angle 72°, obeying local matching rules. Which statement correctly describes the Penrose P3 tiling?

answer: It tiles the plane aperiodically: no translation maps the tiling onto itself, yet the deflation rule produces self-similar tilings at every scale.
note: Penrose P3 (rhombs 36 and 72 degree acute angles) is aperiodic with deflation self-similarity; it has no translation symmetry and 5-fold local symmetry so it is not a wallpaper group tiling.

prompt: Consider the Miller-Rabin test applied to n = 561 with base a = 2. Write 560 = 2⁴ · 35. What does the test show about n = 561?
choices: 2 is a witness that 561 is composite, since 2³⁵ ≢ 1 (mod 561) and no 2^(2ʲ·35) is ≡ −1 (mod 561) for 0 ≤ j ≤ 3.

note: 2^35=263, then 166, 67, 1 mod 561: not 1 at start and no -1 appears, so 2 is a strong witness.

prompt: A graduate student must explain a 12-step inductive proof in a 20-minute seminar talk to an audience that includes analysts who do not know the combinatorial definitions used in the induction. Which plan best follows the standard advice for board talks that explain proofs?

prompt: Consider the convex program: minimize f(x) = x_1^2 + x_2^2 subject to g(x) = x_1 + x_2 − 4 ≥ 0. At the optimum x* = (2, 2), the constraint is active. What does the KKT condition tell us about the Lagrange multiplier λ associated with g?
choices: KKT requires ∇f(x*) = λ ∇g(x*), so (2x_1, 2x_2) = λ(1, 1), giving λ = 4; since λ > 0 the constraint is active and λ measures the shadow price of relaxing the constraint.
KKT requires ∇f(x*) = λ ∇g(x*), so (2x_1, 2x_2) = λ(1, 1), giving λ = 2; λ equals the objective value at the optimum since the constraint is active.
KKT requires ∇f(x*) + λ ∇g(x*) = 0 with λ ≥ 0 for an inequality constraint g(x) ≥ 0, giving λ = −4 which is admissible because only the sign of the product λg matters.
KKT requires only that g(x*) ≥ 0 with complementarity λg(x*) = 0, so λ can be any nonnegative number since the constraint is active.
answer: KKT requires ∇f(x*) = λ ∇g(x*), so (2x_1, 2x_2) = λ(1, 1), giving λ = 4; since λ > 0 the constraint is active and λ measures the shadow price of relaxing the constraint.
note: grad f = (4,4) = lambda (1,1), lambda=4>0, shadow price of the constraint. (Minor loose phrasing 'since lambda>0 the constraint is active' but the result and interpretation are right.)

prompt: In a symmetric (v, k, λ) block design with v = 7, k = 3, and λ = 1 (the Fano plane constructed from PG(2, 2)), how many blocks contain a given point?

Using b k = v r and b = v for a symmetric design, we get r = k · λ = 3 · 1 = 3, but since there are 7 points and 7 blocks each pair is in 2 blocks so r = 7.
answer: In a symmetric design, r = k = 3, so exactly 3 blocks contain any given point.
note: Symmetric (7,3,1) design: r=k=3.

prompt: Consider the fixed-point iteration x_{n+1} = g(x_n) with g(x) = x − x^3/3 near the fixed point x* = 0. Since g'(0) = 1, the linear convergence theorem does not apply. What is the observed order of convergence of the iterates to x* = 0 for x_0 sufficiently small but nonzero?

answer: Since g'(0) = 1 and g''(0) = 0 but g'''(0) = −2 ≠ 0, the iteration converges to 0 sublinearly at order 1 (linear with rate 1), specifically x_{n+1} ≈ x_n − x_n^3/3 so x_n ~ sqrt(3/(2n)), i.e., convergence is of order 1 but with a non-geometric rate.
note: g(x)=x-x^3/3: y=x^2 gives y_{n+1}=y_n-(2/3)y_n^2, y_n~3/(2n), x_n~sqrt(3/(2n)); sublinear, not geometric. Others false.

prompt: Find all functions f: ℝ → ℝ satisfying f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y) for all real x, y and f(xy) = f(x)f(y) for all real x, y. How many such functions are there, and what are they?
choices: Exactly two: f(x) = 0 for all x, and f(x) = x for all x.
Exactly one: f(x) = x for all x.

prompt: A mathematics major is preparing for actuarial and data science positions and has completed coursework in probability, numerical methods, and a statistics capstone with a written project. Which approach best follows the standard advice for building a career portfolio and credentials?

prompt: A fourth grader computes 23 × 14 by writing 23 × 4 = 92, then 23 × 10 = 230, and adding to get 322. choices: The 4 in 14 counts 4 ones, so the first line of the standard algorithm multiplies 23 by 4 ones; the 1 in 14 counts 1 ten, so the next line multiplies 23 by 1 ten, giving 23 tens, or 230, which is shifted one place left.
The standard algorithm multiplies each digit of 23 by each digit of 14 in any order, so the two lines simply record 23 × 4 and 23 × 10 because those are easier facts to recall.
The first line multiplies 23 by 4 because 4 is the larger digit of 14, and the second line multiplies 23 by 10 because the remaining digit must be paired with the base ten.
The two lines come from the distributive law applied to 23 × (4 + 10) only after regrouping 14 as 10 + 4, and the shift left is a convention with no place-value meaning.

note: Standard algorithm: 23 x 4 ones and 23 x 1 ten = 230; shift reflects place value.

prompt: A seventh-grade class spins a fair spinner with four equal sections (A, B, C, D) 40 times and records 14 A's. One student says, 'The spinner must be unfair, since A came up more than the expected 10 times.' Which response best develops understanding of chance and variability while addressing the student's reasoning?
choices: Acknowledge that 14 is more than the expected 10, then have the class simulate many sets of 40 spins to see how often a fair spinner produces 14 or more A's, so they judge whether 14 is unusual rather than merely above average.
Confirm that the spinner must be unfair, since any outcome above the expected count shows a biased device, and have the class recompute the expected value as 14.
Tell the class that 14 is exactly what a fair spinner predicts in the long run, since the law of large numbers says observed counts always match expected counts once the number of trials is large.

answer: Acknowledge that 14 is more than the expected 10, then have the class simulate many sets of 40 spins to see how often a fair spinner produces 14 or more A's, so they judge whether 14 is unusual rather than merely above average.
note: Simulating many sets of 40 spins is the standard way to judge whether 14 is unusual; others are misconceptions (LLN misuse etc.).

prompt: The continued fraction of π is [3; 7, 15, 1, 292, …], so its convergents include 3/1, 22/7, 333/106, and 355/113. Which convergent p/q gives the best rational approximation to π with denominator at most 113, and what does the theory of continued fractions guarantee about the error |π − p/q|?
choices: 355/113, and the theory guarantees |π − 355/113| is smaller than |π − r/s| for every rational r/s with s ≤ 113 other than 355/113 itself.
22/7, and the theory guarantees |π − 22/7| < 1/(2·7²), a better bound than any other convergent with denominator at most 113 gives.
333/106, and the theory guarantees |π − 333/106| < 1/106², while convergents with smaller denominators need not satisfy any such bound.
355/113, and the theory guarantees |π − 355/113| < 1/113², but no claim can be made about other rationals with denominator at most 113.
answer: 355/113, and the theory guarantees |π − 355/113| is smaller than |π − r/s| for every rational r/s with s ≤ 113 other than 355/113 itself.
note: 355/113 is the best rational approximation of pi among denominators <= 113 (best approximation property of convergents); option 4 wrongly says no claim about others.

prompt: In the projective plane, the dual of the statement 'Three distinct points not on a common line determine a unique triangle' is which of the following?

Three distinct lines through a common point determine a unique triangle.
Three distinct points on a common line determine a unique triangle.
Three distinct points not on a common line determine three concurrent lines.
answer: Three distinct lines not through a common point determine a unique triangle.
note: Duality swaps points and lines, collinear and concurrent: three lines not through a common point determine a triangle.

prompt: At a thesis defense, a committee member from another subfield asks: "You assume the coefficient matrix is symmetric throughout — could you explain to me, at the level of the qualifying-exam linear algebra everyone here remembers, exactly where symmetry enters your main convergence proof?" Which response follows the best practice for defending a thesis?
choices: Locate the single step where symmetry is used (the spectral theorem guaranteeing an orthonormal eigenbasis), restate that step in the more basic language the questioner asked for, and note explicitly which later estimates would fail without it.
Recite every place the word "symmetric" appears in the thesis, since a complete defense answer must cover the entire document.
Read the statement of the spectral theorem exactly as written in Section 2 without relating it to where the proof uses it.
Tell the committee that the general nonsymmetric case is outside the scope of the thesis and ask for the next question.
answer: Locate the single step where symmetry is used (the spectral theorem guaranteeing an orthonormal eigenbasis), restate that step in the more basic language the questioner asked for, and note explicitly which later estimates would fail without it.
note: Best practice: locate the step and re-explain at the asker's level; others are poor defense practice.

prompt: A student is presenting a poster at an undergraduate mathematics conference. The poster reports one main theorem with two supporting lemmas, and the thesis behind it runs to eighty pages. Visitors arrive at irregular times and stay for about five minutes. Which plan best fits the standard advice for poster presentations?
choices: State the main theorem and its motivation prominently, summarize the idea of each supporting lemma in one line, and give the full technical proofs only if a visitor asks for them.
Reproduce the eighty-page thesis on the poster in small type, since the poster's purpose is to document the complete written argument.
Put the main theorem and the two lemmas on the poster without any motivating context, since mathematical audiences arrive already knowing the problem.
Arrange the poster as a sequence of eight large panels, each summarizing a different chapter of the thesis in the order it was written.
answer: State the main theorem and its motivation prominently, summarize the idea of each supporting lemma in one line, and give the full technical proofs only if a visitor asks for them.
note: Poster advice: main result and motivation prominent, details on request.

prompt: Suppose Newton's method applied to a smooth function f with a simple root r converges quadratically: e_{n+1} ≈ C e_n^2 where e_n = x_n − r and C = f''(r)/(2f'(r)). If f(x) = x^2 − 2, f'(r) = 2√2, and f''(r) = 2 at r = √2, what is the asymptotic error constant C?
choices: C = f''(r)/(2f'(r)) = 2/(2·2) = 1/2 since f'(r) is approximated as 2.
C = f''(r)/f'(r) = 2/(2√2) = 1/√2 without the factor of 2 in the denominator.

prompt: Two circles Γ₁ and Γ₂ pass through a point P and meet again at Q. Invert about a circle centered at P. Which statement correctly describes the image of this configuration, and what does it give you?
choices: Both circles map to straight lines through the image of Q, so the angle between Γ₁ and Γ₂ at P equals the angle between those two lines, showing the circles meet at the same angle at P and at Q.
Both circles map to circles again, so inversion gives no simplification and the power of P must be computed directly.
Γ₁ and Γ₂ map to two parallel lines, so the circles are tangent at Q and the angle between them is 0.
Both circles map to straight lines not through the image of Q, so the circles meet at right angles at both P and Q.
answer: Both circles map to straight lines through the image of Q, so the angle between Γ₁ and Γ₂ at P equals the angle between those two lines, showing the circles meet at the same angle at P and at Q.
note: Inversion at P sends circles through P to lines through image of Q, preserving angles, so the circles meet at the same angle at P and Q.

prompt: A student is asked why the area of a rectangle is length times width and answers, 'Because that is the formula the teacher gave us.' The student then says a long thin rectangle 10 units by 0.5 units 'cannot have an area of 5, because you cannot fit 5 whole squares inside it.' Which response best builds the conceptual foundation of measurement?
choices: Clarify that area measures how many unit squares cover the region, and that units can be iterated in parts: the rectangle covers 10 rows of half a square, so 5 square units, showing area is not restricted to whole-square counts.
Agree that the area cannot be 5, since a rectangle's area must be a whole number of unit squares, and suggest measuring the long side instead.
Tell the student the formula applies only to whole-number side lengths, and give the area as 10 by counting the long side alone.
Explain that the formula is true because area is defined to be length times width, so no counting interpretation of unit squares is needed.
answer: Clarify that area measures how many unit squares cover the region, and that units can be iterated in parts: the rectangle covers 10 rows of half a square, so 5 square units, showing area is not restricted to whole-square counts.
note: Area as iterated unit squares in parts; 10 rows of half squares = 5.

prompt: Let R = Z and consider the R-modules M = Z/4Z and N = Q/Z. Using the characterization of flatness for modules over a PID via torsion and via Tor₁, which of the following is correct?

prompt: Let f be the germ at z = 1 of a branch of log z with f(1) = 0. prompt: Let X be the wedge sum of two circles (a figure eight), written as two circles C_1 and C_2 joined at a single point p. prompt: Let u be C^2 on a bounded connected domain Ω, continuous on the closure, with Δu ≥ 0 in Ω (subharmonic). Suppose u attains its maximum value at some interior point of Ω. What does the strong maximum principle conclude?

prompt: Solve u_tt = c^2 u_xx on R with c = 3, initial position u(x,0) = f(x) supported in |x| ≤ 1, and initial velocity u_t(x,0) = 0. At time t = 1, on which set of x can u(x,1) be nonzero?

prompt: Let A be a unital C*-algebra and let a ∈ A be self-adjoint with ‖a‖ = 5. What is the norm of a^2?

prompt: A student is writing Chapter 3 of a thesis. The chapter proves two new theorems about bounded operators on a Hilbert space, each stated for compact self-adjoint operators. prompt: A linear system Ax = b is solved by two different numerical algorithms. Both compute an answer x̂ with a small measured residual ‖b − A x̂‖/‖b‖. note: Small residual does not certify accuracy; with kappa=1e8, error bounds scale as ~1e8*eps vs ~1e16*eps, so Q loses about twice as many digits.

prompt: A stationary ARMA(1, 1) time series satisfies X_t = 0.5 X_{t−1} + ε_t + 0.25 ε_{t−1}, where ε_t is white noise with variance σ² = 4. The spectral density of a stationary process is f(ω) = (σ² / 2π) |θ(e^{−iω}) / φ(e^{−iω})|². What is the spectral density of this process at frequency ω = π?

prompt: In the initial value formulation of general relativity, a spacetime is built from a 3-dimensional Riemannian manifold with metric h_ij, an extrinsic curvature K_ij, and matter data, and the evolution is governed by the Einstein equations only if the initial data satisfy constraint equations. prompt: A student's thesis contains a proof adapted from a published paper, rewritten in new notation with some steps filled in, and one theorem whose statement was sharpened during a long email exchange with a postdoc at another university. prompt: A researcher wants to show that a finite, connected, planar graph drawn in the plane satisfies V minus E plus F = 2, where V, E, and F count vertices, edges, and faces. Prove the statement by the probabilistic method, choosing the drawing of the graph at random and computing the expected value of V minus E plus F.
Change to a different formula, V minus E plus F = 1, that is easier to prove for trees, and argue that the two formulas must agree.
answer: Build the graph up one edge at a time and show that the alternating sum V minus E plus F does not change when an edge is added in either of the two ways that preserve connectedness, reducing the claim to a check on the single-vertex graph.
note: Induction on edges (adding a pendant edge or an edge splitting a face leaves V-E+F unchanged) is the standard reduction for Euler's formula.

prompt: Let X be the projective line P^1 over an algebraically closed field, let O_X be its structure sheaf, and let D be the divisor n times the point at infinity on X. What is the dimension over the field of the space of global sections H^0(X, O_X(D)) when n = 5?

prompt: Let B_t be a standard Brownian motion starting at 0, and let X_t = exp(a B_t) for a constant a not equal to 0. Ito's formula expresses X_t as X_0 plus an Ito integral with respect to B plus one further term. What is that extra term, written as an integral from 0 to t?

Σ_m P(Y = y | X = x, M = m) P(M = m)

answer: Σ_m P(M = m | X = x) Σ_{x'} P(Y = y | X = x', M = m) P(X = x')

prompt: Impagliazzo and Wigderson proved that if some function on n-bit inputs computable in time 2^{O(n)} requires Boolean circuits of size 2^{Ω(n)}, then every language in BPP can be decided in deterministic polynomial time: the hard function yields a pseudorandom generator that stretches an O(log n)-bit seed to n bits and fools all polynomial-size circuits. MA = NP: fooling polynomial-size circuits removes the need for Merlin's randomness, so interactive proof certificates can be taken to be deterministic witnesses.
answer: BPP = P: the generator fools the polynomial-size circuit that computes the machine's acceptance probability, so one can try all 2^{O(log n)} = n^{O(1)} seeds in polynomial time and take the majority.
note: Impagliazzo-Wigderson hardness-versus-randomness: BPP=P. Others are false.

prompt: A public health ministry must decide whether to close schools during an epidemic and asks a mathematician to interpret a model that projects hospitalizations. Present all four models as equally valid and let the minister choose among them, since a mathematician should not judge which assumptions are more plausible.

answer: State which assumptions drive the projections, present the range across the modeling groups and the conditions under which each projection holds, and identify which decisions stay the same across all of the models.
note: Communicate assumptions, range across models, and decisions robust to model choice; other options hide uncertainty, abdicate judgment, or stall.

prompt: A science journalist is writing a story about a new theorem and proposes the headline "Mathematician Solves Every Number Problem at Last." Send a written objection to the headline only if the journalist asks, because challenging the wording risks losing the coverage altogether.
Reply with the full technical abstract and no example or analogy, so that every statement the public reads is the researcher's own exact wording.
answer: Ask the journalist to change the headline, and supply a concrete example and an analogy that reflect the true scope of the theorem, while stating plainly which hypotheses are needed and which questions remain open.

prompt: A professor is asked to write a reference letter for a strong postdoc applicant from an underrepresented group who has fewer publications than competing candidates because of a heavy teaching load at a teaching-focused institution. prompt: You fit y = c + dt by least squares to 8 measurements taken at t = 5.00, 5.01, ..., 5.07 seconds. The columns of the design matrix (all 1s, and the t values) are nearly parallel, so the computed slope is unstable. Which change fixes this without changing the fitted line?

prompt: A population model has [jₙ₊₁; aₙ₊₁] = [[0, 3], [1/2, 1/2]] [jₙ; aₙ], where j counts juveniles and a counts adults, starting with positive numbers of each. What happens in the long run?

prompt: A usability manager plans a summative, comparative benchmark study of two versions of an online form. answer: The 'five users' result comes from a formative problem-discovery model: the expected share of distinct problems found by n users is 1−(1−p)^n for per-user detection probability p. answer: In Ericsson and Simon's account, a concurrent report is trustworthy only for information the participant is already heeding in encoded form. prompt: During a Socratic seminar about whether junk food should be banned in cafeterias, four students speak. Which comment best pushes the discussion deeper?
choices: You said the ban would cut waste, but how would we measure whether it actually does?
I liked what Jay said and I agree with it.
I think junk food is bad and that is all there is to say.
Can we stop talking about this now?
answer: You said the ban would cut waste, but how would we measure whether it actually does?

prompt: A candidate for class president writes: "I have served on student council for three years and helped plan every school dance since seventh grade. That is why you can trust me to lead." Which rhetorical appeal is the candidate using most?
choices: Ethos, because the speaker points to experience and trustworthiness
Pathos, because the speaker wants voters to feel excited about school dances
Logos, because the speaker lists three years of service as a fact
Kairos, because the speaker chose the right moment before an election
answer: Ethos, because the speaker points to experience and trustworthiness

prompt: Marcus must write about climate change for two readers: a text message to a friend and a formal letter to the mayor. Which pair of sentences matches each audience?
choices: Text: "yo it's crazy hot out here" / Letter: "Rising temperatures have strained our city's infrastructure."
Text: "Rising temperatures have strained our city's infrastructure." / Letter: "yo it's crazy hot out here"
Text: "Rising temperatures have strained our city's infrastructure." / Letter: "Rising temperatures have strained our city's infrastructure."
Text: "yo it's crazy hot out here" / Letter: "yo it's crazy hot out here"
answer: Text: "yo it's crazy hot out here" / Letter: "Rising temperatures have strained our city's infrastructure."

prompt: Chen is writing about how social media affects teens and uses three sources. Which is the best example of synthesis?
choices: Blending the sources' ideas to argue that effects depend on how teens use social media.
Quoting each source one after the other in three separate paragraphs.
Picking just one source and ignoring the other two.
Listing each source with a short summary and nothing else.

prompt: Which statement is a fact rather than an opinion or an inference?
choices: The city council voted five to two to approve the new park.
The new park will be the best place in town for families to gather.
The council members who voted yes probably care more about parks.
This decision shows that our city values green spaces.
answer: The city council voted five to two to approve the new park.

prompt: What is the main purpose of an analytical essay about a short story?
choices: To explain how the story's techniques create meaning and effect.
To tell the story again in a shorter and clearer form.
To state whether the story is good or bad in the writer's view.
To convince readers to read more stories by the same author.
answer: To explain how the story's techniques create meaning and effect.

prompt: Which research question is the most focused and answerable?
choices: How did the printing press change the spread of news in 15th-century Europe?
What is history?
Why is technology important?
Should people read more books?
answer: How did the printing press change the spread of news in 15th-century Europe?

prompt: Which revision makes this sentence most concise without losing meaning? "Due to the fact that the bus was late, we arrived at the concert after it had already started."
choices: Because the bus was late, we arrived after the concert started.
Due to the fact that the bus ran late, we got to the concert after it had already begun.
Because the bus was late, we arrived at the concert after it had already started.
The bus being late is the reason that we arrived at the concert after it started.
answer: Because the bus was late, we arrived after the concert started.

prompt: A body paragraph in an analytical essay has a clear claim and a strong quotation from the text. What should come next?
choices: Analysis that explains how the quotation supports the claim.
A second, unrelated quotation that also comes from the text.
A restatement of the claim written in slightly different words.
A question to the reader that points toward the next paragraph.
answer: Analysis that explains how the quotation supports the claim.

prompt: A student says, "You can't trust Maya's argument about the new schedule because she always dresses so sloppily." What logical fallacy is this?
choices: Ad hominem, because it attacks the person instead of the argument.
Slippery slope, because it assumes one change will lead to many others.
Straw man, because it misrepresents what the other person actually argued.
False dilemma, because it reduces a complex issue to only two choices.
answer: Ad hominem, because it attacks the person instead of the argument.

prompt: Which sentence would most likely need editing to fix an error rather than revision for ideas?
choices: The team practiced hard, and their they played well in the final game.
The paragraph about funding should come before the paragraph about safety.
The thesis does not match the evidence in paragraph three.
The introduction needs a stronger hook to grab readers.
answer: The team practiced hard, and their they played well in the final game.

prompt: Read this passage: "Maria told Elena that she had forgotten her notes. She looked worried as she searched her bag." Who does "she" refer to in the second sentence, and how can a writer make it clearer?
choices: It is unclear; the writer should name the person instead of using "she" again.
It clearly refers to Maria; no change is needed.
It clearly refers to Elena; no change is needed.
It is unclear; the writer should switch both uses of "she" to "it."
answer: It is unclear; the writer should name the person instead of using "she" again.

prompt: A speaker claims that a new phone app raises test scores, and her only proof is that her younger brother's grades improved after he used it. What is the weakest part of her reasoning?
choices: She uses one person's experience to support a broad claim.
She does not explain how the app works.
She speaks too quickly for the audience to follow.
She uses technical words the audience does not know.
answer: She uses one person's experience to support a broad claim.

prompt: Which sentence uses a gerund as the subject of the sentence?
choices: Reading aloud makes her nervous.
She is reading aloud to the class today.
The reading aloud of poems took an hour.
They asked her to read aloud at the assembly.
answer: Reading aloud makes her nervous.

prompt: Complete the analogy: "delicate : fragile :: talkative : ___". The pair "delicate : fragile" shows a specific relationship. Which word completes the second pair with the same relationship?
choices: garrulous
gossip
quiet
rambling
answer: garrulous

prompt: Priya is explaining how photosynthesis works in a report. Which choice best uses formatting and media to help readers understand?
choices: Adding a labeled diagram of a leaf with arrows showing where light, water, and carbon dioxide enter.
Adding a large photo of a pretty forest just to decorate the page.
Changing all the text color to green to match the topic.
Adding more words to the introduction to make it longer.
answer: Adding a labeled diagram of a leaf with arrows showing where light, water, and carbon dioxide enter.

prompt: A writer arguing for later school start times includes this sentence: "Some argue that later starts would wreck after-school sports schedules." What should the writer do next to strengthen the argument?
choices: Acknowledge the concern, then explain why the change is still worth it, for example by shifting practice times and citing the gains in student health and achievement.
Delete the sentence, since a strong argument never mentions the other side or gives it any space.
Repeat the original claim in louder, more emotional words without answering the objection at all.
Abandon the position and switch the whole essay to describing how after-school sports teams are organized.
answer: Acknowledge the concern, then explain why the change is still worth it, for example by shifting practice times and citing the gains in student health and achievement.

prompt: A student finds a blog post on a natural remedies company's website that claims a new herbal supplement cures migraines. Is this a scholarly source, and why or why not?
choices: No, because it is a promotional post on a company's own site and has not been peer reviewed.
Yes, because it was written by someone who sells health products for a living.
Yes, because it appears on the open web where anyone can read and check it.
No, because anything found on the internet is too old to be reliable.
answer: No, because it is a promotional post on a company's own site and has not been peer reviewed.

prompt: In a speech to parents, a principal says: "As a mother myself, I know how frightening this change feels." Which rhetorical appeal is the principal mainly using, and why?
choices: Ethos: the principal establishes credibility and shared identity with the audience by presenting herself as a fellow parent.
Pathos: the principal mainly stirs the audience's fear and anxiety about the change to make them act emotionally.
Logos: the principal mainly gives factual evidence about how frightening the change will be in practice.
Kairos: the principal mainly seizes the urgent moment of the change to pressure parents into deciding quickly.
answer: Ethos: the principal establishes credibility and shared identity with the audience by presenting herself as a fellow parent.

prompt: A student is writing one essay about two short poems. Both poems are set in winter. Poem A shows a traveler pausing at snowy woods at dusk; Poem B shows snow dust falling from a hemlock tree and lifting a raven's mood. The student wants to compare how each poem treats winter. Which thesis would best guide this comparative essay?
choices: Both poems use winter as a quiet, reflective setting, but Poem A treats winter as a beautiful, longing-filled moment, while Poem B treats winter as a small event that shifts the speaker's mood.
Both poems use winter as a symbol of death and endings.
Poem A is written in rhyme while Poem B uses more imagery.
Both poems describe winter scenery with careful detail and calm rhythms.
answer: Both poems use winter as a quiet, reflective setting, but Poem A treats winter as a beautiful, longing-filled moment, while Poem B treats winter as a small event that shifts the speaker's mood.

prompt: Maya is giving a three-minute talk to her class about why the school day should start later. She has practiced at home and knows her material well. During the talk, she reads every word from her notes, speaks in a fast, flat voice, and does not pause between her reasons. Her slides are fine. What is the most important change she should make to her delivery next time?
choices: Speak from brief notes instead of reading word for word, and pause between reasons so listeners can follow.
Add several more statistics to her slides so the talk includes more evidence.
Memorize the talk word for word and say it as quickly as possible to fit the time limit.
Change the slides to a darker color so the room can read them more easily.
answer: Speak from brief notes instead of reading word for word, and pause between reasons so listeners can follow.

prompt: A student writes: "Either we ban all cars from downtown, or our air will be unbreathable within a year." What fallacy does this commit?
choices: False dilemma: it forces a choice between only two extreme options when other possibilities, such as emissions standards or transit improvements, exist.
Slippery slope: it claims that banning cars will lead step by step to some unrelated disaster down the road.
Straw man: it distorts and exaggerates an opponent's actual position before arguing against it.
Hasty generalization: it draws a broad conclusion about all cities from only one small example.
answer: False dilemma: it forces a choice between only two extreme options when other possibilities, such as emissions standards or transit improvements, exist.

prompt: A columnist writes: "The senator's promise to fix everything overnight was his Achilles' heel; voters saw through it at once." What does the allusion to Achilles' heel suggest about the promise?
choices: It was a single glaring weakness that exposed the senator to attack, referring to the one vulnerable spot on the Greek hero Achilles.
It was an overwhelming show of strength that intimidated his opponents, referring to Achilles' mighty skill in battle.
It was a sudden, unexplained reversal of his position, referring to the way Achilles changed sides in the Trojan War.
It was an unjust punishment handed down by authority, referring to the fate the gods imposed on Achilles.
answer: It was a single glaring weakness that exposed the senator to attack, referring to the one vulnerable spot on the Greek hero Achilles.

prompt: Read the sentence: "She opened the letter slowly—her hands trembled—and read the single line." What do the dashes do here?
choices: They set off an inserted detail that interrupts the main action, adding emphasis to the trembling hands.
They show that words have been left out of a quotation, as in a shortened quote.
They replace a colon to introduce a list of things she read.
They join two independent clauses the way a semicolon would.
answer: They set off an inserted detail that interrupts the main action, adding emphasis to the trembling hands.

prompt: An original source says: "The Great Fire of London destroyed more than 13,000 houses in four days." A student writes: "In just four days, the fire wiped out over thirteen thousand homes in London." The student names the source right before this sentence. What has the student done?
choices: Made a paraphrase, because the student restated one passage's idea in their own words without quotation marks.
Made a summary, because the student condensed a whole text into one short line.
Made a direct quotation, because the student used the source's exact numbers.
Committed plagiarism, because the student did not put the words in quotes.
answer: Made a paraphrase, because the student restated one passage's idea in their own words without quotation marks.

prompt: Read this passage from "The Necklace": "She suffered ceaselessly, feeling herself born for all the delicacies and all the luxuries. She suffered from the poverty of her dwelling, from the worn walls, the abraded chairs, the ugliness of the fabrics. All these things, of which another woman of her rank would never even have been conscious, tortured her and made her angry. The sight of the little Breton peasant who did her humble housework aroused in her regrets which were despairing, and distracted dreams. She thought of silent antechambers hung with Oriental tapestry, lit by tall bronze candelabra, and of two great footmen in knee breeches who sleep in the big armchairs, made drowsy by the heavy warmth of the hot-air stove. She thought of long salons fitted up with ancient silk, of delicate furniture carrying priceless curiosities, and of coquettish perfumed boudoirs made for talks at five o'clock with intimate friends, with men famous and sought after, whom all women envy and whose attention they all desire. She had no dresses, no jewels, nothing. And she loved nothing but that; she felt made for that. She would so have liked to please, to be envied, to be charming, to be sought after." Which claim does this passage best support?
choices: Mathilde's unhappiness comes mainly from her own vanity and self-pity.
Mathilde is trapped by a cruel social system that no one can escape.
Mathilde's suffering is caused mainly by her husband's coldness toward her.
Mathilde grows more generous toward her servant as the story goes on.
answer: Mathilde's unhappiness comes mainly from her own vanity and self-pity.

prompt: Read the argument: "All mammals are warm-blooded. A whale is warm-blooded. Therefore, a whale is a mammal." What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: The conclusion does not follow: being warm-blooded does not prove something is a mammal, since non-mammals can also be warm-blooded. The argument affirms the consequent.
The argument equivocates: it uses the word "warm-blooded" in two different senses in the two premises.
The argument is circular: it assumes that a whale is a mammal within the first premise and then proves it again.
The argument has a false premise: not all mammals are actually warm-blooded, so the first claim is simply untrue.
answer: The conclusion does not follow: being warm-blooded does not prove something is a mammal, since non-mammals can also be warm-blooded. The argument affirms the consequent.

prompt: Read the sentence: "The committee has decided that the report will be written by the team, and the deadline was moved by the chair." What change best fixes the inappropriate shift?
choices: Change "the deadline was moved by the chair" to "the chair moved the deadline" so both clauses are active.
Change "has decided" to "had decided" so both clauses are past perfect.
Change "will be written" to "is written" so both clauses are simple present.
Change "the team" to "by the team" so both clauses use a prepositional phrase.
answer: Change "the deadline was moved by the chair" to "the chair moved the deadline" so both clauses are active.

prompt: Luis is making a short video about teen sleep loss. His first version, for classmates, uses slang, quick jokes, and memes. Now the student council will show his video at a school board meeting where parents, teachers, and administrators will decide whether to change the start time. He must design the video again for this audience and purpose. Which plan best fits?
choices: Use clear narration and on-screen data about grades and safety, images of tired students and morning traffic, and end with a specific request to move the start time.
Keep the same slang and memes so the video stays fun for the board members too.
Show only a black screen with white text so that nothing distracts from the message.
Use the same images but make the video twice as long so it seems more serious.
answer: Use clear narration and on-screen data about grades and safety, images of tired students and morning traffic, and end with a specific request to move the start time.

prompt: Which rule is most important when a speaker presents a claim with evidence to a live audience?
choices: Explain how each piece of evidence supports the claim, and speak clearly enough to be followed.
Read every source aloud in full so the audience hears all the proof.
Memorize the talk word for word and never pause or look up.
Repeat the claim at the start of every sentence to keep it clear.
answer: Explain how each piece of evidence supports the claim, and speak clearly enough to be followed.

prompt: In her writing portfolio, Maya compares an early draft of a story with her final draft and describes what she changed and why. Which comment shows the strongest reflection on her growth?
choices: "I moved the turning point to an earlier scene and cut two pages, because my first draft saved the real change for the very end."
"I fixed some typos and made the font bigger so it would look nicer."
"I think my story is much better now than it was before."
"My friend said the ending was better this way, so I kept it."
answer: "I moved the turning point to an earlier scene and cut two pages, because my first draft saved the real change for the very end."

prompt: A writer wants to sound firm and formal while stating what the school must do. Which sentence uses the subjunctive mood correctly for this purpose?
choices: The board requires that every student submit the form before Friday.
The board requires that every student submits the form before Friday.
The board requires that every student will submit the form before Friday.
The board requires that every student submitted the form before Friday.
answer: The board requires that every student submit the form before Friday.

prompt: Which research question is the most focused and answerable in a short research paper?
choices: In U.S. high schools, does using phones in class lower homework completion rates?
Why is teen stress such a big problem in schools today?
How has social media affected teenagers in every possible way?
Is social media use linked to teen anxiety?
answer: In U.S. high schools, does using phones in class lower homework completion rates?

prompt: Two students, Amina in one town and Jonah in another, must co-write a research essay over two weeks and hand in a single final copy. They also need their teacher to see how the draft changed over time. Which plan uses digital tools and collaboration best?
choices: They draft together in one shared document with tracked changes and comments, and submit the final version from that document to the class site.
They each write half the essay in separate files and email the two halves to the teacher on the due date.
They take turns typing on one laptop at Jonah's house and print the final copy there.
