They write the whole essay in one long text message thread and copy it into a document at the end.
answer: They draft together in one shared document with tracked changes and comments, and submit the final version from that document to the class site.

prompt: During a class talk, Priya reads straight from her note cards the whole time and speaks too quickly for listeners to follow. Which skill does she most need to practice?
choices: Making eye contact and pausing so listeners can follow her talk.
Adding more facts to the middle of the talk to make it longer.
Choosing a more formal and serious topic for the talk.
Printing longer note cards that hold more of her words.
answer: Making eye contact and pausing so listeners can follow her talk.

prompt:
A student writing in APA style lists one of her sources like this:
Brown, J. (2019). Teen sleep and school start times. Journal of Youth Studies, 22(4), 45–60.
Which part of the entry is formatted incorrectly for APA?
choices: The journal title and volume number, because in APA the journal title and volume are italicized together.
The year, because in APA the year must be written out as two thousand nineteen.
The page range, because APA never lists page numbers for journal articles.
The author's name, because APA writes out the full first name.
answer: The journal title and volume number, because in APA the journal title and volume are italicized together.

prompt: Which sentence is a periodic sentence, with the main clause held back until the end?
choices: After the votes were counted, the judges debated, and the crowd grew restless, the winner was finally announced.
The winner was finally announced, after the votes were counted and the judges debated.
The winner was announced, the crowd grew restless, and the judges kept debating.
The votes were counted; the judges debated; the crowd grew restless.
answer: After the votes were counted, the judges debated, and the crowd grew restless, the winner was finally announced.

prompt: A student argues that the school day should start later. Which piece of evidence best supports the claim, rather than merely restating it?
choices: A study from the American Academy of Pediatrics finding that teenagers who start school after 8:30 a.m. show measurably higher test scores and fewer car crashes.
A sentence asserting that starting school later is obviously much better for every student in every way.
A classmate's remark that school starting early feels pretty bad and that everyone already knows it.
A long definition of the word "adolescence" copied from a dictionary with no reference to school schedules.
answer: A study from the American Academy of Pediatrics finding that teenagers who start school after 8:30 a.m. show measurably higher test scores and fewer car crashes.

prompt: A student wants the sentence to build tension and land hard on the point that the plan is dishonest. Which revision uses sentence structure most effectively to create that effect?
choices: Periodic structure: "Although the plan promises savings, claims to protect jobs, and pledges fairness, it is dishonest." The main idea is withheld until the final words, so it lands with emphasis.
Cumulative structure: "It is dishonest, a plan that promises savings, claims to protect jobs, and pledges fairness." The main idea comes first and the details trail after it.
Simple structure: "The plan is dishonest. It promises savings. It claims to protect jobs. It pledges fairness." Short equal sentences give each idea the same weight.
Passive structure: "Savings are promised, jobs are said to be protected, fairness is pledged, and dishonesty is what the plan is." The agent is hidden and the point feels vague.
answer: Periodic structure: "Although the plan promises savings, claims to protect jobs, and pledges fairness, it is dishonest." The main idea is withheld until the final words, so it lands with emphasis.

prompt: A student's argumentative essay claims that the school should require thirty minutes of reading every day, because reading raises test scores. The essay gives two pieces of evidence: a study showing that students who read daily score higher on tests, and a quote from a librarian saying reading is enjoyable. A peer points out that students who read daily may already be stronger students before they start reading. What is the best revision-level response for the writer?
choices: Rework the argument so it addresses the possibility that stronger students choose to read more, and find evidence that meets that objection.
Add the librarian's full name and the date of the study to the works cited page.
Change the word "raises" to "is linked with" in every sentence and leave the rest of the argument as it is.
Read the whole essay aloud, fix any awkward sentences, and print a clean copy.
answer: Rework the argument so it addresses the possibility that stronger students choose to read more, and find evidence that meets that objection.

prompt: A writer wants the second half of the sentence to hit like a punch line, with a sharp break right before it. Read the draft: "The team had one goal [BLANK] winning." Which punctuation mark best creates that effect?
choices: A dash: "The team had one goal—winning." The dash creates a sharp, dramatic pause that spotlights the final word.
A colon: "The team had one goal: winning." The colon is smooth and formal rather than dramatic, so it softens the punch.
A semicolon: "The team had one goal; winning." The semicolon joins two clauses, and 'winning' is not a clause, so the break feels wrong.
A comma: "The team had one goal, winning." The comma is too light to create a noticeable break or emphasis.
answer: A dash: "The team had one goal—winning." The dash creates a sharp, dramatic pause that spotlights the final word.

prompt: A student is writing an analytical paragraph about a novel. The draft says: "In chapter four, the narrator calls the old house 'a cage of glass and light.' He is sad in this chapter because his father has died. The house is very large and expensive. The narrator also owns a horse." The student's claim, stated at the start of the paragraph, is: "The narrator feels trapped by his own wealth." What does this paragraph most need in order to support that claim well?
choices: A sentence that explains how the word "cage" in the quotation connects to the narrator's feeling of being trapped.
A sentence that tells exactly how many rooms the house has and how much it cost.
A sentence that summarizes what happens to the narrator in the rest of the novel.
A sentence that defines the word "cage" as an enclosure made to hold animals or birds.
answer: A sentence that explains how the word "cage" in the quotation connects to the narrator's feeling of being trapped.

prompt: A soda company publishes a glossy report concluding that sugary drinks are harmless, and the report cites no independent scientists. What question should a critical reader ask first to detect bias?
choices: Who created this message and what do they gain if I believe it, since the company profits from the conclusion and has not consulted outside experts?
Is this message long and detailed enough to cover the topic thoroughly, since length is the best sign that a source is trustworthy?
Does this message use enough technical vocabulary to sound credible, since scientific wording signals that a source is unbiased?
Does this message include photographs and charts, since visual design shows that the findings have been verified?
answer: Who created this message and what do they gain if I believe it, since the company profits from the conclusion and has not consulted outside experts?

prompt: A student used this source: Kara Lehman, "The Rise of Remote Work," WorkLife, 12 Mar. 2021, www.worklife.com/remote-work. Which works cited entry in MLA style is correct?
choices: Lehman, Kara. "The Rise of Remote Work." WorkLife, 12 Mar. 2021, www.worklife.com/remote-work.
Lehman, Kara. "The Rise of Remote Work." WorkLife. www.worklife.com/remote-work. 12 Mar. 2021.
"The Rise of Remote Work." Kara Lehman. WorkLife, 12 Mar. 2021, www.worklife.com/remote-work.
Kara Lehman, "The Rise of Remote Work," WorkLife, www.worklife.com/remote-work, 2021.
answer: Lehman, Kara. "The Rise of Remote Work." WorkLife, 12 Mar. 2021, www.worklife.com/remote-work.

prompt: Read the passage: "The bill passed. The crowds cheered. The governor signed it. Nothing changed." Which feature most shapes the style of this passage?
choices: A series of short clauses placed side by side with no joining words or subordination.
A long, periodic sentence that withholds the main idea until the very end.
Dense figurative language built from metaphor, simile, and personification.
Formal academic diction filled with technical terms and specialized vocabulary.
answer: A series of short clauses placed side by side with no joining words or subordination.

prompt: Which revision best shows the editing skill of cutting needless words while keeping the sentence's rhythm and force?
choices: She walked slowly and deliberately toward the waiting, expectant crowd. → She walked toward the crowd.
She walked slowly and deliberately toward the waiting, expectant crowd. → She very slowly and very deliberately walked toward the big waiting expectant crowd.
She walked slowly and deliberately toward the waiting, expectant crowd. → She walked slowly and deliberately toward the waiting and expectant crowd.
She walked slowly and deliberately toward the waiting, expectant crowd. → The crowd was waiting and expectant as she walked toward it slowly.
answer: She walked slowly and deliberately toward the waiting, expectant crowd. → She walked toward the crowd.

prompt: A candidate's advertisement says: "My opponent voted to let dangerous criminals walk free." In fact, the opponent voted for a bill that reduced some mandatory minimum sentences. From the standpoint of responsible communication, what is the main problem with the ad?
choices: It recasts a partial truth as a sweeping claim, trading accuracy for the outrage that wins votes.
It recasts a partial truth as a sweeping claim, but the wording is fair because the opponent did vote for the bill.
It uses strong emotional wording alone, which is always unethical even when the facts behind it are accurate.
It hides the fact that criminals exist, misleading voters about crime rates in the state.
answer: It recasts a partial truth as a sweeping claim, trading accuracy for the outrage that wins votes.

prompt: A technician is writing one document, a troubleshooting guide for a water filter's carbon block, that must serve both the installation crew and the buyers reading the product page. What is the best way to organize it?
choices: Keep one accurate technical core and layer it, opening with plain, benefit-focused language and putting hands-on measurements and specs in clearly labeled sections or appendices.
Write a single set of plain instructions with no technical sections, since the crew can look up measurements elsewhere.
Keep one accurate technical core and layer it, opening with the hands-on measurements and putting the plain, benefit-focused language in an appendix.
Write two separate documents with no shared wording, since the crew and the buyers have nothing in common.
answer: Keep one accurate technical core and layer it, opening with plain, benefit-focused language and putting hands-on measurements and specs in clearly labeled sections or appendices.

prompt: Which sentence uses hyphens correctly?
choices: A self-made expert in nineteenth-century history spoke to the class.
A self made expert in nineteenth century history spoke to the class.
A self-made expert in nineteenth century history spoke to the class.
A self made expert in nineteenth-century history spoke to the class.
answer: A self-made expert in nineteenth-century history spoke to the class.

prompt: A site arguing for a new stadium pairs sweeping drone footage of a crowded city with soaring music and a counter that ticks up the number of promised jobs. It gives no source for the job numbers and shows no costs. What is the strongest judgment of this as an argument?
choices: The visuals and music build excitement, but the case fails because its central claim has no evidence or counterargument.
The drone footage proves the stadium will succeed, since large crowds are shown in the video.
The counting animation makes the job claim reliable, since numbers are always verifiable.
A persuasive case needs only strong feeling, so the missing sources do not weaken it.
answer: The visuals and music build excitement, but the case fails because its central claim has no evidence or counterargument.

prompt: You are leading a seminar of eight students. Two students have spoken for most of the first ten minutes, and three others have said nothing at all. What is the best next move as the discussion leader?
choices: Invite the quieter students by name to share their reading of the text and set a short round so everyone speaks.
Praise the two frequent speakers to keep the energy up and let the others join when ready.
End the discussion early, since a group that will not all talk cannot be helped.
Ask the whole group a harder question and wait, assuming the quiet students will jump in.
answer: Invite the quieter students by name to share their reading of the text and set a short round so everyone speaks.

prompt: Which opening sentence would make a college personal statement stand out as specific and memorable rather than generic?
choices: At 5:40 every morning I unlock the bakery door and punch down the first batch of dough before anyone in my family is awake.
I have always been a hardworking person who gives everything I do my very best effort.
Ever since I was young, I have had a great passion for learning and for helping others.
I believe that challenges are really opportunities in disguise if you look at them the right way.
answer: At 5:40 every morning I unlock the bakery door and punch down the first batch of dough before anyone in my family is awake.

prompt: Two readers send you opposite notes on the same draft. Reader A says your argument is too long and wants you to cut the second body paragraph entirely. Reader B says the second body paragraph is the strongest part and wants you to expand it with more evidence. What is the best way to handle this conflicting feedback?
choices: Re-read the draft with both notes in hand and decide, based on your thesis, which reader is right about that paragraph.
Keep the paragraph exactly as it is and ignore both readers' notes.
Follow Reader A first, since the first feedback you receive is usually best.
Cut the paragraph and add the same evidence to Reader B's favorite paragraph instead.
answer: Re-read the draft with both notes in hand and decide, based on your thesis, which reader is right about that paragraph.

prompt: Source A: Factory records show that weekly hours worked rose between 1900 and 1910. Source B: Letters home from workers in those same years often mention exhaustion and missed family events. Which sentence synthesizes these two sources into one point of its own?
choices: Taken together, the records and the letters suggest that the longer hours of the decade cut deeply into workers' daily lives.
Factory records show that weekly hours worked rose between 1900 and 1910.
Letters home from workers in those years often mention exhaustion and missed family events.
One of these sources deals with factory records, while the other deals with letters from workers.
answer: Taken together, the records and the letters suggest that the longer hours of the decade cut deeply into workers' daily lives.

prompt: A speaker says: "We want a leader who serves the people, not a people who serves the leader." Which figure of speech does this sentence use?
choices: Chiasmus, because the second half reverses the structure of the first half.
Anaphora, because the sentence repeats the same opening words in successive clauses.
Metonymy, because one thing stands in for another thing closely connected to it.
Hyperbole, because the speaker exaggerates in order to make a point.
answer: Chiasmus, because the second half reverses the structure of the first half.

prompt: A city's air quality plan is described in three places. The news article says the plan will "clean up the city's air." The report's chart shows particle pollution falling only 6% over ten years. The interview with the city's health officer says, "It helps, but we are far from safe." What is the most reasonable conclusion?
choices: The plan offers a small improvement that the news headline overstates and the health officer corrects.
The news article proves the plan will fully solve the city's air quality problem.
The health officer's interview contradicts the chart, so the chart's numbers must be wrong.
The three sources agree completely, so there is no need to compare them further.
answer: The plan offers a small improvement that the news headline overstates and the health officer corrects.

prompt: A company's statement reads: "Mistakes were made in the handling of customer funds." The sentence never says who made the mistakes. What is the strongest ethical criticism of this wording?
choices: The passive voice hides who acted, which keeps the responsible people from being held to account.
The sentence is too short to explain the situation honestly and should be much longer.
The statement is unethical because it uses technical financial words that few people know.
The wording fails because it names customer funds, which should have stayed private.
answer: The passive voice hides who acted, which keeps the responsible people from being held to account.

prompt: Which sentence correctly uses the word "meticulous" in a form that fits its meaning and grammar? ("Meticulous" means extremely careful about small details.)
choices: The archivist's meticulous labeling of every box made the collection easy to search.
The archivist meticulous labeled every box, making the collection easy to search.
The archivist's meticulousity was evident in how the boxes had been labeled and shelved.
The archivist worked meticulous, labeling every box before shelving it in the collection.
answer: The archivist's meticulous labeling of every box made the collection easy to search.

prompt: A student is deciding which story to open her speech with, where to place her strongest point, and how to end. Which canon of rhetoric is she working on?
choices: Arrangement, the canon of ordering and organizing the parts of a message.
Invention, the canon of finding and developing the arguments themselves.
Style, the canon of choosing the right words, figures, and sentence patterns.
Delivery, the canon of voice, gesture, and timing in front of an audience.
answer: Arrangement, the canon of ordering and organizing the parts of a message.

prompt: A city council voted 5–4 last night to raise water rates by 9% starting in March. Eight residents spoke against the increase, and the mayor called the vote "a painful but necessary step." Which sentence belongs at the very start of the news story?
choices: The City Council voted 5–4 Tuesday night to raise water rates 9% beginning in March.
The mayor called Tuesday night's vote "a painful but necessary step" for the city.
Eight residents spoke against the increase at Tuesday night's council meeting.
Water rates will change in March after months of debate at City Hall.
answer: The City Council voted 5–4 Tuesday night to raise water rates 9% beginning in March.

prompt: Read the sample annotation entry: "The article describes the causes of the 1918 influenza pandemic. The article draws on hospital records from twelve cities. Though clearly written, it relies on one country's records and so may not represent the rest of the world. The article appeared in the Journal of Medical History in 2004." Which sentence evaluates the source rather than merely summarizing or describing it?
choices: "Though clearly written, it relies on one country's records and so may not represent the rest of the world."
"The article describes the causes of the 1918 influenza pandemic."
"The article draws on hospital records from twelve cities."
"The article appeared in the Journal of Medical History in 2004."
answer: "Though clearly written, it relies on one country's records and so may not represent the rest of the world."

prompt: Read the sentence: "Although the committee had already reviewed the proposal, the chair, who rarely agreed with the majority, asked for one more reading before the vote." Which statement about its structure is correct?
choices: It has one main clause and two subordinate clauses: the "Although" clause before the comma and the "who rarely agreed" clause inside the main clause.
It has two main clauses joined by a comma, since "committee" and "chair" each begin a clause with a subject and a verb.
It has one main clause and one subordinate clause, and "who rarely agreed with the majority" is only a phrase with no verb of its own.
It has three separate clauses, because the three nouns committee, chair, and majority each begin a new clause.
answer: It has one main clause and two subordinate clauses: the "Although" clause before the comma and the "who rarely agreed" clause inside the main clause.

prompt: Both texts below show a human achievement long after its makers are gone. In "Ozymandias," the shattered statue "stands" alone in an empty desert, and the boast "Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!" is all that survives. In Ray Bradbury's "There Will Come Soft Rains," the automatic house keeps sweeping and cooking and reading the time aloud, while the family's silhouettes are burned onto the wall like shadows. What is the strongest point the two texts make together that either one alone does not fully show?
choices: Human power outlives neither nature nor the routines built to serve it.
Machines are far more reliable than stone monuments over time.
Nuclear war is the only danger that can wipe out an entire city.
Ancient rulers treated their people far worse than modern families do.
answer: Human power outlives neither nature nor the routines built to serve it.

prompt: An opinion piece arguing for more school funding appears in the paper two days before the city council votes on the budget. Which rhetorical choice does this timing show?
choices: Kairos: the writer chose a moment when the audience is already focused on the decision at hand.
Ethos: the writer showed that experts in education support the argument for funding.
Logos: the writer presented data proving that the current funding levels are unfair.
Memoria: the writer repeated the argument at set times so the audience would remember it.
answer: Kairos: the writer chose a moment when the audience is already focused on the decision at hand.

prompt: A student is revising a capstone portfolio and has been asked to reflect on growth. Which reflection is most useful to a reader?
choices: In my first research draft I quoted sources without framing them; by the final paper every quotation is introduced and tied to my claim.
I learned a great deal this year and my writing has improved a lot in many different ways.
This portfolio contains my best work from the whole year and I hope the reader enjoys it.
I always proofread my papers carefully, and I have been a strong writer for many years.
answer: In my first research draft I quoted sources without framing them; by the final paper every quotation is introduced and tied to my claim.

prompt: Which is a correct MLA in-text citation for a quotation from page 42 of a book by Jordan Smith?
choices: (Smith 42)
(Smith, p. 42)
(Smith, 42)
answer: (Smith 42)

prompt: A manuscript has just finished its developmental edit. Which task comes at the proofreading stage, near the end of the publishing process?
choices: Catching small surface errors, such as a misspelled word or a broken page number, before printing.
Reworking the book's overall structure and cutting two whole chapters for pacing.
Deciding the book's title, cover art, and which stores will sell it.
Choosing whether the book will be published in print, as an e-book, or both.
answer: Catching small surface errors, such as a misspelled word or a broken page number, before printing.

prompt: Which sentence would work best as the thesis of a literary analysis essay?
choices: Fitzgerald uses the green light at the end of Daisy's dock to show a dream that fades at the moment it is finally reached.
Fitzgerald published the novel in 1925, and the story is set in New York during the Jazz Age.
This paper will summarize the plot of the novel and describe its main characters.
Fitzgerald's use of ethos and pathos makes the narrator sound trustworthy to the reader.
answer: Fitzgerald uses the green light at the end of Daisy's dock to show a dream that fades at the moment it is finally reached.

prompt: You are building a short digital presentation on a city's water safety. Which choice best uses a digital tool to strengthen understanding rather than just decorate the slides?
choices: Use an interactive map that lets viewers click their own neighborhood to see its lead-pipe count.
Add a looping background animation of falling water behind every slide.
Choose a bright color theme and large decorative fonts to hold attention.
Include a photo of a water droplet on each slide for a polished, consistent look.
answer: Use an interactive map that lets viewers click their own neighborhood to see its lead-pipe count.

prompt: Which statement about how English changes and varies is accurate?
choices: Every dialect has consistent rules of its own, so non-standard speech is not illogical or broken.
Only standard English has grammar rules, so other dialects are simply ungrammatical.
Words keep the same meaning over time, so older texts can be read literally without notes.
Slang always replaces the standard word within a generation once young people adopt it.
answer: Every dialect has consistent rules of its own, so non-standard speech is not illogical or broken.

prompt: Read the argument: "Our school's attendance rose from 88 to 94 percent after we started the morning tutoring program, so the tutoring program is working. After all, when a program begins and attendance improves, the program is likely the reason." Which part of this argument is the warrant?
choices: The reasoning that when a program begins and attendance improves, the program is likely the reason.
The claim that the morning tutoring program is working.
The figures showing attendance rose from 88 to 94 percent.
The word "likely," which limits how strongly the claim is stated.
answer: The reasoning that when a program begins and attendance improves, the program is likely the reason.

prompt: Which line properly uses a stage direction to show what the actor does and how the line is spoken?
choices: MAYA (quietly, not looking up): It wasn't mine to lose.
MAYA: It wasn't mine to lose, and she felt very sad about it.
MAYA (a character who has lost something and regrets it): It wasn't mine to lose.
MAYA: It wasn't mine to lose. *audience should feel sympathy here*
answer: MAYA (quietly, not looking up): It wasn't mine to lose.

prompt: A writer uses three sources on the same topic. Which is synthesis rather than summary?
choices: A paragraph that points out how two sources agree on the causes of a problem but disagree on the solutions, and explains what that gap shows.
Three paragraphs, one summarizing each source in turn, with no connection made between them.
A paragraph summarizing one source's main argument in detail.
A long quotation from one source with a short introduction before it.
answer: A paragraph that points out how two sources agree on the causes of a problem but disagree on the solutions, and explains what that gap shows.

prompt: A student searches a scholarly database for "social media college students" and gets 4,000 results. Which change will narrow the results most effectively?
choices: Combine the terms with AND and limit the search to peer-reviewed articles from the last five years.
Add the terms OR Instagram OR TikTok to the search.
Search for "social media OR college students" instead.
Remove "college students" and search only for "social media."
answer: Combine the terms with AND and limit the search to peer-reviewed articles from the last five years.

prompt: A student is writing an analytical essay about a short story in which a character keeps a diary but never shows it to anyone. Which sentence does the deepest analytical work, going beneath what the text says to explain what a detail means?
choices: The character's hidden diary symbolizes the private self she must protect from a household that punishes honesty.
The character writes in a diary every night but never lets anyone read it.
The diary appears in several scenes and becomes important later in the story.
The character's hidden diary is interesting because many people also keep diaries of their own.
answer: The character's hidden diary symbolizes the private self she must protect from a household that punishes honesty.

prompt: A student quotes from page 33 of the book Writing Well by Alan Reed (Chicago: Lake Press, 2018). Which Chicago footnote is correct?
choices: Alan Reed, Writing Well (Chicago: Lake Press, 2018), 33.
Reed, Alan. Writing Well. Chicago: Lake Press, 2018.
Alan Reed, Writing Well (Chicago: Lake Press, 2018).
answer: Alan Reed, Writing Well (Chicago: Lake Press, 2018), 33.

prompt: A student writes this sentence for a college paper: "The author basically slams the government's plan in her article." Which revision has the best academic tone?
choices: The author forcefully criticizes the government's plan in her article.
The author totally destroys the government's plan in her article.
The author is not a fan of the government's plan in her article.
The author takes down the government's plan in her article.
answer: The author forcefully criticizes the government's plan in her article.

prompt: Read the two sentences: "City buses in Springfield now stop running at 9 p.m. This means that many night-shift workers cannot get home without a car." Which words or phrase best signals the link between the two ideas?
choices: This means that
For example,
In conclusion,
First of all,
answer: This means that

prompt: Which sentence blends a quotation into the writer's own sentence most smoothly?
choices: Johnson's study found that "students who spaced their studying performed better" than those who crammed.
Johnson did a study. The exact words were "students who spaced their studying performed better."
The study found something interesting. "Students who spaced their studying performed better."
"Students who spaced their studying performed better." Johnson's study proves this point.
answer: Johnson's study found that "students who spaced their studying performed better" than those who crammed.

prompt: Which sentence is written in the conventions of academic writing for a college class?
choices: The study's results support the claim that sleep affects memory.
OMG, this study totally proves sleep is like, super important.
So yeah, sleep and memory are a thing, as everyone knows.
You guys should really care about what this study found.
answer: The study's results support the claim that sleep affects memory.

prompt: A student is writing a literature review about how professors give feedback on student writing. Which paragraph does what a literature review must do?
choices: Early studies (Leki, 1990; Ferris, 1997) focused on written comments on drafts, while later work (Hyland, 2003) turned to how students actually read those comments. Together they show a shift from teacher talk to student response, but none of them study online feedback, which is the gap my project addresses.

Leki (1990) studies written comments on drafts. Ferris (1997) also studies written comments on drafts. Hyland (2003) studies how students read comments. My paper will add to this work by studying online feedback.

Written comments on drafts have been studied by many scholars over the years, and they all agree that feedback matters a great deal. Teachers should therefore spend more time on comments. I will now explain my own method of giving feedback.

Feedback is a big topic in writing studies. Some scholars like it and some do not. I have read about twelve sources on this topic, and I will summarize each one in turn before I state my own opinion at the end.
answer: Early studies (Leki, 1990; Ferris, 1997) focused on written comments on drafts, while later work (Hyland, 2003) turned to how students actually read those comments. Together they show a shift from teacher talk to student response, but none of them study online feedback, which is the gap my project addresses.

prompt: A student has a broad topic: how social media affects college students. Following the research process, what should the student do next?
choices: Narrow the topic into a focused, researchable question.
Find as many sources as possible on social media and college students.
Write the paper's main argument first so the research has direction.
Choose a citation style before beginning to search for sources.
answer: Narrow the topic into a focused, researchable question.

prompt: A student is writing one entry of an annotated bibliography on the topic of sleep and college grades. Which entry does the job an annotated bibliography entry must do?
choices: Chen (2022) surveys 400 students and finds that under six hours of sleep is linked to lower grades. The study uses a large sample but only self-reported hours, so the link is not proof of cause. It is useful for my paper's section on grade outcomes.
Chen (2022) is a journal article about sleep and grades. It was published in a good journal and covers many students. I found it using the library database and saved it to my folder.
Chen (2022) writes: "Students who slept fewer than six hours had lower GPAs" (p. 44). I think this is true because I also sleep too little and my grades are not great. It supports my main point.

Chen (2022) surveys 400 students and finds that under six hours of sleep is linked to lower grades. The article is 18 pages long and has 32 references. It was published in 2022 in a journal about education.
answer: Chen (2022) surveys 400 students and finds that under six hours of sleep is linked to lower grades. The study uses a large sample but only self-reported hours, so the link is not proof of cause. It is useful for my paper's section on grade outcomes.

prompt: A student writes: "All the students I know check their phones during class, so every college student in the country must do this." What kind of reasoning is this?
choices: Induction from too small a sample
Deduction from a general rule
Analogy between two similar cases
A rebuttal of an opposing claim
answer: Induction from too small a sample

prompt: Which option correctly paraphrases this sentence from a source? "Regular aerobic exercise improves memory performance in older adults." Source: Lee, 2020.
choices: Older adults who do regular cardio tend to show better memory (Lee, 2020).
"Regular aerobic exercise improves memory performance in older adults" (Lee, 2020).
Exercise is good for you, as many people have said.
Regular aerobic exercise improves memory performance in older adults, according to my own research.
answer: Older adults who do regular cardio tend to show better memory (Lee, 2020).

prompt: Which revision makes this sentence clearer and more concise? "Due to the fact that many students were tired, it was the case that the exam scores were lower."
choices: Many students were tired, so their exam scores were lower.
Because of the fact that a lot of students were tired, it was the case that the scores were lower.
Many students, who were very tired students in class, saw scores that were lower.
It is a well-known fact that tired students get lower exam scores.
answer: Many students were tired, so their exam scores were lower.

prompt: A student is interested in social media and college students. Which question is the best research question for a college paper?
choices: How do first-year students at one university describe the ways social media affects their study habits?
Is social media bad for college students?
What is social media, and how does it work?
Should colleges ban social media in the dorms?
answer: How do first-year students at one university describe the ways social media affects their study habits?

prompt: Keisha is writing a 15-page paper with four main sections. Which outline best shows logical flow between sections?
choices: A numbered outline that lists each section's main claim and shows how each section builds on the one before it.
A list of every fact she found, in the order she found them.
A single sentence that states her topic and nothing else.
A draft of the introduction repeated for each section.
answer: A numbered outline that lists each section's main claim and shows how each section builds on the one before it.

prompt: Which sentence would work best as a conclusion to a paper arguing that Springfield should extend bus service?
choices: Extending bus service would help thousands of workers keep their jobs, so the city should act now.
As I said in my introduction, Springfield has buses.
In this paper I have talked about many things.
There are many opinions about buses in Springfield.
answer: Extending bus service would help thousands of workers keep their jobs, so the city should act now.

prompt: A student is preparing for a 30-minute appointment at the college writing center to get help on a draft. Which approach best fits how to use a writing center session?
choices: Bring the draft, the assignment sheet, and two specific questions, such as "Is my main claim clear in paragraph two?" and "Where does my reasoning get thin?"
Bring only the finished draft and let the tutor read it silently for the whole session, then ask the tutor to fix the errors and hand it back.
Bring no draft at all and describe the paper from memory, so the tutor can give general advice about writing that applies to any paper.
Bring the draft and ask the tutor to rewrite the weakest paragraph, since the tutor is a better writer and will produce a stronger version.
answer: Bring the draft, the assignment sheet, and two specific questions, such as "Is my main claim clear in paragraph two?" and "Where does my reasoning get thin?"

prompt: A student is writing a proposal to her college to start a peer tutoring program in the residence halls. Which sentence best fits the purpose of a proposal?
choices: This program would cost little to run and would raise first-year grades, and here is a plan for a one-semester pilot in Hall B.
This program would cost little to run and would raise first-year grades, and I have always believed strongly in helping other students.
This program would cost little to run and would raise first-year grades, and I think the college should be ashamed of its current tutoring services.
This program would cost little to run and would raise first-year grades, and many students around the country have written about tutoring.
answer: This program would cost little to run and would raise first-year grades, and here is a plan for a one-semester pilot in Hall B.

prompt: Which claim is hedged with the right level of caution for an academic paper?
choices: Some research suggests that heavy social media use may be associated with lower well-being among some teenagers.
Heavy social media use causes depression in teenagers.
Heavy social media use definitely lowers well-being in all teenagers.
Everyone knows that heavy social media use harms teenagers.
answer: Some research suggests that heavy social media use may be associated with lower well-being among some teenagers.

prompt: A student is analyzing an advertisement that shows a small, thin figure standing alone under a huge logo in an empty white space. What does this layout argue?
choices: The huge logo and empty space make the brand seem powerful and sure of itself, while the small figure makes the buyer seem to need it.
The huge logo and empty space show that the company had a very large budget for this advertisement when it was made.
The huge logo and empty space show that the company wanted to use as little ink as possible when printing this advertisement.
The huge logo and empty space show that the artist who made it was not very skilled at filling in the space with more details.
answer: The huge logo and empty space make the brand seem powerful and sure of itself, while the small figure makes the buyer seem to need it.

prompt: A student is writing the reflective cover letter for a final portfolio. Which sentence best fits what this kind of self-assessment must do?
choices: Comparing my first draft's vague opening with the revision's specific claim shows that I learned to state my argument early, and I still need work on my transitions.
This portfolio contains my three best papers from this course, and I worked very hard on all of them over the whole semester this term.
This portfolio contains my three best papers, and my grades on them were A, A-minus, and B-plus, which I think shows that I am a good writer.
This portfolio contains my three best papers, and I hope my reader enjoys reading them as much as I enjoyed writing them this semester.
answer: Comparing my first draft's vague opening with the revision's specific claim shows that I learned to state my argument early, and I still need work on my transitions.

prompt: Which reference-list entry is correct in APA style for a 2020 journal article by Rita Lee and Marco Cruz titled "Writing Anxiety and Revision," in the Journal of College Writing, volume 12, issue 3, pages 45–60?
choices: Lee, R., & Cruz, M. (2020). Writing anxiety and revision. Journal of College Writing, 12(3), 45–60.
Lee, R., & Cruz, M. (2020). "Writing anxiety and revision." Journal of College Writing, 12(3), 45–60.
Lee, R., and Cruz, M. (2020). Writing Anxiety and Revision. Journal of College Writing, vol. 12, no. 3, pp. 45–60.
Lee, R. & Cruz, M. (2020). Writing anxiety and revision. Journal of College Writing, 12, 3, 45–60.
answer: Lee, R., & Cruz, M. (2020). Writing anxiety and revision. Journal of College Writing, 12(3), 45–60.

prompt: A student is writing a social science study of how first-year students use the library. Which section order best matches social science conventions?
choices: Introduction and research question, review of prior studies, method for collecting the survey data, results, and discussion of what the results mean.
A personal story about my own first library visit, a review of prior studies, my method for collecting the survey data, and a call to action for the college.
Introduction and research question, method for collecting the survey data, results, discussion of what the results mean, and close reading of a short story about a library.
Abstract, poem about the library, method for collecting the survey data, results, and discussion of what the results mean.
answer: Introduction and research question, review of prior studies, method for collecting the survey data, results, and discussion of what the results mean.

prompt: A student must write a 500-word response for a first-year seminar. Her instructor wants her to explain how a campus policy affects first-year students, and the audience is her professor and classmates. Before she starts writing, which question best fits the rhetorical situation?
choices: What expectations does this audience and this genre place on how I explain the policy?
How many words did I write in my last paper for this class?
Which font and margin settings does the instructor require?
What grade do I want to earn on this assignment?
answer: What expectations does this audience and this genre place on how I explain the policy?

prompt: A student is writing about a bar chart that shows that, among four dorms, Hall A has the highest water use and Hall D the lowest. Which sentence best does the work of writing about data?
choices: Hall A uses the most water, and because it is the only hall without low-flow showerheads, the gap suggests that fixtures, not student habits, drive the difference.
Hall A uses the most water, and Hall D uses the least, and the other two halls fall in between, as the chart shows clearly to anyone who looks at it.
Hall A uses the most water, which is a very interesting fact about water use that I think most readers will find interesting as well.
Hall A uses the most water, and water is a valuable resource that we should all try to save whenever we can in our daily lives.
answer: Hall A uses the most water, and because it is the only hall without low-flow showerheads, the gap suggests that fixtures, not student habits, drive the difference.

prompt: A student is building slides for a ten-minute talk on campus recycling. Which slide best fits the guidance for digital and presentation writing?
choices: One slide with the single sentence "Recycling in Hall A rose 40% after the new bins" in large type, with the bar chart beneath it.
One slide with six paragraphs of text copied from the paper's introduction, in small type, with the bar chart hidden in a corner.
One slide with the single sentence "Recycling in Hall A rose 40% after the new bins" in large type, plus another slide of the full paper pasted in as backup.
One slide with the single sentence "Recycling in Hall A rose 40% after the new bins" in large type, but no chart, because charts distract from the speaker.
answer: One slide with the single sentence "Recycling in Hall A rose 40% after the new bins" in large type, with the bar chart beneath it.

prompt: Ella reads a source and wants to restate the author's point in her own words and sentence structure, in about the same length as the original. Which skill is she using?
choices: Paraphrase
Summary
Quotation
Analysis
answer: Paraphrase

prompt: Which sentence follows the standard advice to use people-first, bias-free language?
choices: Participants with disabilities were less likely to respond to the survey.
The disabled participants were less likely to respond to the survey.
Handicapped participants were less likely to respond to the survey.
The impaired participants were less likely to respond to the survey.
answer: Participants with disabilities were less likely to respond to the survey.

prompt: Which topic fits a literacy narrative?
choices: How a middle-school teacher's feedback changed the way the writer thought about their own writing.
A history of the English spelling reform movement over the past century.
An argument that colleges should require more writing courses of all majors.
A comparison of how two novels portray immigration to the United States.
answer: How a middle-school teacher's feedback changed the way the writer thought about their own writing.

prompt: Read the paragraph: "Many students skip breakfast. This leads to poor focus in morning classes. For example, a 2019 study found that students who ate breakfast scored higher on morning quizzes. So eating breakfast can help students do better in class." Which sentence is the paragraph's claim?
choices: So eating breakfast can help students do better in class.
Many students skip breakfast.
This leads to poor focus in morning classes.
For example, a 2019 study found that students who ate breakfast scored higher on morning quizzes.
answer: So eating breakfast can help students do better in class.

prompt: A student is writing up a lab experiment in the natural sciences. Which sentence best fits the conventions of scientific writing?
choices: The solution was heated to 60°C for ten minutes, and the mean change in pH across the three trials was 0.4 units.
We heated the solution to a pretty warm temperature for a while, and the pH changed quite a bit across our three tries at the experiment.
The solution was heated to 60°C for ten minutes, and the change in pH of 0.4 units surprised and delighted the whole lab group.
The solution was heated to 60°C for ten minutes, which shows that science is a powerful tool for understanding the natural world around us.
answer: The solution was heated to 60°C for ten minutes, and the mean change in pH across the three trials was 0.4 units.

prompt: A student is writing a humanities paper on a short story. Which sentence best fits the conventions of humanities writing?
choices: When the narrator calls the house "a cage," the metaphor links her marriage to her earlier imprisonment, which deepens the story's argument about freedom.
When the narrator calls the house "a cage," this word choice is interesting, and many readers have noticed it over the years since the story was published.
When the narrator calls the house "a cage," I felt sad when I read it, because I have also felt trapped at home during long summers with my family.
When the narrator calls the house "a cage," a survey of 200 readers found that 68% described the house as negative, which supports the reading I offer here.
answer: When the narrator calls the house "a cage," the metaphor links her marriage to her earlier imprisonment, which deepens the story's argument about freedom.

prompt: A student quotes from page 24 of a book by Dana Smith. Which in-text citation is correct in MLA style?
choices: (Smith 24)
(Smith 2019)
(Dana Smith 24)
answer: (Smith 24)

prompt: Two students are co-authoring a research paper in a shared online document and disagree about a paragraph. Which approach best fits collaborative writing practice?
choices: Use the document's comment and version history features to name the disagreement, decide who owns the revision, and set a deadline for the change.
One student quietly deletes the other's paragraph late at night and hopes the other student will not notice the change before the due date.
Both students keep two separate copies of the paper on their own computers and paste their parts together on the night before it is due.
Both students rewrite the whole paper together on a video call, working at the same time and typing into the same document at once.
answer: Use the document's comment and version history features to name the disagreement, decide who owns the revision, and set a deadline for the change.

prompt: A writer argues: "Either we ban all phones on campus, or students will never learn anything." What is the main flaw in this reasoning?
choices: It presents only two choices when more options exist.
It attacks the person instead of the argument.
It appeals to the writer's character instead of logic.
It uses a small sample to make a broad claim.
answer: It presents only two choices when more options exist.

prompt: Which action counts as plagiarism?
choices: The student paraphrases a source's unusual claim and gives no citation for it.
The student paraphrases a source's unusual claim and cites it properly.
The student states a fact that appears in most sources on the topic and gives no citation.
The student quotes a source with a citation but leaves out the page number.
answer: The student paraphrases a source's unusual claim and gives no citation for it.

prompt: A student is drafting a comparative essay on two novels, one set in a small farming town and one set in a large coastal city. Which sentence builds an original point out of the comparison instead of simply listing similarities or differences?
choices: Though the two novels use opposite settings, both show communities policing outsiders, suggesting that conformity pressures are social rather than geographical.
Both novels feature characters who feel like outsiders in their communities.
The first novel takes place in a farming town, while the second takes place in a large coastal city.
This essay will compare the settings and characters of the two novels to show how they are alike and different.
answer: Though the two novels use opposite settings, both show communities policing outsiders, suggesting that conformity pressures are social rather than geographical.

prompt: Marco is revising his draft. He realizes his third paragraph supports a point he no longer makes, so he cuts it and moves a stronger example earlier in the paper. What kind of revision is this?
choices: Re-seeing and rebuilding the draft's argument and structure
Proofreading for spelling and punctuation errors
Editing sentences to make them shorter
Changing the font and margins of the paper
answer: Re-seeing and rebuilding the draft's argument and structure

prompt: Mateo has four weeks to write an 8-page research paper. Which plan best shows good writing process management?
choices: He sets dates to finish his research, a first draft, and a revision, leaving time to revise.
He writes all eight pages the night before the paper is due.
He spends three weeks reading and writes the paper in one sitting.
He waits until he feels inspired and then writes the paper.
answer: He sets dates to finish his research, a first draft, and a revision, leaving time to revise.

prompt: Which thesis statement is focused, debatable, and specific?
choices: Community colleges should offer free evening childcare because it would raise graduation rates for student parents.
This paper is about community colleges and childcare.
Childcare is a very important topic for many people today.
Community colleges are good, and childcare is good too.
answer: Community colleges should offer free evening childcare because it would raise graduation rates for student parents.

prompt: During a peer review, a classmate writes: "Your second paragraph uses a study, but I'm not sure how the study proves your point." Which kind of feedback is this?
choices: Specific feedback that points to a place and names a problem to fix
A summary of the writer's whole paper
A grammar correction on sentence punctuation
General praise that does not help the writer
answer: Specific feedback that points to a place and names a problem to fix

prompt: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
choices: Many students struggle with time management; others have no trouble keeping up.
The study had three limitations; small sample size, short duration, and a narrow age range.
Although the data were inconclusive; the team published their findings.
The researchers repeated the experiment; because the results were unclear.
answer: Many students struggle with time management; others have no trouble keeping up.

prompt: A writer notices that she often writes run-on sentences in her papers. What is the best way to fix this pattern?
choices: She reviews her past papers to find run-ons, then checks each new draft for the same error.
She changes the topic of her next paper to avoid the problem.
She asks her roommate to write her next paper instead.
She ignores the pattern because it is not about her ideas.
answer: She reviews her past papers to find run-ons, then checks each new draft for the same error.

prompt: How many morphemes does the word "unhappiness" contain?
choices: 3 — un-, happy, and -ness
1 — it is a single word with no internal parts.
2 — un- and happiness
4 — un-, hap-, -py, and -ness
answer: 3 — un-, happy, and -ness

prompt: Which statement correctly describes the "copula deletion" (null copula) feature of African American English?
choices: The copula can be omitted in certain present-tense environments, as in "She nice," but not in all syntactic positions.
The copula can be omitted freely in any tense and any clause type.
The copula is never omitted; AAE simply pronounces it more softly.
The copula is omitted only in past-tense sentences, as in "She tired yesterday."
answer: The copula can be omitted in certain present-tense environments, as in "She nice," but not in all syntactic positions.

prompt: Robin Lakoff's early work on "women's language" argued that women's speech in American English is marked by a cluster of features. Which of these did she list as characteristic of that register?
choices: Tag questions and question intonation on declarative statements.
Frequent interruption of other speakers and control of conversational topics.
Use of imperatives and profanity to establish authority.
Wider vowel spaces and higher fundamental frequency in all contexts.
answer: Tag questions and question intonation on declarative statements.

prompt: Which phrase structure best analyzes the passive sentence "The problem was solved yesterday"?
choices: A verb phrase containing a verb and an adverb phrase, with "The problem" as the sentence's subject noun phrase.
A verb phrase containing a verb and a direct object noun phrase, with "yesterday" as the subject.
A verb phrase containing two verbs, with "The problem" as an adverb phrase.
A verb phrase containing a verb and an adverb phrase, with "The problem" as a complement of the verb.
answer: A verb phrase containing a verb and an adverb phrase, with "The problem" as the sentence's subject noun phrase.

prompt: T. S. Eliot argued that a writer should express emotion not by naming it directly but by finding a set of objects or situations that evokes it. What did Eliot call this?
choices: The objective correlative.
The pathetic fallacy.
Negative capability.
The willing suspension of disbelief.
answer: The objective correlative.

prompt: You are writing steps for using a centrifuge in a campus lab. Which instruction is written most clearly and safely?
choices: Close the lid before you start the machine. The centrifuge will not run with the lid open.
Before operating the machine, ensure that the lid is closed, as the unit will not function otherwise.
The lid must be closed prior to operation; failure to do so will result in the machine not running.
Ensure the centrifuge is ready to run by making sure the lid is fully closed first.
answer: Close the lid before you start the machine. The centrifuge will not run with the lid open.

prompt: A poet writes: "We paused before a house that seemed / A sinking of the ground." The sentence runs past the line break without a pause at the end of the first line. What is this technique called?
choices: Enjambment — a sentence or phrase that continues past the end of a line.
Caesura — a pause placed in the middle of a line.
End-stopped — a line that ends with a full pause or punctuation.
Volta — a turn or shift in the poem's argument.
answer: Enjambment — a sentence or phrase that continues past the end of a line.

prompt: A TESOL teacher wants students to know not just the grammar of "Would you like...?" but also when it is polite to use it, with whom, and in which situations. What concept from applied linguistics does this lesson address?
choices: Communicative competence — knowing how to use forms appropriately in social context.
Contrastive analysis — comparing the learner's L1 grammar to English grammar.
Phonological awareness — hearing and manipulating individual speech sounds.
Syntax transfer — carrying L1 sentence patterns into L2 production.
answer: Communicative competence — knowing how to use forms appropriately in social context.

prompt: In an English class, the teacher plays a model exchange for the class to repeat in chorus, then has students run through substitution drills ('She is reading a book' → 'She is reading a newspaper' → 'He is reading a newspaper'), correcting any mispronunciation on the spot and never letting the class fall back on their first language. Which teaching method is this class using?
choices: The audiolingual method — pattern drills and imitation build correct language habits.
The grammar-translation method — learners memorize rules and translate written passages.
Total physical response — learners hear commands and respond with actions before they speak.
The Natural Approach — learners hear comprehensible input and speak only when they are ready.
answer: The audiolingual method — pattern drills and imitation build correct language habits.

prompt: A researcher wants to study how often the word "liberty" appears in speeches from 1780 to 1820 and how it is used in those contexts. Which digital humanities method fits this question best?
choices: Search the digitized speeches with a concordance tool that lists each use of "liberty" with the words around it.
Interview living historians about what liberty meant to people in the early republic.
Close-read one speech from 1800 and write about the single best sentence that uses liberty.
Trace the spelling changes of liberty in a printed dictionary from the same period.
answer: Search the digitized speeches with a concordance tool that lists each use of "liberty" with the words around it.

prompt: A language has only a handful of elderly speakers left, and children are not learning it. Where does this language fall on the commonly used scale of language vitality?
choices: Severely or critically endangered — transmission to children has broken down.
Safe and stable — the language is still being passed to children normally.
Vulnerable — most children speak it, but only in limited settings.
Shifting — the language is expanding into new social domains.
answer: Severely or critically endangered — transmission to children has broken down.

prompt: A student is designing a one-page handout and wants the items on the page to look related to each other. Which design choice best uses alignment and proximity to group information?
choices: Set all three step headings flush left on the same margin, and place each explanation directly below its own heading.
Center every heading and explanation on the page so the page looks balanced from top to bottom.
Use a different font for every heading so that readers can tell the sections apart at a glance.
Add a box around every individual item on the page so nothing looks like it floats loose.
answer: Set all three step headings flush left on the same margin, and place each explanation directly below its own heading.

prompt: A city office sends residents this notice: "Pursuant to Ordinance 112-B, it is required that all residential refuse receptacles be situated at the curb prior to 6:00 a.m. on the designated collection day; receptacles shall be removed from the thoroughfare no later than 7:00 p.m. on the same date." A professional editor rewrites it in plain language. Which revision is best?
choices: Put your trash can at the curb before 6 a.m. on pickup day. Take it back in by 7 p.m. that day.
Refuse receptacles must be situated curbside before 6:00 a.m. on the designated collection day and removed no later than 7:00 p.m.
Because of Ordinance 112-B, residents are required to place their waste containers at the curb prior to 6:00 a.m. and remove them after 7:00 p.m.
Trash cans go at the curb early on collection day and should be brought back in that evening as the ordinance requires.
answer: Put your trash can at the curb before 6 a.m. on pickup day. Take it back in by 7 p.m. that day.

prompt: A novel includes the sentence: "What a fool she had been to think he would call. The whole evening wasted." The narration stays in third person, but the phrasing and judgments are clearly the character's own. What technique is this?
choices: Free indirect discourse — third-person narration that carries a character's voice and thoughts.
Stream of consciousness — a continuous, unedited flow of a character's raw thoughts.
Dramatic monologue — a speech delivered by a character to a silent listener.
Objective correlative — a set of objects that evoke a particular emotion.
answer: Free indirect discourse — third-person narration that carries a character's voice and thoughts.

prompt: The words "pin" and "bin" are a minimal pair in English: they differ in meaning and in exactly one sound. Which statement best explains what makes them a minimal pair?
choices: The sounds [p] and [b] contrast in English because substituting one for the other changes the word's meaning.
The sounds [p] and [b] are allophones of one phoneme because they never distinguish words.
The words form a minimal pair because each contains exactly one morpheme.
The words form a minimal pair because their consonants share the same place of articulation.
answer: The sounds [p] and [b] contrast in English because substituting one for the other changes the word's meaning.

prompt: A student argues: (1) 'This university should require a first-year writing course.' (2) 'Students who take such a course write better research papers.' (3) 'A requirement is justified when it measurably improves a skill the university has promised to develop.' In Toulmin's layout of an argument, what role does sentence (3) play?
choices: It is the warrant — the general principle that licenses the step from the grounds to the claim.
It is the grounds — the specific evidence offered in support of the claim.
It is the backing — extra support given for a warrant that has itself been challenged.
It is the qualifier — a word or phrase that limits how strongly the claim is asserted.
answer: It is the warrant — the general principle that licenses the step from the grounds to the claim.

prompt: A speaker of a nonstandard dialect is praised by her neighbors for sounding "down-to-earth" and "real," while she is passed over for a corporate job because her speech is judged "unprofessional." These two attitudes reflect which pair of concepts?
choices: Covert prestige (group solidarity) and overt prestige (status of the standard variety).
Overt prestige (group solidarity) and covert prestige (status of the standard variety).
Language planning and language policy.
First language acquisition and second language acquisition.
answer: Covert prestige (group solidarity) and overt prestige (status of the standard variety).

prompt: In African American English, what does the sentence "He be working late" mean?
choices: He works late on a regular basis.
He is working late right now.
He will probably work late tonight.
He was working late yesterday.
answer: He works late on a regular basis.

prompt: A creative nonfiction writer structures her entire essay about grief as a set of hospital discharge instructions. What is this kind of essay called?
choices: A hermit crab essay — an essay that borrows an existing form or structure.
A braided essay — an essay that weaves together several narrative threads.
A lyric essay — an essay built from fragments and poetic imagery.
A reported essay — an essay based entirely on interviews and research.
answer: A hermit crab essay — an essay that borrows an existing form or structure.

prompt: A student is turning a broad interest into a research project. Which research question is best for a short humanities paper?
choices: How do the courtroom scenes in three 1930s novels use interruptions in dialogue to mark social rank?
What is the true meaning of justice in literature?
How has dialogue in novels changed over time?
What do courtroom scenes in novels mean?
answer: How do the courtroom scenes in three 1930s novels use interruptions in dialogue to mark social rank?

prompt: A writer opens an argument about campus policy by citing her own ten years of teaching experience and the trust she has built with students. Which appeal is she primarily using?
choices: Ethos — establishing her credibility and good character.
Pathos — arousing the audience's emotions.
Logos — building a chain of logical evidence.
Kairos — seizing the right moment for the argument.
answer: Ethos — establishing her credibility and good character.

prompt: A professional writer is preparing a proposal for a company that has cut its budget and wants to save money this year. Which sentence best shows the writer has adapted the document to this audience and purpose?
choices: This plan cuts cleaning costs by 15% in the first year, paying for itself within eight months.
This plan draws on best practices in facility management that leading firms have adopted worldwide.
This plan reflects our team's long experience in workplace consulting and our commitment to excellence.
This plan proposes several changes to how cleaning services are handled at your facility.
answer: This plan cuts cleaning costs by 15% in the first year, paying for itself within eight months.

prompt: What does "place-based writing" mean in nature and environmental writing?
choices: Writing that roots the essay in a specific, described landscape rather than only abstract argument
Writing that argues a policy position about protecting the natural environment
Writing that uses only first-person reflection instead of reporting or research
Writing that describes every plant and animal present in a location in careful detail
answer: Writing that roots the essay in a specific, described landscape rather than only abstract argument

prompt: Six months into thesis drafting, you realize your evidence has shifted your central claim away from what you proposed. What is the best response?
choices: Revise the framing of the project — introduction, chapter openings, conclusion — to reflect the claim your evidence actually supports, and discuss the shift with your advisor.
Force the argument back toward the original claim so the finished thesis matches what you promised the committee.
Leave the original claim in the introduction and let the body chapters argue the new claim, so both versions appear in the record.
Restart the project from the beginning, since a shift in claim invalidates the work done so far.
answer: Revise the framing of the project — introduction, chapter openings, conclusion — to reflect the claim your evidence actually supports, and discuss the shift with your advisor.

prompt: Lila's essay discusses Kate Chopin's The Awakening. She writes one sentence noting that Judith Butler describes gender as something performed through repeated acts, then spends three paragraphs summarizing Butler's book Gender Trouble before turning to two sentences about Chopin's novel. What is the main weakness in her use of theory?
choices: She restates the theorist's argument instead of using it to build a new reading of the novel.
She puts the theory in the body of the essay instead of in a footnote or an appendix.
She applies a theory of performance to a novel instead of to a play or a film.
She gives the theory before the textual evidence, when theory should always come last.
answer: She restates the theorist's argument instead of using it to build a new reading of the novel.

prompt: At your thesis defense, an examiner asks, "If you had two more years to continue this project, what would you do next?" What is the strongest response?
choices: Identify a specific limitation or unanswered question in the current work and describe a concrete next study, method, or body of evidence that would address it.
Say that the project is complete and that there is nothing further to investigate.
Say that you would change your central claim to match the examiner's stated view of the material.
Say that you would expand each chapter with additional examples so the thesis is more comprehensive.
answer: Identify a specific limitation or unanswered question in the current work and describe a concrete next study, method, or body of evidence that would address it.

prompt: In technical editing, what does "enforcing house style" mean?
choices: Making sure a document follows the organization's chosen rules for spelling, capitalization, formatting, and terminology
Making sure every sentence in the document has a unique structure to keep the reader interested
Making sure the writer's personal voice and tone come through consistently
Making sure the document uses only the most recent edition of every cited source
answer: Making sure a document follows the organization's chosen rules for spelling, capitalization, formatting, and terminology

prompt: What is the main difference between developmental editing and copyediting?
choices: Developmental editing addresses structure, argument, and organization; copyediting addresses grammar, usage, and consistency at the sentence level
Developmental editing fixes grammar and spelling; copyediting rewrites the whole manuscript's structure
Developmental editing prepares the file for printing; copyediting designs the book's cover and layout
Developmental editing negotiates the author's contract; copyediting verifies the accuracy of technical facts
answer: Developmental editing addresses structure, argument, and organization; copyediting addresses grammar, usage, and consistency at the sentence level

prompt: What is "textual criticism," and what problem does it address?
choices: The practice of comparing versions of a text to reconstruct its original or most authoritative form, since manuscripts and early printed books often contain errors or variants
The practice of judging whether a literary work is good or bad based on its style
The practice of translating an old text into modern language for general readers
The practice of writing reviews of scholarly editions for academic journals
answer: The practice of comparing versions of a text to reconstruct its original or most authoritative form, since manuscripts and early printed books often contain errors or variants

prompt: Which pairing of a rhetorical thinker and a central idea is correct?
choices: Kenneth Burke — persuasion works through identification with the audience.
Chaïm Perelman — the enthymeme is the central form of rhetorical proof.
Aristotle — rhetoric is best understood as the art of identification.
Quintilian — persuasion depends on a universal audience of all rational listeners.
answer: Kenneth Burke — persuasion works through identification with the audience.

prompt: Sanskrit has pitár- 'father' and Latin has pater, while English has father (and Gothic had fadar). Which statement explains the first consonant of the English word?
choices: Germanic changed Proto-Indo-European *p to *f, one of the shifts called Grimm's Law.
Germanic changed Proto-Indo-European *b to *p, one of the shifts called Grimm's Law.
Latin and Sanskrit changed an older *f to *p, while Germanic kept the older sound.
English borrowed the word from Latin, which is why the sounds do not match.
answer: Germanic changed Proto-Indo-European *p to *f, one of the shifts called Grimm's Law.

prompt: In a persuasive proposal, what is the function of the "statement of need" or problem section?
choices: To establish the specific problem or gap the project addresses and why it matters to the audience
To list the qualifications and past successes of the person or team writing the proposal
To describe in detail every step of the project's implementation timeline
To summarize the proposal's budget and justify each line item
answer: To establish the specific problem or gap the project addresses and why it matters to the audience

prompt: In computational linguistics, researchers normalize word forms so that inflected variants of a word are grouped together. Two common tools do this in different ways. Which description correctly contrasts them?
choices: A stemmer applies chopping rules that can leave non-words such as 'poni', while a lemmatizer uses a dictionary to return a real form such as 'pony'.
A lemmatizer applies chopping rules that can leave non-words such as 'poni', while a stemmer uses a dictionary to return a real form such as 'pony'.
Both tools apply chopping rules and both can leave non-words such as 'poni', but the lemmatizer runs faster on large texts.
Both tools consult a dictionary and both return only real words such as 'pony', but the stemmer runs faster on large texts.
answer: A stemmer applies chopping rules that can leave non-words such as 'poni', while a lemmatizer uses a dictionary to return a real form such as 'pony'.

prompt: What is a "codex," and why does it matter in the history of the book?
choices: A book with pages bound along one side, which replaced the scroll and changed how readers navigated texts
A collection of laws written on stone tablets in the ancient world
A secret code used by printers to protect their work from piracy
A catalog listing every book held in a medieval library
answer: A book with pages bound along one side, which replaced the scroll and changed how readers navigated texts

prompt: In the phrase "the student of physics with long hair", which analysis does X-bar theory give?
choices: "Of physics" is the complement of student, and "with long hair" is an adjunct.
"Of physics" is an adjunct of student, and "with long hair" is the complement.
Both phrases are complements of the noun student.
Both phrases are specifiers of the noun student.
answer: "Of physics" is the complement of student, and "with long hair" is an adjunct.

prompt: At dinner, Ana asks, "Is there any more bread?" Ben answers, "The corner shop is open until nine." What is Ben doing with his reply?
choices: Flouting the maxim of relevance so that Ana infers there is no bread but some can be bought.
Flouting the maxim of quantity by giving Ana more information than she asked for.
Flouting the maxim of manner by using a longer sentence than the situation needs.
Violating the maxim of quality, since the shop's hours have nothing to do with the question.
answer: Flouting the maxim of relevance so that Ana infers there is no bread but some can be bought.

prompt: In the Old English sentence "Se cyning lufode þone bisceop" ('The king loved the bishop'), which word form shows that 'bisceop' is the object of the verb?
choices: þone, the accusative form of the article
se, the nominative form of the article before cyning
-ode, the past tense ending on the verb lufode
the place of bisceop after the verb lufode
answer: þone, the accusative form of the article

prompt: What is "high-context" versus "low-context" communication, and why does it matter in intercultural professional writing?
choices: High-context communication relies heavily on shared background and indirect cues; low-context communication states meanings explicitly, so writers may need to adjust directness for their audience
High-context communication uses formal titles; low-context communication uses first names, which matters for choosing a greeting
High-context communication is spoken; low-context communication is written, which matters for choosing a channel
High-context communication uses many visuals; low-context communication uses mostly text, which matters for document design
answer: High-context communication relies heavily on shared background and indirect cues; low-context communication states meanings explicitly, so writers may need to adjust directness for their audience

prompt: Nia designs the language Vela. In Vela the noun never changes form, but each verb carries one prefix for the subject and another for the object, as in mu-ka-sen 'she saw me'. Which statement about this design is correct?
choices: The design is natural: real languages such as Swahili mark both subject and object on the verb.
The design is unnatural: real languages mark the subject on the verb but never the object.
The design is unnatural: a language must mark case on nouns before it can mark agreement on the verb.
The design is unnatural: only languages with completely free word order mark the object on the verb.
answer: The design is natural: real languages such as Swahili mark both subject and object on the verb.

prompt: In W. W. Greg's influential account of copy-text editing, what does the distinction between "substantives" and "accidentals" separate?
choices: Substantives are the significant words and word-forms of a text; accidentals are presentation features such as spelling, punctuation, capitalization, and italics.
Substantives are readings supported by external documentary evidence; accidentals are readings inferred from the internal context alone.
Substantives are changes made with the author's approval; accidentals are changes introduced without authorization by a compositor.
