These interviews hint that perhaps some students might possibly prefer online feedback sometimes.
Students everywhere prefer online feedback, and these interviews confirm what everyone already knows.
answer: These interviews suggest that, among the students in this study, online feedback was often preferred.

prompt: A student teacher's mentor asks: "Why did you put the paragraph-revision exercise before the sentence-level editing exercise in today's lesson?" Which response best reflects sound teaching practicum reasoning?
choices: Revising ideas and organization first prevents students from polishing sentences they will later delete or rewrite entirely
Sentence-level editing is harder, so students should build confidence with paragraph work first
Most textbooks recommend teaching revision and editing in that order
The school's curriculum requires paragraph work to be covered before sentence work in every unit
answer: Revising ideas and organization first prevents students from polishing sentences they will later delete or rewrite entirely

prompt: A language has the sounds [k] and [x]. [k] appears at the start of words and after a nasal, as in [kaɾ], [kot], and [aŋka]. [x] appears only between a vowel and a consonant, as in [axta]. No two words differ in meaning only because one has [k] and the other has [x]. Which analysis fits the data?
choices: They are allophones of a single phoneme, with [x] the allophone between a vowel and a consonant and /k/ a reasonable underlying form, since [k] occurs in more environments.
They are allophones of a single phoneme, with /x/ as the underlying form, because the more restricted allophone is always the underlying one.
They are two separate phonemes, because they are different sounds pronounced in different ways.
They are in free variation, because speakers of the language pronounce either one freely in any position.
answer: They are allophones of a single phoneme, with [x] the allophone between a vowel and a consonant and /k/ a reasonable underlying form, since [k] occurs in more environments.

prompt: A digital humanities team builds an interactive map of every place mentioned in 500 Victorian novels, with color-coded dots for real and fictional locations. What does this project BEST demonstrate about digital humanities methods?
choices: Computational tools let scholars see large-scale patterns across many texts that would be impossible to detect by reading alone
Digital tools replace the need for close reading once a text collection is large enough
Interactive maps are the only form of digital humanities scholarship that counts as rigorous
Building a map proves that the places mentioned in novels correspond to real historical locations
answer: Computational tools let scholars see large-scale patterns across many texts that would be impossible to detect by reading alone

prompt: A multimedia news story lets readers click through an interactive map, play recorded interviews, and scroll through a photo essay alongside the written article. What core principle of multimedia composition does this design serve?
choices: Each element should do the communicative work it is best suited for, so no single medium carries information another could express better
All elements should repeat the same information in different formats so readers receive the message multiple times
The written article should contain all the story's key facts, with other elements serving only as decoration
The longest element should appear first so readers spend the most time with the richest content
answer: Each element should do the communicative work it is best suited for, so no single medium carries information another could express better

prompt: Readers show an unexpected slowdown on the word 'fell' in the sentence 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' What does this slowdown show about how people parse sentences?
choices: They had first taken 'raced' as the main verb, and 'fell' forced them to reanalyze the sentence.
They slowed because 'fell' is a rarer word and takes longer to recognize than 'raced' and 'barn'.
They slowed because racing horses past barns is an odd event that is hard to picture and imagine.
They slowed because the sentence breaks a rule of grammar by having two verbs with no conjunction.
answer: They had first taken 'raced' as the main verb, and 'fell' forced them to reanalyze the sentence.

prompt: In Chicago notes-and-bibliography style, a student quotes from page 77 of Samuel Ortiz's book Writing and Power (Chicago: Lakeview Press, 2018). What does the first footnote entry for this quotation look like?
choices: 1. Samuel Ortiz, Writing and Power (Chicago: Lakeview Press, 2018), 77.
1. Ortiz, Samuel. Writing and Power. Chicago: Lakeview Press, 2018, 77.
1. Samuel Ortiz, Writing and Power (Chicago: Lakeview Press, 2018).
1. Samuel Ortiz, 'Writing and Power' (Chicago: Lakeview Press, 2018), 77.
answer: 1. Samuel Ortiz, Writing and Power (Chicago: Lakeview Press, 2018), 77.

prompt: In the sixteenth century, Peter Ramus reorganized the traditional system of rhetoric. What was the main change he made?
choices: He assigned invention and arrangement to dialectic, leaving rhetoric to cover style and delivery alone.
He placed memory at the center of rhetoric, arguing that all good invention begins with what the speaker remembers.
He divided speeches into judicial, deliberative, and epideictic kinds, a set of categories earlier writers had lacked.
He replaced the study of style with a theory of the three appeals: the speaker's character, emotion, and argument.
answer: He assigned invention and arrangement to dialectic, leaving rhetoric to cover style and delivery alone.

prompt: In a self-paced reading experiment, each participant reads 24 critical sentences, 12 in the experimental condition and 12 in the control condition. The items are split across lists so that each critical sentence appears in each condition for a different group of participants. Why is this done?
choices: So that the effect cannot be caused by the particular sentences, since each sentence appears in both conditions across the groups.
So that participants cannot guess which sentences are experimental, since all sentences in a list have the same length.
So that each participant reads fewer sentences and therefore stays alert from the beginning to the end.
So that the same participants can run through the experiment twice without recognizing any of the sentences.
answer: So that the effect cannot be caused by the particular sentences, since each sentence appears in both conditions across the groups.

prompt: A report draft has a clear main claim, but its sections are jumbled and one section offers no evidence at all. Which kind of editing does it need first?
choices: Substantive editing, which reorganizes sections and fills gaps in support.
Copyediting, which corrects grammar, punctuation, and word choice throughout.
Proofreading, which catches typos, spacing, and formatting errors on the page.
Style editing, which makes terms and references match a guide such as APA.
answer: Substantive editing, which reorganizes sections and fills gaps in support.

prompt: A team has transcribed 500 hours of recorded community oral histories and wants researchers to search every word. What is the key next step in building a text-mining workflow?
choices: Convert the transcripts into clean, consistently formatted digital text that software can process.
Print the transcripts and file them in the archive reading room.
Ask each narrator to summarize their interview in a short letter.
Select background music for the audio clips on the website.
answer: Convert the transcripts into clean, consistently formatted digital text that software can process.

prompt: Shoppers on a website often leave before buying. The team wants to watch real users try to place an order and hear what confuses them as they go. Which method fits this goal best?
choices: A moderated usability test in which users complete a purchase while thinking aloud.
A survey asking users to rate how attractive the checkout page looks to them.
A focus group in which users discuss their general online shopping habits.
An analysis of how long each page takes to load on average.
answer: A moderated usability test in which users complete a purchase while thinking aloud.

prompt: While reading a French article on modern fiction for her literature review, a student meets the sentence 'Cette approche est actuellement la plus répandue.' What does the word 'actuellement' mean in this sentence?
choices: currently
actually
actively
in fact
answer: currently

prompt: A technical report includes a 25-row table of raw measurements, but most readers only need the three key findings. Which revision best applies the principle of visual emphasis?
choices: Move the three key findings into a highlighted panel near the top and place the full table later.
Set the table in a smaller type size so all 25 rows fit on one page.
Bold every row of the table so that no measurement is missed.
Convert the table into running prose so it flows like the rest of the report.
answer: Move the three key findings into a highlighted panel near the top and place the full table later.

prompt: In one town, a linguist finds that speakers in their twenties use a certain vowel variant far more often than speakers in their seventies, though both groups grew up in the same town. What does this pattern most likely show?
choices: A change in progress in the community, with the younger speakers at the leading end of it.
A normal effect of aging, since people gradually drop sounds and variants as they grow older.
A stable regional difference, since the two groups must have learned their speech in different places.
An effect of being recorded, since younger speakers always relax their speech more than older speakers.
answer: A change in progress in the community, with the younger speakers at the leading end of it.

prompt: A master's student has found one important 2010 article that later scholars in her field keep building on, and she needs to see how the discussion has moved since it appeared. Which search strategy will most directly show her the later work that responds to that article?
choices: Looking the article up in a citation database and reading the later works that cite it.
Searching the library catalog for books whose titles repeat the words in the 2010 article's title.
Typing the article's keywords into a general web search engine and reading the highest-ranked results.
Reading the works listed in the 2010 article's own reference list to see what research came before it.
answer: Looking the article up in a citation database and reading the later works that cite it.

prompt: A new teaching assistant reads a student essay whose argument is thin and undeveloped and which also contains comma splices and misspellings. She has time to write only one substantial comment on the paper. What should she address?
choices: The argument and its evidence, since higher-order concerns come before sentence-level problems.
The comma splices, since cleaner sentences make it easier for a reader to follow the student's thinking.
The misspellings, since these are the fastest problems for the student to fix and act on right away.
Every problem in one long list, since the student learns most from a complete set of corrections.
answer: The argument and its evidence, since higher-order concerns come before sentence-level problems.

prompt: After the defense, a committee member says the thesis's two case studies support the claim about rural clinics but not the sweeping claim about all rural health care. What is the best final revision?
choices: Revise the conclusion so the claim is limited to the kind of rural clinics the case studies actually represent.
Add a paragraph explaining why the two case studies stand for all rural health care.
Delete the conclusion and end the thesis with the last case study.
Switch to the non-thesis capstone option to avoid the limitation.
answer: Revise the conclusion so the claim is limited to the kind of rural clinics the case studies actually represent.

prompt: A microbiologist is writing a methods section for a specialist journal. Which choice best fits this audience?
choices: Give exact parameters, such as "incubated at 37 °C for 24 hours," so other labs can repeat the work.
Replace technical terms with everyday comparisons so that any reader can follow the section.
Omit exact temperatures and times, since specialists already know the standard values.
Define basic terms such as "bacteria" and "culture" for readers new to the field.
answer: Give exact parameters, such as "incubated at 37 °C for 24 hours," so other labs can repeat the work.

prompt: In the sentence 'Leah handed the keys to Marcus,' which set of thematic roles is correct?
choices: Leah is the agent, the keys are the theme, and Marcus is the goal.
Leah is the theme, the keys are the patient, and Marcus is the agent.
Leah is the agent, the keys are the goal, and Marcus is the theme.
Leah is the goal, the keys are the theme, and Marcus is the patient.
answer: Leah is the agent, the keys are the theme, and Marcus is the goal.

prompt: A researcher wants to find which verbs English speakers most strongly prefer with the noun 'evidence' — the words that collocate with it. Which tool and measure best answer this question?
choices: A concordance search in a large corpus, with a measure of how strongly the two words attract each other beyond chance.
A word frequency list from a large corpus, which ranks every word in the language by how often it occurs.
A general web search for 'evidence,' counting how many pages use the noun at least once in their text.
A thesaurus entry for 'evidence,' which lists the words that mean roughly the same thing as the noun.
answer: A concordance search in a large corpus, with a measure of how strongly the two words attract each other beyond chance.

prompt: A linguist searches a large corpus of casual conversation and finds no examples of a certain type of sentence, so she concludes that the sentence type is ungrammatical in the language. What is the main problem with her conclusion?
choices: A perfectly grammatical form can simply be missing from a corpus, so its absence there proves nothing about grammaticality.
Corpus data cannot settle questions of grammaticality at all, since corpora only record what speakers happen to have said.
Grammaticality can be established only by comparing the language with its older, historically related languages.
Only written texts can show grammaticality, since spoken data is full of slips, hesitations, and errors.
answer: A perfectly grammatical form can simply be missing from a corpus, so its absence there proves nothing about grammaticality.

prompt: Ann says to a colleague, 'Could you cover my Friday shift?' Bea answers, 'Um... well... I'd really like to, but I'm up against a deadline.' In conversation analysis, what does Bea's turn show?
choices: A dispreferred second pair part, signaled by the delay and hedging before the refusal.
A repair initiation, in which Bea signals that she did not hear or understand Ann's request.
A topic shift, in which Bea moves the conversation away from Ann's request to her own work.
A first pair part, in which Bea opens a new sequence with a request of her own.
answer: A dispreferred second pair part, signaled by the delay and hedging before the refusal.

prompt: A computational model of sentence processing predicts reading times with 95% accuracy on the researcher's test items. However, the model predicts the longest reading times at the ends of sentences, while human readers slow down at the beginnings. What should the researcher conclude?
choices: High overall accuracy is not enough; the model fails to reproduce the human pattern and should be revised and re-evaluated against the target behavioral data.
The model is successful, because 95% accuracy is above the threshold that the field accepts for publication.
The human reading-time data must be unreliable and should be set aside in favor of the model's own predictions.
The model should be retrained on more sentences from the same corpus until its accuracy reaches 100%.
answer: High overall accuracy is not enough; the model fails to reproduce the human pattern and should be revised and re-evaluated against the target behavioral data.

prompt: Your university is reviewing your writing center, and the director of another unit asks how you know the center helps students rather than simply serving many of them. Which evidence best addresses that question for a writing center?
choices: Session records showing that, over repeated appointments, the same students' drafts improve on specific target skills noted by tutors
A semester-end tally showing the center logged more appointments than any other tutoring unit on campus
Positive comments collected in an optional comment box at the center's front desk
A report listing how many tutors completed the center's training program during the year
answer: Session records showing that, over repeated appointments, the same students' drafts improve on specific target skills noted by tutors

prompt: Which research question is best designed for a single doctoral dissertation?
choices: How do second-year doctoral students at one U.S. university describe the feedback they receive on their dissertation drafts?
What is the single most effective way to give feedback on doctoral dissertation writing?
Why has feedback on doctoral writing failed at universities throughout the history of graduate study?
Does every kind of feedback improve dissertation writing for every doctoral student in every program?
answer: How do second-year doctoral students at one U.S. university describe the feedback they receive on their dissertation drafts?

prompt: You are writing a 1,200-word piece for a general magazine about research in your field. Which lead best serves that audience?
choices: A brief concrete scene of a person facing the problem your research addresses, told in plain language
A two-sentence summary of your study's literature review, so readers understand where the research began
A statement of your research question followed by a note on how your findings extend current theory
A definition of your field's key technical term, since readers need the concept before they can see its importance
answer: A brief concrete scene of a person facing the problem your research addresses, told in plain language

prompt: A doctoral student who reads in a second language takes two hours to read one assigned article from the first page to the last, looking up every unfamiliar word, and she arrives at the seminar with no notes. What is the best advice for graduate-level reading?
choices: Match the strategy to the goal: preview each article's argument and structure first, then read closely only the sections needed for the seminar question.
Read each article slowly from beginning to end and look up every unfamiliar word so that vocabulary grows steadily over the term.
Memorize the main articles in full so that every claim can be quoted word for word in later writing of her own.
Read only the first and last pages of every article, since the rest of the text simply repeats the claims made there.
answer: Match the strategy to the goal: preview each article's argument and structure first, then read closely only the sections needed for the seminar question.

prompt: You are revising your dissertation's introduction and conclusion months after the last chapters were written, and you notice that some of your key terms now mean something slightly different in your analysis than they did in your first draft. What is the strongest way to handle this?
choices: Restate and sharpen the definitions once in the introduction, then check each chapter's key passages against those definitions
Leave the introduction exactly as first written, since changing it would mean admitting your argument shifted
Add a footnote in the conclusion explaining that your terminology was inconsistent during drafting
Rely on your readers to see from the analyses alone how the terms were ultimately used
answer: Restate and sharpen the definitions once in the introduction, then check each chapter's key passages against those definitions

prompt: A digital humanities project will analyze the language of 50,000 historical newspaper pages scanned from microfilm. Before any analysis begins, which step is most important for the validity of the results?
choices: Checking how accurately the scanning software recognized the text, since errors may differ across years and page conditions
Choosing the earliest available newspaper issues so that the dataset covers the longest possible time span
Deleting the most frequent words from the corpus so that rarer words will be easier to count
Picking the analysis software with the largest user community, since popularity signals reliable output
answer: Checking how accurately the scanning software recognized the text, since errors may differ across years and page conditions

prompt: A doctoral student reads steadily for two years and writes only when she feels she has read everything. By the end of her third year she has no chapters drafted. What is the best way to structure a multi-year project?
choices: Set regular writing goals and dated milestones across the whole timeline, treating drafting and revising as ongoing work alongside reading and data collection.
Wait for a semester with no other duties and write the entire dissertation in one intensive block of time.
Finish all reading and data collection first, and begin writing only when the last source has been consulted.
Write only when new ideas arrive, since a fixed schedule produces thin and mechanical prose.
answer: Set regular writing goals and dated milestones across the whole timeline, treating drafting and revising as ongoing work alongside reading and data collection.

prompt: A historian of rhetoric studies the rhetorical education of women in nineteenth-century America but finds very few texts written by women in the archive. What is the strongest historiographical response?
choices: Treat the archive's silence as a fact to be explained, widen the search to letters, school records, and other institutional sources, and discuss how the archive's makeup shapes the story that can be told.
Conclude that women received no rhetorical education in the nineteenth century, since the archive holds no evidence of it.
Fill the gaps by assuming women's education resembled men's education and writing the missing sections by analogy.
Rely only on the printed texts that survive, since a source that is not in the archive cannot count as historical evidence.
answer: Treat the archive's silence as a fact to be explained, widen the search to letters, school records, and other institutional sources, and discuss how the archive's makeup shapes the story that can be told.

prompt: A linguist and an education researcher plan a joint study of classroom talk. The linguist wants a controlled experiment on recorded speech; the education researcher wants a year of observation in one classroom. What should the team do first?
choices: Discuss what each approach assumes about knowledge and evidence, and decide how the two designs will relate to each other within one study.
Let each researcher run a separate study and combine the two sets of findings in a single paragraph at the end.
Choose whichever method is cheaper and faster so that the team can collect data and publish within a year.
Have the linguist design both studies, since experimental methods produce more objective evidence than observation.
answer: Discuss what each approach assumes about knowledge and evidence, and decide how the two designs will relate to each other within one study.

prompt: You are preparing materials for a tenure-track position at a small liberal arts college that emphasizes undergraduate teaching. Which teaching statement best fits that institution?
choices: A discussion of how you teach introductory courses to students from many majors, with concrete examples and evidence of their learning
A statement centered on how your graduate seminars train students to produce publishable research in your specialty
A list of the courses you hope to teach someday, each with a one-line description of its main readings
A summary of your dissertation research, ending with a note that you are happy to teach whatever is needed
answer: A discussion of how you teach introductory courses to students from many majors, with concrete examples and evidence of their learning

prompt: Three doctoral students collaborate on a study. Student A designed the study and collected the data, Student B ran the analysis, and Student C wrote the first draft of the article. All three want to be listed first author. What is the most responsible way to handle authorship?
choices: Agree on authorship criteria before submission, base credit on each person's contribution to the whole project, and record the decision where all three can see it.
Give first authorship to whoever submits the article to the journal first, since submission is the most visible contribution.
List all three names as first authors so that no one's feelings are hurt by a lower position on the paper.
Give first authorship to the student with the most publications so far, since that makes acceptance more likely.
answer: Agree on authorship criteria before submission, base credit on each person's contribution to the whole project, and record the decision where all three can see it.

prompt: A graduate student's grant budget requests $6,000 for transcription on a project that includes 40 interviews. A reviewer notes that the budget gives no explanation of this cost. What is the best fix?
choices: Add a budget justification that shows how the amount was calculated and why the expense is necessary for the project.
Move the transcription costs into the indirect cost category so that reviewers will not have to examine them.
Delete the item and plan to do the transcription work unpaid after the grant period has ended.
Increase the requested amount so that reviewers will assume the cost has been carefully supported.
answer: Add a budget justification that shows how the amount was calculated and why the expense is necessary for the project.

prompt: As writing program administrator, you learn that adjunct instructors across your first-year writing sections are giving very different grades on the same assignment: some fail essays that others would grade as strong. What is the best first step?
choices: Hold a norming session where all instructors score the same sample essays and discuss where their judgments diverge
Email instructors the assignment rubric and remind them to apply it consistently when grading
Drop the assignment from the shared syllabus so that grading differences cannot affect course grades
Average the grades an essay receives from two instructors before returning it to the student
answer: Hold a norming session where all instructors score the same sample essays and discuss where their judgments diverge

prompt: A first-year doctoral student asks a professor what separates a dissertation from a very long seminar paper. Which answer best describes the doctoral standard?
choices: A dissertation must offer an original contribution to knowledge that other scholars in the field can use, question, or build on.
A dissertation must summarize everything that has been written on the topic so that readers have a complete overview of it.
A dissertation must prove a brand-new theory that replaces all the existing theories used in the field.
A dissertation must be at least 200 pages long and rely mainly on unpublished archival sources.
answer: A dissertation must offer an original contribution to knowledge that other scholars in the field can use, question, or build on.

prompt: Early in the research phase, a finding appears that does not fit the framework in your prospectus, and the more data you collect, the more it grows. What is the best course of action?
choices: Examine whether the exception reveals a limit or problem in the framework, and discuss it with your advisor before continuing
Remove the cases showing the exception so that the remaining data supports the framework in the prospectus
Keep collecting exactly the data described in the prospectus and leave the exception unmentioned in the dissertation
Switch to a completely new dissertation topic, since the prospectus can no longer be fulfilled
answer: Examine whether the exception reveals a limit or problem in the framework, and discuss it with your advisor before continuing

prompt: A department wants to know whether its revised curriculum actually improved what students can do. Which plan gives the strongest evidence?
choices: Comparing student work from before and after the revision, scored with the same rubric by scorers who do not know which year the work came from
Asking graduates one year after graduation whether they feel the curriculum prepared them well
Comparing the average grades students earned before and after the curriculum revision
Reviewing the new syllabi to confirm they cover the topics the revision was designed to add
answer: Comparing student work from before and after the revision, scored with the same rubric by scorers who do not know which year the work came from

prompt: A team is testing whether readers can follow a medication schedule printed in a grid. In one trial, a participant reads the grid aloud, finds the correct dose, and says, "This is fine, it makes sense." Later she gives the wrong dose amount. What does this trial show?
choices: What participants say about a document's clarity cannot be trusted on its own without watching what they actually do
Thinking aloud during a task should not be allowed, since speaking interferes with reading a table
One trial is too small to be used, since usability testing requires at least ten participants per session
Printed grids are a poor format for medication instructions and should be replaced by plain paragraphs
answer: What participants say about a document's clarity cannot be trusted on its own without watching what they actually do

prompt: A writing program director studies how her own tutors respond to student writers. She observes their sessions, interviews them, and also conducts their annual reviews. What most threatens the study's trustworthiness, and how should she address it?
choices: Her dual role may shape what the tutors say and do, so she should document her positionality, use peer debriefing or an audit trail, and build in checks such as member checking.
The sample is too large for qualitative work, so she should cut the study to two tutors so the data stay manageable.
Her familiarity with the program is a weakness, so she should avoid learning anything about the tutors beforehand.
Observation cannot be combined with interviews, so she should choose one method and drop the other entirely.
answer: Her dual role may shape what the tutors say and do, so she should document her positionality, use peer debriefing or an audit trail, and build in checks such as member checking.

prompt: A researcher compares 20 different word types across two conditions with 20 separate t-tests and reports only the three results with p < .05. What is the main problem, and what should the researcher do?
choices: Running many tests raises the chance of a false positive, so the researcher should adjust the significance level (for example, with a Bonferroni or false discovery rate correction) or pre-specify a few planned comparisons.
Running many tests lowers the chance of a false positive, so the researcher should keep all 20 tests and report every p-value below .05 as a finding.
The tests are too conservative, so the researcher should switch to 20 one-tailed tests to make the significant results easier to publish.
The sample is too small for 20 tests, so the researcher should simply add more word types without changing the analysis plan.
answer: Running many tests raises the chance of a false positive, so the researcher should adjust the significance level (for example, with a Bonferroni or false discovery rate correction) or pre-specify a few planned comparisons.

prompt: An assistant professor finished a dissertation on translation in the early modern period and wants later projects to add up to a recognizable research program rather than a set of one-off articles. Which approach best builds that program?
choices: Ask one recurring question across related projects, such as how translation shaped early modern authority, so each new project answers a piece of the same larger argument.
Write on whatever topic seems most likely to be accepted by a journal in the next year, keeping the projects loosely related in period.
Repeat the dissertation's exact question in every later project so the whole career stays within one narrow topic.
Pursue unrelated projects in several fields to signal independence from the dissertation advisor's area.
answer: Ask one recurring question across related projects, such as how translation shaped early modern authority, so each new project answers a piece of the same larger argument.

prompt: In a four-site, multi-year funded study, the sites begin collecting data in slightly different ways, and the results no longer line up. What should the project lead do first?
choices: Revisit the shared protocol, retrain all site teams together, and run calibration exercises until the sites record and score consistently.
Analyze each site's data separately and let readers combine the results themselves.
Stop the study and start over with a smaller single-site design.
Let each site keep its own method and note the differences as a limitation at publication.
answer: Revisit the shared protocol, retrain all site teams together, and run calibration exercises until the sites record and score consistently.

prompt: A content strategy lead at a national nonprofit notices that the organization's posts get many page views but almost no newsletter signups. What should the lead do first?
choices: Revisit the organization's goals and the audience's path, then redesign the calls to action and content formats so the work serves the signup goal.
Publish posts more often, since a higher volume of page views should eventually raise signups.
Switch to longer, more academic posts to impress readers with the organization's expertise.
Drop the signup goal from the plan, since page views alone are enough to show the content is working.
answer: Revisit the organization's goals and the audience's path, then redesign the calls to action and content formats so the work serves the signup goal.

prompt: A scholar is organizing a two-hour conference panel on digital methods in literary study. Which planning step best supports a session that holds together and uses its time well?
choices: Circulate the papers in advance, name a chair and a respondent who can link the talks, and reserve about a third of the session for discussion.
Rank the submissions by strength alone and accept the top four, whatever their topics are.
Give each of five speakers a full twenty minutes so everyone can present a complete argument.
Let each speaker set their own topic and skip opening remarks so no time is spent on framing.
answer: Circulate the papers in advance, name a chair and a respondent who can link the talks, and reserve about a third of the session for discussion.

prompt: A faculty member is writing the personal statement for a tenure dossier, which must connect research, teaching, and service. Which approach best serves the case?
choices: Frame research, teaching, and service as parts of one scholarly identity, showing how each area supports the others and how the work will continue.
Give equal space to every committee assignment, so the record shows the full amount of service performed.
Present research first as the only area that counts at tenure, and treat teaching and service as brief afterthoughts.
Summarize each area separately and let the external letter writers decide how the three areas fit together.
answer: Frame research, teaching, and service as parts of one scholarly identity, showing how each area supports the others and how the work will continue.

prompt: A writer directs a monthly reading series whose attendance has been falling for a year. Which move best reflects sound arts programming leadership?
choices: Survey current and lapsed attendees, then adjust programming and partnerships to fit the community, with a realistic budget and calendar.
Invite only the biggest-name writers available and raise ticket prices to cover their fees.
Cut the season to a single event a year to reduce the organizing team's workload.
Keep the format unchanged and rely on social media to bring the audience back.
answer: Survey current and lapsed attendees, then adjust programming and partnerships to fit the community, with a realistic budget and calendar.

prompt: A writing program director must assess whether students' writing improves across the four years of the undergraduate program. Which design best supports valid, useful evidence?
choices: Sample student writing at several points in the program, score it with a shared rubric by trained readers, and use the results to revise courses.
Rely on end-of-term student ratings of their own writing, collected in each course.
Use grades in first-year writing alone and treat them as a measure of four-year growth.
Compare average scores across institutions without matching the writing tasks or the scoring criteria.
answer: Sample student writing at several points in the program, score it with a shared rubric by trained readers, and use the results to revise courses.

prompt: A postdoc has two years of fellowship funding and a dissertation on Victorian periodicals. They need a research plan for the next several years. Which plan best fits what a strong early-career research agenda looks like?
choices: One focused project on how serialization shaped Victorian authorship, sized to yield two articles and a book proposal within the two-year term.
Four separate projects spanning different centuries and genres, chosen to show hiring committees the widest possible range.
One project so large it cannot be finished during the fellowship, so it will still be running at the next job search.
A plan to finish every leftover thread from the dissertation, including topics the scholar no longer pursues, before moving on.
answer: One focused project on how serialization shaped Victorian authorship, sized to yield two articles and a book proposal within the two-year term.

prompt: A scholar receives a "revise and resubmit" from a strong journal. Two reviewers ask for a major new reading of one text, and a third asks the author to cut the section they are most attached to. The editor's letter calls the essay promising. What is the strongest response?
choices: Revise along the editor's and reviewers' lines, add a point-by-point response letter, and address the requested cut directly in that letter.
Withdraw the essay and submit it elsewhere, since the requested changes would alter the argument too much.
Resubmit the essay unchanged with a letter explaining why the reviewers misread the section at its heart.
Add the new reading the reviewers ask for and keep the original section, noting in the letter that both appear.
answer: Revise along the editor's and reviewers' lines, add a point-by-point response letter, and address the requested cut directly in that letter.

prompt: A linguistics team is ready to deposit transcripts, audio recordings, and metadata from a documentation project in a public repository. The funder requires open access to the data, but some recordings are of ceremonies that community members asked to keep restricted. Which deposit plan best meets both obligations?
choices: Post the metadata and transcripts openly under a Creative Commons license, and restrict the sensitive recordings to approved users.
Keep every file off the repository and send copies only to individual researchers who email to request them.
Put all the files in the repository under all-rights-reserved terms so the community can ask for takedowns later.
Deposit the sensitive recordings openly and hold back the metadata and transcripts until the community signs off.
answer: Post the metadata and transcripts openly under a Creative Commons license, and restrict the sensitive recordings to approved users.

prompt: Your department is running a public lecture series and wants disabled scholars and low-income community members to attend. Which plan removes the most barriers?
choices: Live captioning, an accessible venue, free registration, and a remote attendance option.
A discount code for students who email the chair to request it before the series begins.
Larger-font printed programs and a note inviting anyone with accessibility needs to contact a staff member.
Weekday evening events, with recordings posted online for anyone who cannot attend in person.
answer: Live captioning, an accessible venue, free registration, and a remote attendance option.

prompt: A department committee is revising the undergraduate major, and members disagree sharply about which requirements to keep. Which approach best reflects productive shared-governance work?
choices: Ground the debate in the program's stated goals and student evidence, and record the decision and its rationale.
Let the most senior members settle the matter quickly so the committee can move on to other business.
Postpone the decision until every member fully agrees, so no minority view has to be recorded.
Skip documenting the debate, since written records only create hard feelings later.
answer: Ground the debate in the program's stated goals and student evidence, and record the decision and its rationale.

prompt: A scholar is drafting a teaching statement for a job application. Which approach best fits what search committees expect from the statement?
choices: Link two or three concrete classroom choices to evidence of student learning, showing a consistent teaching approach.
List every course taught in order, with the readings and main assignments named for each one.
State broad values such as rigor and inclusivity without describing how they show up in the classroom.
Focus mainly on defending low student evaluations and arguing that they are unfair measures of teaching.
answer: Link two or three concrete classroom choices to evidence of student learning, showing a consistent teaching approach.

prompt: A poet who founded an influential small press thirty years ago is stepping back from running it. What best protects the press's editorial role in literary culture after the founder leaves?
choices: Appoint editors trained within the press and give it a written editorial mission and dependable funding that outlast the founder.
Sell the list to a large commercial publisher, whose scale will keep the books in print and reaching readers.
Have the founder keep final say over every acquisition after the handover, so the taste does not change.
Widen the list to publish in many more genres, so that the press no longer depends on one person's taste.
answer: Appoint editors trained within the press and give it a written editorial mission and dependable funding that outlast the founder.

prompt: You are chairing a tenure review at another university. The candidate's book is praised by letter-writers, but three of the five letters come from the candidate's own former teachers. What is the most rigorous response?
choices: Seek independent letters from scholars with no supervisory tie to the candidate before judging the record.
Discount the case entirely, since former teachers can never write useful letters.
Accept the letters as they stand, since reputation of the letter-writers is what matters.
Compare the number of letters with the other cases the committee has seen this year.
answer: Seek independent letters from scholars with no supervisory tie to the candidate before judging the record.

prompt: A five-year study of letters between two modernist poets has uncovered a previously unknown literary friendship. Which feature would most lift this work to prize level?
choices: It uses the correspondence to revise how scholars understand modernist influence across national borders.
It prints every letter in full with careful notes on handwriting and dating.
It reviews everything the two poets published before the study began.
It describes the archive's holdings in detail for future visitors.
answer: It uses the correspondence to revise how scholars understand modernist influence across national borders.

prompt: A national argument-writing initiative has run for three years with grant money and strong early results in its pilot regions. The grant ends next year. What is the best way to keep the gains going at national scale?
choices: Build the training and materials into existing teacher-education programs and state subject associations, so they continue without the grant.
Keep the national office team running all training and seek a second large grant to continue the same model.
Publish a full report of the pilot results so that other regions can copy the methods on their own.
Turn the initiative into an annual national conference where teachers present their strongest argument-writing lessons.
answer: Build the training and materials into existing teacher-education programs and state subject associations, so they continue without the grant.

prompt: You are invited to give a distinguished lecture on the future of literary study. Which choice most strengthens the lecture's argument?
choices: A clear claim about where the field is heading, supported by a few well-chosen examples the audience can weigh.
A full survey of everything you have published, so the audience sees your record.
A reading of one poem in exhaustive detail, so the audience sees your method at work.
A summary of every current debate in the field, so the audience sees the whole picture.
answer: A clear claim about where the field is heading, supported by a few well-chosen examples the audience can weigh.

prompt: A newspaper asks you to comment on a public controversy about whether English spelling should be simplified. What is the best way to bring your scholarship into the conversation?
choices: Explain the evidence about how spelling systems change and resist reforms, while distinguishing established findings from your own view.
State your personal opinion clearly, since the public wants to know where experts stand.
Decline the request, since scholars should leave national debates to journalists.
List the scholars who agree with you, so readers can check the majority view.
answer: Explain the evidence about how spelling systems change and resist reforms, while distinguishing established findings from your own view.

prompt: A major publisher asks you to edit a definitive edition of a poet's collected works. As a scholar acting as cultural steward, what matters most?
choices: Establishing reliable texts with clear editorial principles, so future readers and scholars can trust and build on the edition.
Choosing the poems that best represent the poet's achievement for general readers.
Writing interpretive introductions that show why the poet matters to our moment.
Producing the edition quickly, before another editor publishes a rival version.
answer: Establishing reliable texts with clear editorial principles, so future readers and scholars can trust and build on the edition.

prompt: You are directing a new historical dictionary of English. Which decision should come first?
choices: Set the principles for which words are included and how their histories will be dated and evidenced.
Hire the lexicographers, since a good team will settle the design as it works.
Choose the entries by frequency, since the most common words matter most.
Design the printed layout, since the dictionary's look shapes how it is used.
answer: Set the principles for which words are included and how their histories will be dated and evidenced.

prompt: A senior scholar writes a manifesto arguing that English studies has spent decades debating authorial genius while neglecting who was allowed to publish at all. Which sentence best converts this diagnosis into a research agenda others can pursue?
choices: These questions about access and permission should reorganize the archive, the canon, and the methods we teach, and I name five studies that would test them.
This manifesto argues that access matters more than genius, and I hope the field agrees with me.
I have always felt strongly about exclusion in publishing, and this essay explains why.
Studies of access and permission are interesting, though debates about authorial genius remain central.
answer: These questions about access and permission should reorganize the archive, the canon, and the methods we teach, and I name five studies that would test them.

prompt: As editor of a major journal, you receive a submission that is brilliantly argued but relies on a single unpublished letter no other scholar can consult. What is the best editorial response?
choices: Ask the author to address the evidentiary access problem before the journal commits to the argument.
Reject it immediately, since unpublished sources cannot support journal articles.
Accept it as it stands, since brilliance of argument outweighs evidence problems.
Send it to reviewers without comment and let them decide about the letter.
answer: Ask the author to address the evidentiary access problem before the journal commits to the argument.

prompt: As head of a national association for English studies, you learn that a member has been found to have fabricated evidence in a major study. What is the best action for the association?
choices: Follow a fair, transparent process that examines the evidence and states a clear standard for scholarly integrity.
Expel the member at once, since the association's reputation must be protected.
Leave the matter to the member's home university and take no position.
Settle the matter privately among the association's officers without a record.
answer: Follow a fair, transparent process that examines the evidence and states a clear standard for scholarly integrity.

prompt: A framework for reading narrative time is published in 1990. By 2025, hundreds of studies use its terms, several scholars have revised its categories, and two rival frameworks define themselves against it. What does this reception show about the framework?
choices: That it is field-defining theory, since later scholars adopt, extend, and contest its terms.
That it is field-defining theory, since the field has now proven its claims true.
That it is only a useful method, since scholars have revised its original categories.
That it is a passing trend, since rival frameworks have defined themselves against it.
answer: That it is field-defining theory, since later scholars adopt, extend, and contest its terms.

prompt: You edit a book series on the history of the novel. A proposal offers a superb study of an important but already crowded topic, while another offers a solid study that opens an area the series has never covered. Which proposal best fits the series?
choices: The solid study that opens the uncovered area, since a series defines its subject by mapping what is missing.
The superb study of the crowded topic, since quality of execution should decide every case.
Neither, since a series should wait until a proposal excels in both coverage and quality.
Whichever author agrees to revise the proposal to match the series cover and format.
answer: The solid study that opens the uncovered area, since a series defines its subject by mapping what is missing.

prompt: A rhetorician coined a term for a new area of study — "civic data rhetoric" — and about a dozen researchers now use it. The scholar wants the area to last rather than fade as a trend. Which plan gives it the best chance of becoming a lasting subfield?
choices: Set up a recurring venue with clear methods and guiding questions, and train doctoral students who carry the work to other universities.
Keep the term flexible and give it new meanings each year, so that more scholars can say their work belongs to it.
Publish one large book that settles the area's main questions, then move on to other research.
Present the work mainly through invited talks at other fields' conferences, rather than building its own scholarly home.
answer: Set up a recurring venue with clear methods and guiding questions, and train doctoral students who carry the work to other universities.

prompt: An English educator is asked to advise on a new national framework for teaching writing in grades 6 through 12. Which approach makes the framework most likely to be adopted and used well across many regions?
choices: Center the framework on a small set of clear, teachable goals, with sample student work and room for local curricula to reach them.
Write a detailed sequence of daily lessons that every teacher follows in the same order across the country.
List every skill students should master at each grade level, so that nothing important is left out.
Describe broad aims such as critical thinking and clear expression, so that each region can shape its own meaning.
answer: Center the framework on a small set of clear, teachable goals, with sample student work and room for local curricula to reach them.

prompt: Which capital letter is made with one tall straight line and two short slanted lines that touch the tall line in the middle?
choices: K
L
M
N
answer: K

prompt: I have one dog. My friend has two more dogs. Now we have three of them. Which word fills the blank? Now we have three ____.
choices: dogs
dog
doges
dogg
answer: dogs

prompt: Which mark goes at the end of this sentence? Where did you put my red ball
choices: A question mark
A period
An exclamation point
A comma
answer: A question mark

prompt: Say the word sun out loud. Which letter matches the LAST sound you hear?
choices: n
s
u
m
answer: n

prompt: Which mark goes at the end of this sentence? Can we play at the park
choices: A question mark
A period
An exclamation point
A comma
answer: A question mark

prompt: Which word begins with an r-blend (two consonants like br, cr, dr, fr, gr, or tr)?
choices: drum
flag
clap
slip
answer: drum

prompt: Finish the word: I clean the floor with a m__.
choices: op
ap
ip
up
answer: op

prompt: Which phrase uses a or an correctly?
choices: an egg
a egg
an cat
a ant
answer: an egg

prompt: Maria is writing a piece that gives FACTS about cats. Which sentence is a good START that names her topic and tells a fact?
choices: Cats are small animals that people keep at home as pets.
I love cats so much!
Cats are the best pets of all.
Do you like cats too?
answer: Cats are small animals that people keep at home as pets.

prompt: Which word has the same vowel sound as the oy in toy?
choices: coin
cow
saw
boat
answer: coin

prompt: Which word has the long o sound spelled with a silent e at the end?
choices: rope
rod
room
rot
answer: rope

prompt: Which word begins with a silent k, where you do not say the k sound?
choices: knit
kite
king
kick
answer: knit

prompt: Which greeting of a friendly letter is punctuated correctly?
choices: Dear Uncle Ben,
Dear, Uncle Ben
Dear Uncle, Ben
Dear Uncle Ben.
answer: Dear Uncle Ben,

prompt: Choose the correct past tense word to finish the sentence. Last night, Leo ______ a letter to his grandma.
choices: wrote
writed
written
writes
answer: wrote

prompt: Which noun is an abstract noun, naming a feeling or idea that you cannot touch?
choices: joy
hat
lake
cousin
answer: joy

prompt: Add -ing to the word make. Which spelling is correct?
choices: making
makeing
makking
makin
answer: making

prompt: Which sentence puts the comma in the right place after the introductory clause?
choices: When the rain stopped, we went outside.
When, the rain stopped we went outside.
When the rain, stopped we went outside.
When the rain stopped we went, outside.
answer: When the rain stopped, we went outside.

prompt: The Greek root graph means "write" or "draw." Which word is built from this root?
choices: autograph
airport
interrupt
grape
answer: autograph

prompt: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
choices: The storm knocked out the power; we lit candles and played cards.
Because the storm knocked out the power; we lit candles and played cards.
We packed three things for the picnic; sandwiches, apples, and juice.
The storm knocked out the power; and lit candles to play some cards.
answer: The storm knocked out the power; we lit candles and played cards.

prompt: A student's draft says only, 'She was nervous.' Which revision best develops the moment as a story scene by using specific description and a slower pace?
choices: Her fingers trembled around the page, and the words blurred as the door handle slowly turned.
She felt very nervous, and she was really worried about what would happen next.
She was nervous because nervous is just how people feel when they are afraid.
Nervousness is an emotion that many people feel when something big is about to happen.
answer: Her fingers trembled around the page, and the words blurred as the door handle slowly turned.

prompt: Which sentence uses the opening participial phrase correctly, with no dangling modifier?
choices: Walking to school, Jake saw a squirrel dart across the path.
Walking to school, a squirrel darted in front of Jake.
Walking to school, the squirrel was seen by Jake.
Walking to school, the rain started to fall on the path.
answer: Walking to school, Jake saw a squirrel dart across the path.

prompt: Read this sentence from a short story: "Marta kept the cracked teacup on the shelf long after she had thrown away every other dish from the old house." Which sentence best explains WHY this detail matters, rather than just repeating what it says?
choices: By saving only the cracked cup, Marta shows she values what ties her to the past over what is perfect or useful, which hints at her grief.
Marta kept the teacup on the shelf even after she threw away all of the other dishes from the old house.
The cup is cracked, which means it was probably dropped at some point before Marta moved away.
Teacups are a common household object, and many people keep one or two of them on a shelf.
answer: By saving only the cracked cup, Marta shows she values what ties her to the past over what is perfect or useful, which hints at her grief.

prompt: A student uses Chicago style with footnotes. She quotes page 42 of the book Rivers of Change by Maria Ortiz, published in 2011 in Chicago by Lake Press. Which first note is formatted correctly? (Asterisks mark italics.)
choices: 1. Maria Ortiz, *Rivers of Change* (Chicago: Lake Press, 2011), 42.
1. Ortiz, Maria. *Rivers of Change*. Chicago: Lake Press, 2011. 42.
1. Ortiz, M. (2011). *Rivers of Change*. Chicago, IL: Lake Press, p. 42.
1. Maria Ortiz, *Rivers of Change*, Lake Press, Chicago, 2011, p. 42.
answer: 1. Maria Ortiz, *Rivers of Change* (Chicago: Lake Press, 2011), 42.

prompt: Read the sentence: "The detective watched the suspect with binoculars." It is ambiguous mainly because the phrase "with binoculars" can attach to two different parts of the sentence. What are the two readings?
choices: The detective used binoculars to watch the suspect, or the suspect was the one who had binoculars.
The suspect was watched in the past, or the suspect is still being watched right now.
The detective watched the suspect closely for a long time, or watched only for a moment.
The suspect saw the detective first, or the detective saw the suspect first.
answer: The detective used binoculars to watch the suspect, or the suspect was the one who had binoculars.

prompt: You are a US-based scholar. Your book argues for a new reading of a well-known 1985 novel that is still under copyright. You quote three short passages, a few lines each, to support close readings, and you cite the edition you used. What should you do about permission?
choices: Assess whether the quotations qualify as fair use, weighing your scholarly purpose, the small amount quoted, and the effect on the novel's market
Nothing is needed, because any quotation under 300 words is automatically free of copyright restriction
Contact the estate only if the copyright was not renewed after its first term, since renewal decides protection
Cite the edition in a footnote, since proper citation of a source replaces the need for any copyright analysis
answer: Assess whether the quotations qualify as fair use, weighing your scholarly purpose, the small amount quoted, and the effect on the novel's market

prompt: Which word in this sentence needs a capital letter? My dog likes to run in the park on monday.
choices: monday
dog
park
run
answer: monday
note: Days of the week are capitalized; monday is the only lowercase proper noun. Taught in Proper Nouns (U4).

prompt: In the book title "where the wild things are", which word should stay lowercase when the title is written correctly?
choices: the
where
wild
are
answer: the
note: In title case, short article the stays lowercase mid-title; where is first word, wild and are (verb) are capitalized. Capitalizing Titles (U2).

prompt: You make your pencil go up and down, up and down across the page like this: / / / / . Which pre-writing stroke is this?
choices: straight lines
circles
curves
dots
answer: straight lines
note: Straight-line pre-writing strokes, U9.

prompt: You drew a picture of a little cat. You want to tell what happened in your picture to make a story. Which one is a story about your picture?
choices: The little cat climbed the tree and got stuck.
A little cat.
The cat is orange.
I have a cat at home.
answer: The little cat climbed the tree and got stuck.
note: Only option telling an event; drawing and dictating a story U14.

prompt: You drew a picture of a rainy day. You want to tell what you think about rainy days and why. Which one shows what you like or do not like and why?
choices: I do not like rainy days because I cannot play outside.
It is raining today.
A rainy day is when water falls from the sky.
My picture has gray clouds in it.
answer: I do not like rainy days because I cannot play outside.
note: Only option giving a like/dislike plus reason; opinion U14.

prompt: Which word has the two sounds /f/ and /t/ at the very end, like in 'soft'?
choices: gift
giff
gish
gilt
answer: gift
note: Ending blend -ft; U15.

prompt: Which sentence is a tongue twister?
choices: She sells seashells by the seashore.
My friend has a shell from the sea.
The shells at the store were shiny.
She went to the shore on Saturday.
answer: She sells seashells by the seashore.
note: Only alliterative tongue twister; U20.

prompt: Maya wants her classmates to bring their blankets to the animal shelter. What kind of speaking is she doing?
choices: She is trying to persuade them to do something.
She is trying to teach them new facts about blankets.
She is trying to make them laugh with a funny story.
She is only telling them about her favorite color.
answer: She is trying to persuade them to do something.
note: Asking classmates to bring blankets is persuading; U19.

prompt: One mouse ran across the floor. Then two ______ ran across the floor. Which word goes in the blank?
choices: mice
mouses
mouse
mices
answer: mice
note: Irregular plural mice; U2.

prompt: Read the two sentences. The dog will bark at the cat. The bark on the tree is rough. What does the word bark mean in these two sentences?
choices: It means two different things in the two sentences.
It means the same thing in both sentences.
It means the dog is running in both sentences.
It means the tree is loud in both sentences.
answer: It means two different things in the two sentences.
note: Multiple-meaning word bark; U12.

prompt: You read this fact in a book: "A frog can jump very far." Which sentence shows that you put the fact in your own words?
choices: A frog can leap a long way in one hop.
A frog can jump very far.
Frogs are animals that live near water.
A frog can jump very far. A frog can jump very far.
answer: A frog can leap a long way in one hop.
note: Paraphrase keeps the fact; C changes the fact; U17.

prompt:
You listen to a short talk about bees. The speaker says: "Bees live in a hive with one queen. Worker bees gather nectar from flowers. The nectar becomes honey, which feeds the whole hive."

What is the MAIN idea the speaker wants you to understand?

A. Bees gather nectar and turn it into honey for the hive.
B. There is one queen in every hive.
C. Bees visit flowers.
D. Honey is sweet.
choices: Bees gather nectar and turn it into honey for the hive.
There is one queen in every hive.
Bees visit flowers.
Honey is sweet.
answer: Bees gather nectar and turn it into honey for the hive.
note: A captures the talk's main point; others are details; U20.

prompt:
Choose the word that correctly completes the sentence.

The students packed ______ lunches before the field trip.

A. they're
B. there
C. their
D. they are
choices: their
they're
there
they are
answer: their
note: Possessive their among homophones; U13.

prompt:
Sam is taking notes for a report on dolphins. He has a card labeled "What Dolphins Eat." Which fact belongs on this card?

A. Dolphins eat fish and squid.
B. Dolphins live in all the world's oceans.
C. Dolphins are mammals that breathe air.
D. A baby dolphin is called a calf.
choices: Dolphins eat fish and squid.
Dolphins live in all the world's oceans.
Dolphins are mammals that breathe air.
A baby dolphin is called a calf.
answer: Dolphins eat fish and squid.
note: Only fact about diet; notes and categories U16.

prompt:
Read these two lines:

"The stars were bright above the town, / The sleepy moon came gently down."

What does the word "sleepy" do in these lines?

A. It gives the moon a gentle, restful feeling.
B. It tells the exact time the moon rose.
C. It shows that the stars were angry.
D. It proves that the town was empty.
choices: It gives the moon a gentle, restful feeling.
It tells the exact time the moon rose.
It shows that the stars were angry.
It proves that the town was empty.
answer: It gives the moon a gentle, restful feeling.
note: Picture word giving the moon a restful feeling; imagery U19.

prompt:
Read the sentence: The puppy slept soundly in its bed.

Which question does the adverb "soundly" answer?

A. How did the puppy sleep?
B. When did the puppy sleep?
C. Where did the puppy sleep?
D. What did the puppy sleep in?
choices: How did the puppy sleep?
When did the puppy sleep?
Where did the puppy sleep?
What did the puppy sleep in?
answer: How did the puppy sleep?
note: soundly tells how; adverbs U7.

prompt:
Nina needs to write a note to the school librarian to ask about a book. Which sentence sounds BEST for this kind of note?

A. Hey! Can I grab that book or what?
B. I wanna know if you got the book I asked about.
C. Would you please tell me if the book I want is ready to borrow?
D. Gimme the book when you see it, okay?
choices: Would you please tell me if the book I want is ready to borrow?
Hey! Can I grab that book or what?
I wanna know if you got the book I asked about.
Gimme the book when you see it, okay?
answer: Would you please tell me if the book I want is ready to borrow?
note: Only polite/formal option; U9.

For these reasons, everyone should try riding a bike.
answer: Biking is one of the best ways to travel around town.

prompt:
Which sentence combines these two choppy sentences into ONE smooth sentence?

"The puppy has brown spots. The puppy likes to nap in the sun."

A. The spotted puppy likes to nap in the sun.
B. The puppy has brown spots, and the puppy likes to nap in the sun.
C. The puppy has brown spots. It likes to nap in the sun.
