prompt: A senior scholar is invited to write a state-of-the-field essay covering twenty years of scholarship on a major poet. Which set of moves would make the essay field-defining rather than merely bibliographic?
choices: Naming the assumption that has organized most of the work, showing where following it has stopped yielding results, and proposing a question the field has not asked.
Listing the books and articles published in the period with a one-sentence summary of each, and noting which are most frequently cited.

prompt: Earl Miner's Comparative Poetics observes that Japanese poetic theory grew out of lyric poetry and personal expression, while Western poetic theory grew out of public, mimetic kinds such as epic and drama. prompt: An editor of a twentieth-century novel adopts the first edition's spelling and punctuation throughout, but where a later edition authorized by the author carries wording that the editor judges better, the editor prints the later wording and records the change in an editorial note. prompt: A student is writing a report about the history of hot-air balloons and finds: (1) a museum website article about the first balloon flight in France in 1783, and (2) a book about early air travel that describes the same flight but focuses on how crowds reacted. The passage shows that city life is objectively faster and colder than life in any village.
Her cultural background has little effect, since she describes the new city in plain, factual words.
The passage shows only that she dislikes shopping and has no interest in other people.
answer: Her knowledge of village life sets what she notices and finds strange in the new city.

prompt: A poem runs nineteen lines in five groups of three plus a final group of four. Two lines repeat again and again throughout it — one closing the first group of three and the last line of the poem, the other in the middle of the middle groups. Which form is this? A. A villanelle B. A sonnet C. A ballad D. An ode
choices: A
A sonnet
A ballad
An ode
answer: A

prompt:
Read the passage.

A 1901 handbook for railroad workers describes how to signal a train. It was written by the railroad company's own safety office and printed for use by its employees.

What should a reader keep in mind most when using this handbook as a source about rail work?
choices: It was written by the company to instruct its own workers, so it may not tell about injuries or failures.
It is too old to contain any useful details, since all handbooks from 1901 are wrong.
It must be trusted completely, since only experts were allowed to write handbooks in 1901.
It is unreliable mainly because it describes work that no one performs any longer.
answer: It was written by the company to instruct its own workers, so it may not tell about injuries or failures.

prompt:
Read the passage.

(1) A town's factory closed in 1980. (2) For years afterward, the town's tax income fell and its school budget was cut. (3) Some say the school cuts caused the factory to close.

What does the text actually support about the factory and the school?
choices: The tax and school changes are described as coming after the closing, so the text does not support the claim that they caused it.
The school cuts are described as the reason the factory closed.
The text shows that the factory closed because of the school budget.
The text proves that the two events happened at the same time.
answer: The tax and school changes are described as coming after the closing, so the text does not support the claim that they caused it.

prompt: In a play, two servants trade puns about "sole" and "soul" while hiding from their masters, the young lovers end up married after a case of mistaken identity, and the final scene brings every quarrel to an end. Which Shakespearean type of play is this? A. A comedy, which ends in marriage or reconciliation and leans on wordplay and mix-ups. B. A tragedy, which ends in the hero's downfall and death. C. A history, which follows kings and the making of a nation. D. A romance only, which stays in a made-up land of magic.
choices: A
A tragedy, which ends in the hero's downfall and death.
A history, which follows kings and the making of a nation.
A romance only, which stays in a made-up land of magic.
answer: A

prompt: Two stories both tell about a single family dinner. Story P gives the whole dinner across twenty pages of narration. Story Q jumps straight to the one moment when the father finally answers his daughter's question, with everything before and after left out. What does Story Q mainly show about how a short story is built? A. It is compressed: it chooses one telling moment and lets the reader infer the rest. B. It is compressed: it must run only two pages to count as a short story. C. It avoids conflict: a short story cannot include an argument. D. It avoids setting: a short story never tells the reader where events happen.
choices: A
It is compressed: it must run only two pages to count as a short story.
It avoids conflict: a short story cannot include an argument.
It avoids setting: a short story never tells the reader where events happen.
answer: A

prompt: A memoirist is writing about the day she left home at eighteen. She already has the plain facts: the time of the train, the weather, who came to say good-bye. What else must she bring to these facts for the piece to be a memoir and not just a diary entry? A. Her present voice reflecting on why that day mattered and what it means to her now. B. The exact words of every person at the station, whether she remembers them or not. C. A made-up ending that would make the story more exciting. D. A list of sources she read about other people leaving home.
choices: A
The exact words of every person at the station, whether she remembers them or not.
A made-up ending that would make the story more exciting.
A list of sources she read about other people leaving home.
answer: A

prompt: A young hero crosses into a strange land, wins a treasure with the help of a guide, and must finally cross back home to her ordinary village, changed by the trip. Which stage of the hero's journey does the return home represent? A. The return, where the hero brings back what she learned to the ordinary world. B. The call to adventure, where the hero first hears of the quest. C. The trials, where the hero faces tests and enemies. D. The refusal, where the hero turns down the quest at first.
choices: A
The call to adventure, where the hero first hears of the quest.
The trials, where the hero faces tests and enemies.
The refusal, where the hero turns down the quest at first.
answer: A

prompt: Read the passage: "Devon was fiercely loyal to his friends and just as fiercely proud. When his team cheated to win, he refused to tell on them — and when the coach praised him alone for the victory, he could not bring himself to say he did not deserve it." How do Devon's traits work together to drive the plot? A. His pride and his loyalty pull him toward protecting the team and staying silent, which is what keeps the secret growing. B. His pride alone makes him tell the coach the truth right away and end the story. C. His loyalty makes him quit the team, so the coach has to choose a new captain. D. He has only one trait, so the events depend on other characters instead.
choices: A
His pride alone makes him tell the coach the truth right away and end the story.
His loyalty makes him quit the team, so the coach has to choose a new captain.
He has only one trait, so the events depend on other characters instead.
answer: A

prompt: On stage, one character is left alone and speaks aloud: "Now I am alone. Oh, what a rogue and peasant slave am I!" Why does the playwright use this kind of speech here? A. A soliloquy lets the character bare thoughts the other characters cannot hear, so we learn what he truly feels. B. A soliloquy is a speech shouted to the whole court, so every character hears it. C. A soliloquy is a stage direction telling the actor to stand alone and say nothing. D. A soliloquy is a song the character sings to keep the mood light.
choices: A
A soliloquy is a speech shouted to the whole court, so every character hears it.
A soliloquy is a stage direction telling the actor to stand alone and say nothing.
A soliloquy is a song the character sings to keep the mood light.
answer: A

prompt: A poem runs three lines: the first has five syllables, the second seven, and the third five. It shows one small moment in nature and stops, without rhyme or argument. Which form is this, and what does that form do? A. A haiku: it holds a single brief moment in very few words. B. A free verse poem: it sets its line lengths to make a pattern of beats. C. A ballad: it rhymes the second and fourth lines to tell a tale. D. An ode: it addresses its subject in a long, formal praise.
choices: A
A free verse poem: it sets its line lengths to make a pattern of beats.
A ballad: it rhymes the second and fourth lines to tell a tale.
An ode: it addresses its subject in a long, formal praise.
answer: A

prompt: Read the sentence: "The firefighters were powerless against the blaze, and that powerless feeling was what finally saved them, because it made them call for help before it was too late." This is a paradox because the sentence A. says two things that seem to contradict each other — being powerless somehow saved them — yet both are true at once. B. compares firefighters to something unlike them using the word "like" or "as." C. gives human qualities to the blaze, such as the blaze reaching for them. D. describes the fire in words that mean the opposite of what is really meant.
choices: A
compares firefighters to something unlike them using the word "like" or "as."
gives human qualities to the blaze, such as the blaze reaching for them.
describes the fire in words that mean the opposite of what is really meant.
answer: A

prompt: A novel opens with an old sailor on shore telling his shipmates, "Let me tell you about the young man I once was." The rest of the book is the story of his voyage as he tells it to them. What is this structure, and what does it let the author do? A. It is a frame story: the outer narrator sets up the tale and can comment on it, shaping how we judge the young sailor. B. It is a flashback only: the novel moves back in time with no outer narrator at all. C. It is a frame story: the shipmates interrupt so often that the voyage is told in the wrong order. D. It is a flashback only: the old sailor appears just to remind us the voyage happened in the past.
choices: A
It is a flashback only: the novel moves back in time with no outer narrator at all.
It is a frame story: the shipmates interrupt so often that the voyage is told in the wrong order.
It is a flashback only: the old sailor appears just to remind us the voyage happened in the past.
answer: A

prompt:
Read the passage.

(1) Some argue that city parks are a luxury the budget cannot afford. (2) Yet a park is not a luxury like a fountain or a statue. (3) A park cleans the air, cools the streets in summer, and gives children a safe place to play.

Which statement best describes how sentence 3 develops the claim of the passage?
choices: It gives concrete ways a park serves the city, so that sentence 2's claim is backed up with reasons.
It repeats in other words what sentence 2 already said, adding no new support for the claim.
It introduces a new claim about summer weather that is separate from the argument about parks.
It admits that parks are too expensive, which weakens the argument begun in sentence 2.
answer: It gives concrete ways a park serves the city, so that sentence 2's claim is backed up with reasons.

prompt:
Read the excerpt from a speech.

"We have petitioned; our petitions have been answered only by insult. We have warned them; they have ignored our warnings. Shall we try argument once more? We have tried it for ten years."

What is the main purpose of this repeated wording?
choices: To build the sense that every peaceful option has been exhausted, making action seem necessary.
To admit that the speaker's side has made mistakes and should back down.
To give a step-by-step list of instructions for the listeners to follow.
To entertain the audience with a story before getting to the main point.
answer: To build the sense that every peaceful option has been exhausted, making action seem necessary.

prompt: An essay argues that schools should teach financial literacy. In one paragraph the author lists three studies showing teens cannot read a pay stub. The next paragraph begins, "But numbers alone do not make the case," and turns to a student's story about her first paycheck. What is that turning sentence doing? A. It signals a turn in the author's reasoning, connecting the research to a different kind of evidence. B. It announces that the first paragraph was false and should be ignored. C. It changes the subject from schools to the history of money. D. It quotes the student before her story actually appears.
choices: A
It announces that the first paragraph was false and should be ignored.
It changes the subject from schools to the history of money.
It quotes the student before her story actually appears.
answer: A

prompt: Read this passage: "The judge knew the law perfectly and applied it perfectly, and that is exactly why the verdict was unjust." Why is this passage paradoxical?
choices: It claims that doing something perfectly led to a result that is the opposite of perfect justice.
It claims the judge both knew the law and did not know the law.
It says the verdict was just and unjust in the same words.
It argues that no verdict can ever be truly fair.
answer: It claims that doing something perfectly led to a result that is the opposite of perfect justice.

prompt: Read these lines from a Romantic poem: "The child is father of the Man; / And I could wish my days to be / Bound each to each by natural piety." (Wordsworth, "My Heart Leaps Up"). What does the line "The child is father of the Man" mean?
choices: The feelings and wonder of childhood shape the adult a person later becomes.
Children understand nature better than their parents ever can.
Every adult must be reborn in order to live a pure life.
A man should treat children with the respect owed to a parent.
answer: The feelings and wonder of childhood shape the adult a person later becomes.

prompt: An essayist drafts a piece about grief. He begins with the morning his father died, jumps to a story about fishing as a boy, then circles back to the funeral, and ends on the same fishing river. A peer reviewer says the essay would be stronger if it followed a clear timeline from the death to the funeral. What is the best response to this feedback?
choices: The timeline order might be clearer but would strip out the essay's real subject, the way memory itself jumps between moments
The reviewer is right, because no strong essay ever leaves the order of events in question
The reviewer is wrong, because personal essays should never mention events from childhood
The reviewer is right, because readers cannot follow an essay unless it ends where it begins
answer: The timeline order might be clearer but would strip out the essay's real subject, the way memory itself jumps between moments

prompt: Read this passage from a contemporary story: "Everything I tell you about that winter is true, except the parts I have made up, which are the truest of all. There was no cabin by the lake. I want you to picture it anyway: the smoke, the ice on the bucket." What is the narrator mainly doing to the reader?
choices: Admitting the story is invented while asking the reader to feel its truth.
Confusing the reader about which character is speaking.
Correcting an earlier version of the story he published.
Describing a real place while hiding its true location.
answer: Admitting the story is invented while asking the reader to feel its truth.

prompt: Read this sentence from an old essay: "It is a strange thing that the poor, who have least to give, are found oftener at the door of the needy than the rich, who have most, and that the rich man, when he passes the beggar, calleth that prudence which the poor man nameth cowardice." The word "calleth" is an older form of a verb. Who does this action — "calleth that prudence"?
choices: the rich man
the poor man
the beggar
the needy at the door
answer: the rich man

prompt: In a book about urban life, the essayist writes: "Of course the car gave the worker freedom; no one denies the pleasure of a road that ends where he chooses. Yet that freedom quietly purchased a city where nothing essential is within walking distance." What role does the phrase "Of course" play in the argument?
choices: It grants a point to the other side before the author shows its hidden cost
It introduces a claim the author believes is too obvious to need support
It signals that the author will abandon the topic of city planning entirely
It shows the author doubts the truth of everything said in the sentence
answer: It grants a point to the other side before the author shows its hidden cost

prompt: Read this passage: "Creon refuses to let the traitor be buried. His son begs him to yield and warns that the gods and the city are turning against him. Creon relents, but only after he has rushed to the tomb and found his son dead beside it. The chorus remarks that wisdom comes to men late and in sorrow." What does the chorus's remark say about how Creon gained his understanding?
choices: He learned wisdom only after suffering made him change, so it came too late to help.
He was wise from the start, but others refused to listen to him.
He learned wisdom from the gods before he made any decision.
He gained understanding by carefully reasoning through the law.
answer: He learned wisdom only after suffering made him change, so it came too late to help.

prompt: In a documentary about a strike, the film shows footage of workers marching, then holds for ten full seconds on a shot of an empty factory floor before a company spokesperson speaks. What does that held shot most likely contribute to the film's argument?
choices: It lets the silence and emptiness weigh on viewers before the company's defense, subtly shaping how that defense is heard
It shows that the film crew forgot to edit out a blank section of footage
It proves that the company's spokesperson refused to appear on camera
It signals that the documentary is a comedy rather than a serious account
answer: It lets the silence and emptiness weigh on viewers before the company's defense, subtly shaping how that defense is heard

prompt: An essay about voting rights begins: "Access to the ballot is not a favor bestowed by generous officials; it is the plainest form of consent a citizen can give." The author later returns to this idea, asking each time what "consent" requires of both the citizen and the state. How does this repetition of the key term serve the essay?
choices: It lets the author steadily deepen the idea of consent from a simple privilege to a two-sided duty
It shows that the author could not think of other wording for the same idea
It signals that the essay is mainly a history of voting laws across centuries
It makes clear that consent means exactly the same thing in every part of the essay
answer: It lets the author steadily deepen the idea of consent from a simple privilege to a two-sided duty

prompt: Read this passage: "The new library was called 'adequate' by the committee, which is to say it was called nothing at all." The narrator's main point is that the word "adequate" is —
choices: so lukewarm that it praises the library by barely acknowledging it
a strong compliment that shows the committee's true admiration
a neutral description that the narrator accepts without comment
a sign that the committee found the library too large and showy
answer: so lukewarm that it praises the library by barely acknowledging it

prompt: Read this excerpt from an essay on technology: "We are told the smartphone is a neutral tool, a simple extension of the hand. But no tool that watches its owner while it works can be called neutral." What is the main rhetorical move in the second sentence?
choices: It challenges the opposing claim by offering a new definition of what makes a tool neutral
It admits that the smartphone is useful and then drops the criticism entirely
It restates the first sentence in simpler words for readers who missed it
It shifts the subject from technology to a different topic altogether
answer: It challenges the opposing claim by offering a new definition of what makes a tool neutral

prompt: A novel from Nigeria centers on two brothers: one who left for London and speaks in careful, formal English, and one who stayed and speaks in a lively local mix of English and pidgin. A feminist reader notices that the brothers' mother and wives rarely get to speak for themselves, and when they do, the men quickly explain what they meant. What does this pattern most clearly ask a reader to examine?
choices: How the women's own voices are crowded out by the men who speak for them
How the brothers' different dialects show that one of them is uneducated
How the formal English of the London brother makes him the story's hero
How the setting of London changes the plot more than the setting of Nigeria
answer: How the women's own voices are crowded out by the men who speak for them

prompt: Two sources describe a flood in 1927. Source A, a levee board memo, blames unusually heavy rain. Source B, diaries of Black sharecroppers, describes levees on their side of the river being left unrepaired while richer districts were protected. A historian argues the disaster was caused by decisions about whose land got saved. What evidence would best support the historian's claim?
choices: Records showing which levee sections were repaired before the storm and which were left unfinished
Weather records showing that the rain that year was the heaviest in decades
More diaries from residents describing how frightened they were of the water
A newspaper editorial arguing that floods are natural disasters that no one controls
answer: Records showing which levee sections were repaired before the storm and which were left unfinished

prompt: A theorist writes: "Although the state secures consent through institutions that appear neutral, it does so, in Gramsci's account, in ways that serve the interests of the ruling group." Which paraphrase keeps the meaning of the sentence?
choices: The state wins people's agreement through institutions that look neutral, but that agreement still serves the ruling group.
The state rules only by force and never by winning people's agreement.
The state's institutions are truly neutral and serve everyone equally.
Gramsci argues that the ruling group openly controls the state by force.
answer: The state wins people's agreement through institutions that look neutral, but that agreement still serves the ruling group.

prompt: A news headline reads: "City Council Slams Residents with Massive New Tax Burden." The story reports that the council voted to raise the property tax rate from 1.0% to 1.1%. What does the headline's wording do?
choices: It uses loaded words that frame the increase negatively instead of stating the change plainly.
It reports the tax change in neutral language and leaves judgment to readers.
It repeats a resident's own description of the tax increase.
It gives the exact numbers so that readers can judge the change themselves.
answer: It uses loaded words that frame the increase negatively instead of stating the change plainly.

prompt: A student is reading The Tale of Genji, an 11th-century Japanese novel written by Murasaki Shikibu and read today in English translation. She notices that the characters rarely say what they feel directly, and instead show feelings through poems they write to each other. What is the best way for her to use this observation?
choices: Treat the indirect style and the poems as the characters' way of speaking to each other, and read them as part of the plot.
Decide that the novel is poorly written and skip the poems.
Assume that all Japanese writing is the same and stop reading carefully.
Rewrite the characters' speeches so they say what they feel directly.
answer: Treat the indirect style and the poems as the characters' way of speaking to each other, and read them as part of the plot.

prompt: A table shows the number of students enrolled at a college: 2018: 1,200; 2019: 1,300; 2020: 1,250; 2021: 1,400. Which statement does the table support?
choices: Enrollment rose overall from 2018 to 2021, with a small dip in 2020.
Enrollment rose in every year from 2018 through 2021.
The table shows that the 2020 dip was caused by the pandemic.
Enrollment stayed about the same across all four years.
answer: Enrollment rose overall from 2018 to 2021, with a small dip in 2020.

prompt: Aisha is reading a 300-page book on the history of public health for a paper on quarantine policy. One chapter covers quarantine laws in detail, and the others cover sanitation, hospitals, and nursing. What is the best way for her to read this book for her paper?
choices: Read the quarantine chapter closely and skim the others for background.
Read every chapter with equal care so that she misses nothing at all.
Read only the introduction and conclusion and skip the chapters.
Skim all of the chapters at the same speed and take no notes.
answer: Read the quarantine chapter closely and skim the others for background.

prompt: Dev has 90 pages of reading due tomorrow, and he keeps putting off starting because the pile feels endless. Which plan best builds his stamina and gets the reading done?
choices: Break the work into short timed blocks with a set page goal and brief breaks.
Wait until late tonight so that last-minute pressure forces him to push through.
Read all 90 pages in one sitting with no breaks so that he finishes faster.
Put off the hardest reading and read only the pages he already finds interesting.
answer: Break the work into short timed blocks with a set page goal and brief breaks.

prompt: Two novels, one written in 1901 in India and one written in 2010 in Nigeria, both tell the story of a young person who leaves a small town for a big city. What is the best first step for a reader comparing these two works from different time periods and places?
choices: Note what each work says about leaving home in its own setting, and then look for similarities and differences.
Judge both works only by the rules of the newest novel.
Focus only on the Indian novel, since it was written first.
Skip the older novel, since it is too old to be useful.
answer: Note what each work says about leaving home in its own setting, and then look for similarities and differences.

prompt: An editorial argues: "The university should require a statistics course for every major. Graduates who took statistics earn more in their first jobs, and employers say they value data skills." What is the author's main claim?
choices: The university should require a statistics course for every major.
Graduates who took statistics earn more in their first jobs.
Employers say that they value data skills in new hires.
Students should choose majors that lead to higher salaries.
answer: The university should require a statistics course for every major.

prompt: While reading an argument that industrialization improved life for most workers, Nia writes in the margin: "? — what about child labor in the mines? does his evidence cover that?" What does this annotation help her do?
choices: It records a challenge to the author's evidence that she can check or raise later.
It restates the passage's point so she can remember it later.
It defines an unfamiliar term in her own simple words.
It copies the author's main claim for review before an exam.
answer: It records a challenge to the author's evidence that she can check or raise later.

prompt: After reading a section of her biology textbook, Priya closes the book and says the section's main points out loud from memory, then opens the book to check what she left out. Which efficient textbook reading step is this?
choices: Reciting the section from memory to see what she retained.
Previewing the section's headings before reading it closely.
Scanning the section quickly for one single fact she needs.
Annotating the section with margin notes while she reads it.
answer: Reciting the section from memory to see what she retained.

prompt: While reading a chapter on supply and demand, Omar stops after each paragraph and writes a one-line note in his own words, such as "when supply drops and demand stays, prices rise." What is the main benefit of this habit?
choices: It lets him check his understanding as he reads and gives him notes to study later.
It helps him finish the assigned reading in much less time than usual.
It means he will not need to reread or review the chapter at all.
It keeps him from having to work out the author's main idea himself.
answer: It lets him check his understanding as he reads and gives him notes to study later.

prompt: While reading a long article online, Sam clicks every blue link he sees, and an hour later he cannot recall the article's main point. What should he do instead?
choices: Finish reading the article first and note which links to check afterward.
Click each link as it appears so that he never forgets to follow it.
Read the linked pages first and then come back to the article later.
Avoid online articles altogether and look for texts without links.
answer: Finish reading the article first and note which links to check afterward.

prompt: In the introduction of a journal article on sleep and memory, the author writes: "This article argues that sleep loss harms memory consolidation more in older adults than in younger adults." What is the role of this sentence in the article?
choices: It states the article's central claim, which the rest of the article supports.
It reports the study's main numerical result taken from the data.
It describes the method the researchers used to collect their data.
It quotes an earlier researcher whose work the article sets out to test.
answer: It states the article's central claim, which the rest of the article supports.

prompt:
Read this poem:

I taste a liquor never brewed —
From Tankards scooped in Pearl —
Not all the Frankfort Berries
Yield such an Alcohol!

Inebriate of air — am I —
And Debauchee of Dew —
Reeling — thro' endless summer days —
From inns of molten Blue —

When Landlords turn the drunken Bee
Out of the Foxglove's door —
When Butterflies — renounce their drams —
I shall but drink the more!

Who is the "I" or speaker of this poem, and what is she describing?
choices: A woman who feels drunk on the beauty of a summer day outdoors
A bartender describing how much alcohol the customers have drunk
A bee that has been kicked out of a flower after drinking too much nectar
A landlord who is complaining about guests who drink too much
answer: A woman who feels drunk on the beauty of a summer day outdoors

prompt: Three studies on exercise and mood are on the table: two find that regular exercise improves mood, and the third finds no effect. When she writes about the research, what should the student do?
choices: Report that most studies find an effect while one does not, and consider why they differ.
Report only the two studies that agree, since they are the stronger evidence.
Report the single most recent study as the final answer to the question.
Report that the question has no answer at all because the studies conflict.
answer: Report that most studies find an effect while one does not, and consider why they differ.

prompt: Read the last two lines of this poem: "When Butterflies — renounce their drams — / I shall but drink the more!" What does the poet's use of words about drinking ("drams," "drink") and the dashes between phrases mainly add to these lines?
choices: They turn the speaker's joy in nature into a playful drinking joke, and the dashes add the pauses of excited speech.
They warn the reader that alcohol is dangerous and should be avoided.
They show that the speaker is a real drunkard who needs medical help.
They make the poem sound formal and serious, like a school rules list.
answer: They turn the speaker's joy in nature into a playful drinking joke, and the dashes add the pauses of excited speech.

prompt: A student reads two versions of the same tale. Charles Perrault writes it down in 1697 in French for the court of Louis XIV and adds a tidy moral at the end; the Brothers Grimm publish their version in German in 1812 after collecting it from tellers. What is the main difference between these two kinds of texts?
choices: Perrault's is a literary fairy tale shaped for readers, while the Grimms' is a written record of an oral folk tale.
Perrault's is a folk tale passed down orally, while the Grimms' is an original literary invention.
Perrault's version is written in verse, while the Grimms' version is written in prose.
Perrault's tale has no magical elements, while the Grimms' version adds magic to a true story.
answer: Perrault's is a literary fairy tale shaped for readers, while the Grimms' is a written record of an oral folk tale.

prompt: Which novel is narrated by a man born at the exact moment of India's independence in 1947, who grows up with magical powers and whose life somehow mirrors the life of his new country?
choices: Midnight's Children by Salman Rushdie
A House for Mr Biswas by V. S. Naipaul
The God of Small Things by Arundhati Roy
Waiting for the Barbarians by J. M. Coetzee
answer: Midnight's Children by Salman Rushdie

prompt: A student writes a paper on Wordsworth's "Michael" about how the poem's shepherds, valleys, and flocks shape the meaning of the story, and about what our responsibility is to the places we describe. Which approach is she taking?
choices: Ecocriticism
Psychoanalytic criticism
Structuralism
Marxist criticism
answer: Ecocriticism

prompt: A scholar's article argues its claim in its opening paragraph, uses quotations from the novel as evidence, answers a rival critic by name in the third paragraph, and closes by noting what still needs study. A student reading the article asks, "What is her claim, and does her evidence support it?" What skill is the student practicing?
choices: Reading criticism for its argument, evidence, and place in a scholarly conversation
Summarizing the plot of the novel the article discusses in her own words
Judging whether the article's author had admirable personal beliefs
Choosing the theory that most scholars currently agree is correct
answer: Reading criticism for its argument, evidence, and place in a scholarly conversation

prompt: A play follows one family through a single long day at their Connecticut summer house in 1912, as the mother's morphine addiction and the sons' troubles slowly come to light. Much of it is drawn from the playwright's own family. Which drama is this?
choices: Long Day's Journey into Night by Eugene O'Neill
A Raisin in the Sun by Lorraine Hansberry
Death of a Salesman by Arthur Miller
Topdog/Underdog by Suzan-Lori Parks
answer: Long Day's Journey into Night by Eugene O'Neill

prompt: A student is sorting four novels by period. Which one is a work of postwar British fiction from the late twentieth century, told by an aging English butler who slowly reveals, in a calm and careful voice, how he wasted his life by never saying what he felt?
choices: The Remains of the Day by Kazuo Ishiguro
Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen
A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man by James Joyce
Lord of the Flies by William Golding
answer: The Remains of the Day by Kazuo Ishiguro

prompt: A student reads Frankenstein and argues that Victor creates the creature and then rejects it because he fears what it reveals about himself, and that the creature's rage mirrors its maker's. This reading focuses on doubles, guilt, and buried desire. Which theory is she using?
choices: Psychoanalytic criticism
Marxist criticism
Structuralism
New Historicism
answer: Psychoanalytic criticism

prompt: Read this passage from an American Romantic story: "A young man leaves his wife Faith at the door of their village and walks into the dark forest, where he meets a figure who carries a staff that looks like a great black snake." In this story, what do the forest and the snake-like staff most likely do?
choices: They work as symbols of temptation and the darkness of the human heart
They stand for the real geography of colonial New England towns.
They are simply props the villain uses and carry no further meaning.
They are jokes that show the story is mainly a comedy.
answer: They work as symbols of temptation and the darkness of the human heart

prompt: Which novel tells the story of several Ojibwe families on and near a North Dakota reservation across many decades, moving the narration from one character to another and weaving in trickster figures and old stories?
choices: Love Medicine by Louise Erdrich
Ceremony by Leslie Marmon Silko
House Made of Dawn by N. Scott Momaday
The Absolutely True Diary of a Part-Time Indian by Sherman Alexie
answer: Love Medicine by Louise Erdrich

prompt: Read this passage: "Of Man's first disobedience, and the fruit / Of that forbidden tree whose mortal taste / Brought death into the World, and all our woe, / With loss of Eden, till one greater Man / Restore us..." The speaker asks a heavenly being for help telling the story and for the strength to justify God's ways. Which description best fits this opening?
choices: An epic invocation by the narrator, asking divine aid for the poem ahead
A dramatic aside spoken by a character to the audience mid-scene
A lyric lament in which a jilted lover speaks about lost love
A satirical proposal in which the speaker pretends to be serious
answer: An epic invocation by the narrator, asking divine aid for the poem ahead

prompt: A student runs a computer program that makes a word cloud from Moby-Dick. The words "white," "whale," and "sea" appear largest. What can this result do for her reading, and what can it NOT do?
choices: It can point out which words are most frequent so she reads those passages more closely, but it cannot tell her what the words mean in context
It can prove the author's intended theme of the novel, but it cannot show which words are most frequent
It can translate the novel's hardest passages, but it cannot compare this novel with other novels
It can judge whether the novel's style is good or bad, but it cannot point out repeated words and images
answer: It can point out which words are most frequent so she reads those passages more closely, but it cannot tell her what the words mean in context

prompt: A student reads a nineteenth-century novel about a strike in a mill town. She notices how the laws of property, the wealth of the mill owners, and the poverty of the workers decide what the characters can do. Before this unit, she might have called this a "story about hard work." What sharper claim does her new reading let her make?
choices: The novel's conflicts grow out of the class relations and economic system of its time
The novel's conflicts grow out of the author's unresolved feelings about his parents
The novel's conflicts grow out of fixed patterns built into language itself
The novel's conflicts grow out of each reader's private response to the characters
answer: The novel's conflicts grow out of the class relations and economic system of its time

prompt: Read these two lines of poetry: "The tide comes in. The tide goes out. / The boats sleep in the bay." A student counts the beats in the first line and finds four strong beats, each one separated by softer syllables. Which term best describes this pattern of beats?
choices: Meter
Rhyme scheme
Stanza break
Alliteration
answer: Meter

prompt: In a short novel from Mexico, a man goes to the town of Comala looking for his father and finds it filled with whispering ghosts, repeating voices, and fragments of stories that do not connect in the usual way. Which book is this?
choices: Pedro Páramo by Juan Rulfo
The Aleph by Jorge Luis Borges
Hopscotch by Julio Cortázar
The Stranger by Albert Camus
answer: Pedro Páramo by Juan Rulfo

prompt: Beowulf is an Old English poem about a hero who fights a monster, the monster's mother, and finally a dragon. Which feature belongs to the earliest English poetry as seen in Beowulf?
choices: Lines built on strong beats with a pause in the middle of the line
Lines arranged in groups of four with a set rhyme scheme
A story told in letters written back and forth between friends
Short free-verse lines with no set beat pattern
answer: Lines built on strong beats with a pause in the middle of the line

prompt: Read this passage from a Renaissance play: "Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships, / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?" A hero-scholar speaks alone on stage about a face he has seen. The lines do not rhyme and run in a steady five-beat pattern. Which description fits this passage?
choices: A soliloquy in blank verse
A dialogue in rhyming couplets
A prose confession to a priest
A choral ode sung by the whole cast
answer: A soliloquy in blank verse

prompt: A crime novel opens with a seemingly perfect country house. As the detective questions the family, the reader learns the butler is not who he claims, a locked room was opened from the inside, and everyone had a motive. The pleasure of the story comes from following these clues toward a hidden solution. Which convention is at work?
choices: The closed circle of suspects whose hidden secrets are gradually exposed
The lonely outsider whose disgust at society drives him to crime
The eerie suspense created by decayed settings and supernatural dread
The repeated scene replayed until the reader must choose the next action
answer: The closed circle of suspects whose hidden secrets are gradually exposed

prompt: A Gothic poem describes a ruined abbey at midnight, a flickering candle, a mysterious hooded figure in the chapel, and the narrator's growing terror. Yet after a closer look, the ghost turns out to be a smuggler in disguise. The poem's main effect comes from which pair of features?
choices: Atmosphere of suspense built from eerie settings, plus a mystery that thrills the reader
Precise evidence gathered from suspects, plus a logical solution that closes the case
Ordinary family life rendered in everyday language, plus a focus on inner growth
Heroic battles in imaginary lands, plus invented languages and maps of far-off places
answer: Atmosphere of suspense built from eerie settings, plus a mystery that thrills the reader

prompt: A writer publishes a book about the years they spent caring for a sick parent. The writer admits that some conversations in the book are recreated from memory and may not be word-for-word true. Which statement best describes how we read this kind of life writing?
choices: We read it as the writer's shaping of their own life, where memory and form matter as much as exact facts.
We treat it as a novel, since any change to the facts makes it fiction.
We treat it as a history book and check every detail against public records.
We ignore the writer's life entirely and look only at the style.
answer: We read it as the writer's shaping of their own life, where memory and form matter as much as exact facts.

prompt: Before studying the major schools of literary theory one by one, a class looks at a single map listing Formalism, Structuralism, Marxism, Psychoanalysis, Feminism, and Reader-Response side by side. What is the main purpose of getting this overview first?
choices: To see how the schools relate to one another before studying each one's methods in depth
To decide once and for all which school gives the only right reading of a text
To memorize the dates and biographies of the founder of each school
To collect every opinion critics have ever published about one single novel
answer: To see how the schools relate to one another before studying each one's methods in depth

prompt: In Dante's Divine Comedy, the poet journeys through Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise as they were understood in the medieval Christian world. Who guides him through Hell in the first part of the poem?
choices: The Roman poet Virgil
The Trojan hero Aeneas
The Greek poet Homer
The philosopher Aristotle
answer: The Roman poet Virgil

prompt: Read this short essay opening: "I have never trusted cats. Let me be precise: I have never trusted the way a cat will sit in a doorway and judge you, then leave the room as if you had failed a test you never knew you were taking." How does the second sentence work in the essay's structure?
choices: It narrows and rephrases the first claim with a more exact example.
It introduces a new character who speaks the rest of the essay.
It contradicts the first claim and takes it back.
It quotes a famous author to prove the first claim.
answer: It narrows and rephrases the first claim with a more exact example.

prompt: Read this passage: "From the hill, I watched the wedding below. I could see Anna lift her veil, though she could not see me watching from so far away." The story lets us see Anna, but only know the thoughts of the person on the hill. Which term names the choice of whose eyes we see through?
choices: Focalization
Plot climax
Rhyme scheme
Stage direction
answer: Focalization

prompt: Which novel opens in 1838 on the Ganges, where a poor Indian farmer's daughter ends up aboard an old slave ship converted to carry indentured laborers to Mauritius, joining a group of very different people thrown together by the opium trade and the British Empire?
choices: Sea of Poppies by Amitav Ghosh
A Passage to India by E. M. Forster
Things Fall Apart by Chinua Achebe
Midnight's Children by Salman Rushdie
answer: Sea of Poppies by Amitav Ghosh

prompt: A poet writes: "Let us go then, you and I, / When the evening is spread out against the sky / Like a patient etherized upon a table." The speaker goes on to worry about rolled cuffs, coffee spoons, and whether he dares to eat a peach. Which American Modernist poem is this?
choices: "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" by T. S. Eliot
"Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening" by Robert Frost
"I Hear America Singing" by Walt Whitman
"Because I could not stop for Death" by Emily Dickinson
answer: "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" by T. S. Eliot

prompt: Which novel follows a Dominican American boy from New Jersey who is obsessed with comic books, tells his family's story across the dictatorship of Trujillo in the Dominican Republic, and adds long scholarly footnotes to the main story?
choices: The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao by Junot Díaz
The House on Mango Street by Sandra Cisneros
Their Eyes Were Watching God by Zora Neale Hurston
Beloved by Toni Morrison
answer: The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao by Junot Díaz

prompt: A writer argues: "Civil rights legislation of the 1950s passed in part because it served the interests of white political and business leaders at the time — for instance, improving the nation's image abroad during the Cold War. Progress came where it matched those interests." Which idea from critical race theory is the writer using?
choices: Interest convergence, the claim that racial progress advances only when it aligns with white self-interest
Counter-storytelling, the practice of using personal narrative to challenge the dominant account of events
Microaggressions, the everyday slights that cumulatively mark a group as lesser in daily life
Cultural appropriation, the taking of a marginalized group's cultural forms by a dominant group
answer: Interest convergence, the claim that racial progress advances only when it aligns with white self-interest

prompt: A student writing an honors thesis on a Victorian novel must first "map the critical conversation" around the text. Which research plan best does that, rather than simply collecting opinions?
choices: Search several databases for recent scholarship on the novel, note which critics build on or argue with which earlier critics, and identify where the debate now stands and what remains unresolved.
Search for one major critic's book on the novel, summarize that critic's argument fully, and use it as the thesis's single framework throughout.
Search for every article ever written on the novel, list each critic's view in chronological order, and let the thesis become a summary of all of them.
Search for the author's biography and letters, reconstruct what the author intended, and treat that intention as the settled meaning that critics should match.
answer: Search several databases for recent scholarship on the novel, note which critics build on or argue with which earlier critics, and identify where the debate now stands and what remains unresolved.

prompt: In Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, the chapter "The Whiteness of the Whale" (1851) has Ishmael say that whiteness in nature is "a dumb blankness, full of meaning," and that it appalls him more than any color. What does an ecocritic most likely find valuable in this passage?
choices: It refuses to treat the nonhuman whale as a stable symbol carrying human meaning, letting it stay strange
It offers a pastoral vision in which nature restores the human speaker to health and wholeness
It gives the whale a full inner life, letting readers see the animal as a conscious subject like themselves
It shows nature as sacred creation, so that the whale figures the divine order of the universe
answer: It refuses to treat the nonhuman whale as a stable symbol carrying human meaning, letting it stay strange

prompt: Thomas Nagel's 1974 essay "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?" argues that even if we knew every physical fact about a bat's sonar, we would still not know what its experience feels like from the inside. A scholar uses this to argue something about fiction. What would that argument most likely be?
choices: That first-person narration matters because subjective experience cannot be captured by any objective, third-person description
That characters are best understood functionally, as systems of inputs and outputs rather than as inner lives
That we can know a character's mind completely once we know the physical facts of the brain described in the text
That a character's inner states are nothing over and above the behaviors and reports the text gives us
answer: That first-person narration matters because subjective experience cannot be captured by any objective, third-person description

prompt: A critic writes: "Spivak advises subaltern groups to act as though a fixed identity — 'woman,' 'the subaltern' — were real, in order to win political ground, while knowing all along that the category is a historical construction. The strategy is useful but temporary." What is this strategy called?
choices: Strategic essentialism, acting through a fixed identity category while knowing it is a construct
Hybridity, the mixing of colonizer and colonized cultures that produces a third, unstable space
World-systems analysis, mapping core and periphery economies that structure global literary markets
Alterity, the irreducible otherness of a group that can never be fully represented by outsiders
answer: Strategic essentialism, acting through a fixed identity category while knowing it is a construct

prompt: A literary critic writes: "In a 1590s English grammar book and a 1600s merchant's manual, the same rule keeps appearing: children and servants must be taught to speak only when spoken to, and in set forms. The rule shows up in plays of the period too, in the way servants' lines are written as short, formulaic replies. What a society counts as 'good speech' is produced by institutions, not discovered in nature." Which critical approach is this critic practicing?
choices: Foucauldian discourse analysis, tracing how institutions produce a regime of truth about speech
Deconstruction, showing that the word 'good' undoes the binary of good and bad speech
Formalist close reading, isolating the paradox built into the servants' formulaic replies
Marxist base-and-superstructure analysis, treating the grammar book as a direct copy of economic relations
answer: Foucauldian discourse analysis, tracing how institutions produce a regime of truth about speech

prompt: A student writing about a recent novel sets the book beside news coverage, social media, and political speeches from the year it appeared, and argues that the novel responds to and reshapes that moment. Which habit of reading contemporary fiction does this show?
choices: Reading the novel in relation to its cultural moment, so that its form and themes are seen as engaging with current debates.
Treating the novel as a timeless fable with no connection to any particular historical situation.
Judging the novel against a single classic text and deciding which of the two is superior.
Focusing only on the author's biography and private feelings, ignoring everything outside the life.
answer: Reading the novel in relation to its cultural moment, so that its form and themes are seen as engaging with current debates.

prompt: William Morris's News from Nowhere (1890) was written as an answer to Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward (1888). Bellamy's future Boston is a centrally planned industrial state; Morris's future England is a green, craft-based society with no state machinery at all. What does Morris's novel do as utopian writing?
choices: It contests another utopia's vision of the good society, offering a rival account of work and nature
It warns against a planned society by exaggerating its horrors until the reader recoils from it
It imagines a single perfected society so fully that no further argument about the future is possible
It describes an unreachable ideal that exists only to show how far the present falls short
answer: It contests another utopia's vision of the good society, offering a rival account of work and nature

prompt: In Jean Toomer's Cane (1923), prose, poetry, and dramatic sketches are set side by side to evoke Black life in the rural South and the urban North. Which feature of Harlem Renaissance writing does this mixing of forms best show?
choices: An effort to break with inherited European forms and build new ones adequate to Black experience.
A strict commitment to sonnets and ballad meters as the truest vehicles for Black experience.
A refusal to engage with questions of Black identity or with the textures of American place.
A turn away from American subjects toward imitation of classical Greek and Latin models.
answer: An effort to break with inherited European forms and build new ones adequate to Black experience.

prompt: In Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818), Victor Frankenstein says, "Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge." Which Romantic theme does this warning most directly express?
choices: The danger of overreaching ambition that severs the seeker from human feeling and natural limits.
The Romantic celebration of nature as a restorative force that heals the mind through beauty.
The belief that scientific knowledge, once discovered, must be shared freely with all of society.
The Romantic ideal of the poet as an isolated genius who suffers for a hostile public.
answer: The danger of overreaching ambition that severs the seeker from human feeling and natural limits.

prompt: A novelist writes: "My grandmother fled Warsaw in 1943. I was born in 1971 and was never there, but the photographs on her mantel and the stories she told at night are the truest things I know. When I write the fire, I am writing from her memory as if it were my own." Which concept names the narrator's relationship to a past she did not live through?
choices: Postmemory, the relationship of a later generation to a trauma transmitted through stories and images
Screen memory, an everyday recollection that conceals a more painful one from the rememberer
Flashbulb memory, a vivid and durable recall of the moment a shocking piece of news was heard
Collective memory, a shared group recollection that shapes a community's identity over time
answer: Postmemory, the relationship of a later generation to a trauma transmitted through stories and images

prompt: In T. S. Eliot's "The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock" (1915), the speaker says, "I have measured out my life with coffee spoons," and asks, "Do I dare / Disturb the universe?" What do these lines mainly show about the speaker?
choices: A life narrowed to trivial routine, and a mind too anxious to act on any larger desire.
A joyful celebration of ordinary daily pleasures that make ordinary life meaningful.
A confident hero preparing to make a decisive change in his world.
A satirical attack on waiters and coffee houses as the ruin of modern society.
answer: A life narrowed to trivial routine, and a mind too anxious to act on any larger desire.

prompt: A Kenyan novelist writes in English about local life, drawing on oral storytelling rhythms and on the traditions of the East African novel. Which idea about Global Anglophone literature does this best illustrate?
choices: English-language literature outside Britain and America is shaped by local traditions and forms, not simply a copy of Western models.
Global Anglophone writing is best understood as a single worldwide style with the same conventions everywhere.
Writing in English means the author has abandoned local language, memory, and oral tradition entirely.
Works written outside Britain and America can only be studied as documents of history, never as literature.
answer: English-language literature outside Britain and America is shaped by local traditions and forms, not simply a copy of Western models.

prompt: A medieval Latin word, hospes, can mean "guest," "host," or "stranger," depending on context. A critic seizes on this: a text built on this word cannot cleanly separate the person who welcomes from the person who is welcomed, and so the ethics of hospitality in the passage cannot be settled. What is this critic's method called?
choices: Deconstruction, showing that a word contains two opposed meanings at once and suspends the binary
Deconstruction, showing that a text's rhetoric cancels its grammar and blocks any meaning at all
Formalist paradox, treating the double meaning as a deliberate device that resolves into a theme
Unreliable narration, treating the double meaning as a clue that the narrator is hiding the truth
answer: Deconstruction, showing that a word contains two opposed meanings at once and suspends the binary

prompt: In George Eliot's Middlemarch (1871–72), the narrator pauses the story to reflect at length on the characters' motives and on the small provincial world they share. What does this intrusive, reflective narration chiefly do for the Victorian novel?
choices: It lets the narrator interpret and judge the characters' inner lives and social world, giving the reader moral analysis rather than bare events.
It keeps the reader from knowing the characters' thoughts, so that their inner lives stay a mystery throughout.
It signals that the story is unreliable and that no interpretation of the characters can be trusted.
It breaks the fictional illusion by reminding the reader that the novel is only a made-up artifact.
answer: It lets the narrator interpret and judge the characters' inner lives and social world, giving the reader moral analysis rather than bare events.

prompt: A scholar compares a novel published in London in 1850 with an edition printed in Philadelphia the same year and finds different chapter breaks, changed names, and several altered passages. Which conclusion about transatlantic publishing does this evidence best support?
choices: Books crossing the Atlantic were often reshaped by local publishers and markets, so the two editions are distinct textual objects, not simple copies.
The American edition must be a pirated copy with errors, and the British edition alone reflects the author's true text.
Since the novel was written in English, all editions of it everywhere must print exactly the same text.
Differences between editions only occur in translations, never between two English-language printings.
answer: Books crossing the Atlantic were often reshaped by local publishers and markets, so the two editions are distinct textual objects, not simple copies.

prompt: A student is scanning Chaucer's verse in the original Middle English. Which statement correctly describes how a final -e on a word, as in 'grete' or 'Aprille', is normally treated in scanning?
choices: It is usually sounded as a light extra syllable, but elided before a word beginning with a vowel or a weak h
It is always silent, as in Modern English, so it never counts as a syllable in a line
It is always sounded as a full syllable, even when the next word begins with a vowel
It is sounded only on verbs, and never on nouns or adjectives, which keep a silent -e
answer: It is usually sounded as a light extra syllable, but elided before a word beginning with a vowel or a weak h

prompt: A critic writes: "In the village of this novel, every girl is expected to want marriage, and the narrator treats that want as natural. But the text keeps showing marriage as an economic arrangement forced on women. Adrienne Rich's argument applies here: heterosexuality is not a desire women happen to feel, but an institution that is imposed on them." What does Rich's argument hold?
choices: Compulsory heterosexuality, the claim that women's attraction to men is institutionally enforced, not simply innate
The male gaze, the claim that women in fiction are arranged as objects to be looked at by a male viewer
The second shift, the claim that women's paid work is followed by unpaid domestic work at home
The feminine mystique, the claim that postwar culture trapped women in idealized domesticity
answer: Compulsory heterosexuality, the claim that women's attraction to men is institutionally enforced, not simply innate

prompt: In Chaucer's General Prologue, the Knight is described: "A Knyght ther was, and that a worthy man, / That fro the tyme that he first bigan / To riden out, he loved chivalrie." What does "worthy" mean in this Middle English context, as the lines use it?
choices: Of high standing and honor — a man of rank whose conduct matches his status as a knight.
Rich in money and property, since the following lines list the many lands he owns.
Morally good in a modern sense, meaning kind and gentle toward everyone he meets.
Physically strong and impressive in body, as shown by his skill in tournaments.
answer: Of high standing and honor — a man of rank whose conduct matches his status as a knight.

prompt: A Renaissance poet writes of a sailor swallowed by a whale who emerges after three days, and the poem treats the event as a figure for an earlier scripture story. A critic explains that an Old Testament event in the poem is a foreshadowing of a later one, so that the two scenes are understood as one pattern in sacred history. What is this critical device called?
choices: Typology, where an Old Testament event prefigures and is fulfilled by a later one
Allegory, where each character and setting stands for an abstract moral quality throughout
Natural theology, where the design of the whale is read as evidence of a divine creator
Kenosis, where the divine is shown emptying itself into the vulnerable body of the creature
answer: Typology, where an Old Testament event prefigures and is fulfilled by a later one

prompt: A first-person narrator says: "I have never once been jealous of my sister. I only want what is best for her. Of course I told her fiancé that she had been ill, and that he should not tire her with a long engagement." A reader works out that the narrator is deeply jealous and is acting against her sister. Which cognitive concept names the mental work the reader is doing here?
choices: Theory of mind, inferring a character's hidden beliefs and desires from what she says and does
Visual mental imagery, picturing the scene of the sister and her fiancé in the mind's eye
Mirror neurons, feeling the narrator's jealousy as a physical response in the reader's own body
Affective contagion, catching the narrator's mood without any process of inference at all
answer: Theory of mind, inferring a character's hidden beliefs and desires from what she says and does

prompt: A student writes: "In a postmodern novel, the narrator addresses the reader, contradicts the plot, and openly calls attention to the book as a made thing. The reader can never settle on one stable meaning." A professor objects that this treats postmodernism as pure nonsense. Which revision best applies the unit's approach to postmodernism?
choices: Acknowledge that the disruption is deliberate, then argue what the instability reveals about the fiction's themes and its cultural moment.
Remove all discussion of instability and describe only the plot and the characters' emotions.
Argue that any text with an unreliable narrator is automatically a postmodern masterpiece.
State that postmodern texts have no meaning at all and therefore cannot be analyzed.
answer: Acknowledge that the disruption is deliberate, then argue what the instability reveals about the fiction's themes and its cultural moment.

prompt: A student is writing about how the elegy, a poem of mourning, has been written from ancient Greece to the present. Which approach treats the elegy as a genre with a history and theory rather than as a label for any sad poem?
choices: Tracing how elegiac conventions, such as lament and consolation, are revised or resisted by poets in different periods.
Deciding which poems count as sad enough to be included in the study.
Ranking elegies by the fame of the poets who wrote them.
Focusing only on the personal grief the poet experienced while writing.
answer: Tracing how elegiac conventions, such as lament and consolation, are revised or resisted by poets in different periods.

prompt: A doctoral student must evaluate a book's method before citing it. Which question assesses the METHOD rather than the argument or the gaps?
choices: How were the primary texts selected, and what does that selection let the author claim?
What is the author's main claim about the relationship between the two genres?
Which scholars does the author disagree with most directly in the introduction?
What follow-up study would build on this book's findings?
answer: How were the primary texts selected, and what does that selection let the author claim?

prompt: A student is studying a nineteenth-century novel as it was first published: in monthly installments in a magazine, with advertisements and illustrations surrounding each installment. Which question belongs to literature and media rather than to a reading of the novel's plot alone?
choices: How did serialization shape the pacing of the plot and the way readers encountered the story over time?
Which character in the novel undergoes the most change by the final chapter?
How does the novel's use of irony shape the narrator's reliability?
What does the novel suggest about marriage and money in its period?
answer: How did serialization shape the pacing of the plot and the way readers encountered the story over time?

prompt: A descriptive bibliographer examines a hand-press book and finds that the printed pages carry a faint pattern of horizontal lines spaced about two centimeters apart, with a small crest visible in one corner of a sheet. What does this evidence tell her about the book's paper?
choices: It is laid paper, made on a wire sieve, and the crest is a watermark identifying the papermaker or mill.
It is wove paper from a mould with a fine wire cloth, and the crest is a decorative stamp added by the binder.
The lines are roller marks left by the printing press, and the crest is a stationer's device printed with the type.
The lines are ruling drawn by a scribe before printing, and the crest is the library mark of an early owner.
answer: It is laid paper, made on a wire sieve, and the crest is a watermark identifying the papermaker or mill.

prompt: A codicologist turns through a handwritten book and notices that most of the units of leaves sewn together are made of four sheets folded once, giving eight leaves, but two units are made of a single folded sheet, giving two leaves. How should she describe the book's structure?
choices: Its gatherings are mostly quaternions, with two gatherings of one folded sheet, so a collation formula would record that mixture.
Its gatherings are all of four sheets folded twice, so the book is uniformly quarto in structure.
It is a roll of single sheets stitched at one edge, so gatherings play no part in describing it.
Its gatherings are mostly single sheets, with two units of four sheets, the reverse of what she first saw.
answer: Its gatherings are mostly quaternions, with two gatherings of one folded sheet, so a collation formula would record that mixture.

prompt: A student studies a printed play script and notices that the same scene is staged very differently in three modern productions: one uses a bare stage, one a realistic nineteenth-century drawing room, and one a contemporary office. Which question belongs to performance studies rather than to close reading of the printed text alone?
choices: How does each staging's choice of setting and design shape the audience's understanding of the play's conflict?
How does the playwright's use of blank verse shape the rhythm of the dialogue?
What sources did the playwright consult when constructing the plot?
Which words in the scene are ambiguous in their dictionary meaning?
answer: How does each staging's choice of setting and design shape the audience's understanding of the play's conflict?

prompt: A scholar is given a seventeenth-century book with no bookplate. On the flyleaf someone has written "E. Browne, ex dono authoris, 1671," and the same hand has signed two other pages. What can she conclude from this?
choices: The book was given by its author to a reader named E. Browne in 1671, and the inscriptions are provenance evidence tracing early ownership.
E. Browne was the printer of the book, and the note records the date the sheets came off the press.
The note is a bookseller's price code, so it shows which shop sold the book but nothing about its readers.
The note is a shelf mark added by a modern library, so it dates from long after the book was printed.
answer: The book was given by its author to a reader named E. Browne in 1671, and the inscriptions are provenance evidence tracing early ownership.

prompt: A digital archive displays a scan of a broadside along with a record that lists its creator, the year 1848, its physical size, the archive that holds it, and the terms under which it may be reused. A researcher wants to know how such records help her find and trust the scan. What is the best description of that record?
choices: It is the item's metadata: descriptive, technical, and rights fields that make the scan findable, identifiable, and usable.
It is the item's OCR transcript: the printed text converted to searchable characters so it can be read without the scan.
It is the item's finding aid: a list of everything in the archive's collection, arranged by box and folder.
It is the item's collation: a record of its gatherings, leaf count, and format as a physical object.
answer: It is the item's metadata: descriptive, technical, and rights fields that make the scan findable, identifiable, and usable.

prompt: A researcher observes that working-class families in her study use literacy at home in ways that differ from the practices valued at school, and she argues that calling one set of practices "better literacy" is a judgment made by those with power. What view of literacy does this represent?
choices: A sociocultural view, treating literacy as a social practice shaped by power and identity rather than as a single neutral skill.
A cognitive view, treating literacy as a set of mental processes for decoding and comprehension that are the same for every reader.
A psychometric view, treating literacy as a measurable ability that can be scored and ranked on a standardized scale.
A linguistic view, treating literacy as mastery of grammar and vocabulary in a language, independent of who uses it.
answer: A sociocultural view, treating literacy as a social practice shaped by power and identity rather than as a single neutral skill.

prompt: A student is tracing how the study of Renaissance literature changed across the twentieth century. Which question belongs to the history of the discipline rather than to a single reading of a play?
choices: How did the rise of New Criticism in the mid-twentieth century shift attention from an author's biography to the verbal structure of the text?
What does the imagery of disease in this particular tragedy suggest about the city it depicts?
Which sources did this playwright draw on when writing the plot of this play?
How does the soliloquy in this scene reveal the speaker's state of mind?
answer: How did the rise of New Criticism in the mid-twentieth century shift attention from an author's biography to the verbal structure of the text?

prompt: A teacher must pick a book for a struggling fourth grader. She runs a readability formula that counts sentence length and syllables, and it rates the book as easy. When she reads the book herself, she finds it has an unusual story structure, little context for its historical setting, and several abstract terms. What is the best conclusion?
choices: The formula measures only surface features of the text, so its rating must be weighed against qualitative features such as structure, knowledge demands, and vocabulary.
The formula is right, so the book is a good fit for the struggling reader and the other features can be ignored.
The formula measures only illustrations and layout, so it says nothing at all about how hard a book is.
The formula is more reliable than a teacher's judgment, so the qualitative features are counted only for gifted readers.
answer: The formula measures only surface features of the text, so its rating must be weighed against qualitative features such as structure, knowledge demands, and vocabulary.

prompt: A student reads an English translation of a novel from the Japanese and notices that the translation renders a range of politeness levels and honorifics into plain English prose. What does this observation suggest about the translation?
choices: That social register encoded grammatically in the source language is partly lost or relocated into diction in the translation.
That the original novel was written in a mixture of Japanese and English.
That the translator chose to write a new novel rather than to translate.
That the original novel was composed in a poetic form rather than in prose.
answer: That social register encoded grammatically in the source language is partly lost or relocated into diction in the translation.

prompt: In a study of first graders, children are asked to name rows of printed digits as fast as they can. The children who are slowest on this task are also the ones who read the least accurately a year later. What does this result show?
choices: That speed at a fast, automatized naming task predicts later reading accuracy, so slow naming is a warning sign of reading difficulty.
That knowing letter names is the strongest single predictor of later reading, since digit naming depends on the alphabet.
That children who read more slowly understand more of what they read, so slow naming marks careful readers.
That the number of words a child knows in speech predicts reading accuracy, since naming digits tests vocabulary.
answer: That speed at a fast, automatized naming task predicts later reading accuracy, so slow naming is a warning sign of reading difficulty.

prompt: A distant-reading study counts how often a word appears in each of two thousand novels. The word "the" scores extremely high almost everywhere, while "harpoon" scores high in only a small number of whaling novels. How does TF-IDF help here?
choices: It lowers the weight of words like "the" that appear in nearly every text and raises the weight of words concentrated in a few, so distinctive vocabulary stands out.
It converts every word to its root form, so "harpoons" and "harpooned" are counted together with "harpoon."
It removes words that appear in more than one novel, leaving only words unique to a single text.
It arranges each novel in chronological order so that changes in word use can be plotted over time.
answer: It lowers the weight of words like "the" that appear in nearly every text and raises the weight of words concentrated in a few, so distinctive vocabulary stands out.

prompt: A graduate student reads a scholarly article and needs to state its central claim as the author frames it. Which question targets the article's ARGUMENT?
choices: What conclusion does the author draw from the evidence, and how do the section headings lead to it?
What earlier scholarship on this topic does the author cite in the literature review?
Which archives and databases did the author search to assemble the corpus?
Which related topics does the author explicitly leave for future research?
answer: What conclusion does the author draw from the evidence, and how do the section headings lead to it?

prompt: In a film, a factory whistle blows and the workers on the line look up as the shift ends. A moment later the shot changes to a woman waiting at a window in a different city, and the sound of the whistle continues over her shot as well. How is the whistle sound used here?
choices: It is sound from the factory scene whose source is on screen there, carried over the next shot as a sound bridge linking the two scenes.
It is a score element added by the director to build mood, with no source anywhere in the story world.
It is dubbed dialogue recorded after shooting to correct the workers' voices in the factory scene.
It is a flashback cue signalling that the woman is remembering the factory from an earlier time.
answer: It is sound from the factory scene whose source is on screen there, carried over the next shot as a sound bridge linking the two scenes.

prompt: A student applies Bakhtin's concept of heteroglossia, developed in his essays on the novel, to a nineteenth-century novel in which several social voices and dialects compete within the narration. Which question follows from treating heteroglossia as a formal property of the novel rather than as a theme?
choices: How does the narration stage competing social languages within the prose itself, rather than merely reporting that characters speak in dialect?
Does the novel express Bakhtin's own political views about the Russian peasantry?
Which characters in the novel best represent the ideals of the community?
Does the novel show that one social class is more virtuous than the others?
answer: How does the narration stage competing social languages within the prose itself, rather than merely reporting that characters speak in dialect?

prompt: A school gives every fifth grader a test that reports how each student compares with a national sample of fifth graders, and separately a test that reports how each student performs on a fixed list of skills for that grade. What is the key difference between these two tests?
choices: One is norm-referenced and ranks students against a national sample; the other is criterion-referenced and reports mastery of a fixed set of grade-level skills.
